meta.title: Historical Events
meta.subtitle: Turning points across world history — searchable.

glossary.heading: Periods — how the historical eras are bounded

terms.Ancient (to 500 CE): From the earliest records through the fall of the western Roman empire.
terms.Medieval (500–1500): The middle ages across Europe, the Islamic world, and Asia.
terms.Early modern (1500–1800): The age of exploration, reformation, and revolutions.
terms.20th century onward: World wars, decolonisation, and the digital age.

meta.footer: A placeholder topic seeded with sample events. Dates are scholarly estimates where exact dates are unknown.

entries.name: Founding of Rome
entries.desc: Traditional date for the founding of the city of Rome, later the centre of the Roman Republic and Empire.
entries.tldr: Roman tradition, recorded by writers like Livy, dates the city's founding to 753 BCE by the legendary twins Romulus and Remus, said to have been raised by a she-wolf after being abandoned as infants. Romulus reputedly killed Remus in a dispute over the city's boundaries and became its first king. Archaeological evidence points to earlier settlement on the Palatine Hill, but the legendary date became the anchor of the later Roman calendar, counted 'ab urbe condita.'

entries.name: Battle of Marathon
entries.desc: Athenian-led victory over the first Persian invasion of Greece, a defining moment for the Greek city-states.
entries.tldr: A Persian force sent by King Darius I to punish Athens for backing a revolt in Ionia landed on the plain of Marathon, northeast of the city. Heavily outnumbered, the Athenians, joined only by a small contingent from Plataea, charged the Persian line at a run to reduce archery exposure, and their strengthened flanks enveloped the Persian center. According to a famous but likely legendary tradition, a runner raced to Athens to announce the win before collapsing dead, the inspiration for the marathon race. The victory boosted Athenian confidence and became a symbol of Greek resistance to Persia.

entries.name: Unification of China under Qin
entries.desc: Qin Shi Huang united the warring states into the first centralised Chinese empire.

entries.name: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
entries.desc: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus, conventionally marking the end of the western Roman Empire.
entries.tldr: The Western Roman Empire's collapse is conventionally dated to 476 CE, when the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus and declined to appoint a successor, instead ruling Italy himself as king. The empire had been weakening for decades under pressure from Germanic migrations, civil wars, and economic decline, so the deposition capped a long process rather than a sudden event. The Eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople, survived for another thousand years as the Byzantine Empire, marking the boundary between antiquity and the Middle Ages.

entries.name: The Hijra
entries.desc: Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina, the starting point of the Islamic calendar.
entries.tldr: In 622 CE the Islamic prophet Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca, where they faced persecution from the ruling Quraysh tribe, to the city of Yathrib, later renamed Medina. There Muhammad established the first Muslim community and became its political and religious leader, drafting the Constitution of Medina to govern relations among its tribes and faiths. The migration transformed a persecuted minority into a self-governing polity capable of eventually returning to and controlling Mecca. Caliph Umar later designated the year of the Hijra as the start of the Islamic lunar calendar.

entries.name: Norman Conquest of England
entries.desc: William of Normandy's victory at Hastings reshaped English language, law, and aristocracy.
entries.tldr: William, Duke of Normandy, crossed the Channel and defeated King Harold II's army at the Battle of Hastings, where Harold was reportedly killed by an arrow to the eye, an image immortalized in the Bayeux Tapestry. William subdued remaining Anglo-Saxon resistance and had himself crowned king in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. He replaced the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy with Norman lords, commissioned the Domesday Book to survey his kingdom's wealth, and infused English with thousands of French-derived words still in use today.

entries.name: Fall of Constantinople
entries.desc: Ottoman capture of the Byzantine capital, often taken to mark the end of the Middle Ages.
entries.tldr: On 29 May 1453, after a seven-week siege, Ottoman forces under the young Sultan Mehmed II breached the ancient land walls of Constantinople using massive siege cannon and overwhelming numbers. The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI, died fighting in the final assault, and the city was pillaged before Mehmed restored order and made it his new capital, renamed Istanbul. The fall extinguished the Byzantine Empire after more than a thousand years and conventionally marks the end of the medieval period. Fleeing Greek scholars carried classical manuscripts west, feeding the Renaissance.

entries.name: Columbus Reaches the Americas
entries.desc: First of Columbus's voyages, opening sustained European contact with the Americas.
entries.tldr: In August 1492, Genoese navigator Christopher Columbus sailed west from Spain with three ships, seeking a new route to Asia, and made landfall in the Bahamas that October. He believed he had reached the East Indies and never fully accepted that he had found a previously unknown continent to Europeans. The voyage opened sustained contact between Europe and the Americas, triggering centuries of colonization, the Columbian Exchange of crops and diseases, and the enslavement and decimation of indigenous populations. It is conventionally treated as the opening event of the early modern era.

entries.name: Arrival of the First Fleet
entries.desc: British ships established the first European colony in Australia at Sydney Cove.
entries.tldr: Under Captain Arthur Phillip, eleven ships carrying over a thousand people, including roughly 780 convicts, arrived at Botany Bay in January 1788 before relocating to the better-watered harbor at Sydney Cove. There, on 26 January 1788, Phillip raised the British flag and founded the penal colony of New South Wales, beginning continuous European settlement in Australia. The arrival displaced the Eora Aboriginal people, and violence and disease soon devastated their communities. The date is now Australia Day.

entries.name: French Revolution Begins
entries.desc: Storming of the Bastille opened a decade of upheaval that toppled the French monarchy.
entries.tldr: On 14 July 1789, Parisian crowds stormed the Bastille fortress-prison seeking gunpowder and reacting to fears that royal troops were massing to crush the new National Assembly. Though the prison held only a handful of inmates, the assault became a symbol of popular sovereignty triumphing over royal despotism. The date is now France's national holiday, and the storming is conventionally treated as the opening act of a revolution that would abolish the monarchy within three years.

entries.name: Meiji Restoration
entries.desc: Restoration of imperial rule in Japan and the start of rapid modernisation.
entries.tldr: A coalition of samurai from rival domains overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate and restored the young Emperor Meiji as nominal ruler, ending over two and a half centuries of feudal military government. The new government abolished the samurai class's legal privileges, adopted Western industrial technology, built a conscript army and navy, and rewrote Japan's legal and educational systems within a single generation. The pace was so fast that Japan defeated China in 1895 and, a decade later, Russia, the first non-Western power to beat a European empire in a modern war.

entries.name: Berlin Conference
entries.desc: European powers formalised the partition and colonisation of Africa.
entries.tldr: Convened by German chancellor Otto von Bismarck in 1884-85, the conference gathered fourteen European powers plus the United States to regulate colonization and trade in Africa. No African representatives were invited, yet the delegates set rules of 'effective occupation' that triggered the frantic Scramble for Africa. Borders were drawn largely along straight lines with little regard for existing ethnic or political boundaries, dividing peoples and kingdoms arbitrarily. Many of today's African state borders still trace directly back to lines agreed in Berlin.

entries.name: Partition of India
entries.desc: Independence and division of British India into India and Pakistan.
entries.tldr: As British rule over India ended, the departing colonial administration divided the subcontinent along religious lines into a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim-majority Pakistan, the latter split into two wings a thousand miles apart. The boundary, drawn hastily by British lawyer Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited India before, was announced only after independence, triggering one of history's largest mass migrations as roughly 15 million people crossed the new borders. Communal violence killed an estimated one to two million people amid widespread massacres and displacement.

entries.name: Apollo 11 Moon Landing
entries.desc: First crewed landing on the Moon, by the United States' Apollo programme.
entries.tldr: On 20 July 1969, NASA's Apollo 11 mission achieved the first crewed landing on the Moon when the lunar module Eagle, piloted by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, touched down in the Sea of Tranquility. Armstrong became the first human to step onto the lunar surface, famously describing it as "one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind," while Michael Collins orbited above in the command module. The astronauts returned safely to Earth on 24 July, fulfilling Kennedy's 1961 pledge to reach the Moon.

entries.name: Siege of Van
entries.desc: Defense of Van (1915), the Armenian population's self-defense against Ottoman forces during the Armenian genocide.
entries.tldr: In April 1915, as Ottoman authorities began the mass killing of Armenians, the Armenian population of Van organized an armed self-defense against besieging Ottoman forces. Outnumbered residents held improvised defenses for about a month until a relieving Russian army and Armenian volunteers arrived and broke the siege. The defense became one of the few instances in which an Armenian community avoided the genocide underway elsewhere in the empire. Van was later depopulated when those forces withdrew, and the episode remains central to Armenian historical memory.

entries.name: Battle of Fahl
entries.desc: Major battle in the Muslim conquest of Byzantine Syria, fought by Rashidun Caliphate forces near Pella (Fahl).
entries.tldr: Fought near the town of Pella, known in Arabic as Fahl, in the Jordan Valley, this battle was part of the early Rashidun Caliphate's conquest of Byzantine Syria after the death of Muhammad. Arab Muslim forces defeated a Byzantine garrison that had reportedly flooded the surrounding marshland to slow their advance, a tactic that instead trapped many defenders in retreat. The victory secured the Jordan Valley for the Caliphate and cleared the way for the decisive Battle of Yarmouk soon after.

entries.name: Polish–Muscovite War
entries.desc: The Polish–Muscovite War (1605–18), a conflict between the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Tsardom of Russia.
entries.tldr: Part of what Russian history calls the Time of Troubles, when the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth exploited Muscovy's succession crisis, backing rival pretenders to the tsar's throne. Polish forces occupied the Kremlin from 1610 to 1612 before a popular uprising drove them out, an event Russia still marks as a national holiday. The war ended with the Truce of Deulino, which ceded the Smolensk and Chernihiv regions to the Commonwealth. It marked the high point of Commonwealth power over Russia before Muscovy's later resurgence.

entries.name: Treaty of Hünkâr İskelesi
entries.desc: Treaty between the Russian Empire and the Ottoman Empire establishing a mutual defence alliance.
entries.tldr: Signed in 1833 after Russia sent naval and military aid to help the Ottoman Empire repel an invasion by its rebellious vassal Muhammad Ali of Egypt, this treaty established a formal defensive alliance between the two empires. A secret clause obliged the Ottomans to close the Dardanelles to foreign warships at Russia's request, giving Russia a decisive edge in the Black Sea. The treaty alarmed Britain and France, who saw a dangerous expansion of Russian influence over the weakening Ottoman state. It lasted only until 1841, when other powers replaced it with a multilateral convention.

entries.name: Battle of Madagascar
entries.desc: Allied campaign to capture the Vichy French-controlled island of Madagascar during World War II.
entries.tldr: Concerned Japan might use Vichy-controlled Madagascar as a naval base to threaten Allied shipping in the Indian Ocean, British and Commonwealth forces launched Operation Ironclad to seize the island's ports. British marines captured the harbor of Diego Suarez in a rapid amphibious assault in May 1942, though Vichy forces resisted sporadically across the island for months. The campaign was Britain's first major amphibious operation of the war and a rehearsal for later joint operations. Vichy Madagascar formally surrendered in November 1942, and rule passed to Free French authorities.

entries.name: Battle of Guandu
entries.desc: Cao Cao's decisive victory over Yuan Shao's larger forces, a turning point of the late Eastern Han dynasty.
entries.tldr: In 200, Cao Cao, commanding a much smaller army, defeated the powerful northern warlord Yuan Shao at Guandu by exploiting intelligence about Yuan's supply depot at Wuchao and launching a night raid that burned the grain stores his rival's army depended on. The resulting panic and desertions turned a defensive standoff into a rout. The victory broke Yuan Shao's power in the north and set Cao Cao on the path to dominating northern China as the Eastern Han dynasty collapsed.

entries.name: Battle of Puebla
entries.desc: Mexican victory over French forces at Puebla during the second French intervention in Mexico.
entries.tldr: On 5 May 1862, Mexican forces under General Ignacio Zaragoza defeated a larger and better-equipped French army attempting to seize the city of Puebla during France's intervention in Mexico. Though France returned with reinforcements the following year and captured Puebla, the initial victory became a powerful symbol of Mexican resistance to foreign intervention. It is commemorated annually as Cinco de Mayo, a holiday now more widely celebrated in the United States than in Mexico itself. The battle briefly delayed French plans to install Maximilian I as emperor of Mexico.

entries.name: Battle of Auray
entries.desc: Decisive confrontation of the Breton War of Succession, part of the Hundred Years' War.
entries.tldr: Fought on 29 September 1364 near the Breton town of Auray, the battle decisively ended the Breton War of Succession, fought in parallel with the wider Hundred Years' War. An English-backed force under John of Montfort and captain John Chandos defeated the French-backed army of Charles of Blois, who was killed in the fighting, while the celebrated knight Bertrand du Guesclin was captured. Montfort's win secured him the Duchy of Brittany as John IV, and du Guesclin, once ransomed, went on to become France's foremost military commander.

entries.name: Pig War
entries.desc: Largely bloodless 1859 border confrontation between the United States and the British Colony of Vancouver Island.
entries.tldr: Tensions between American and British settlers on San Juan Island, whose ownership both the United States and Britain claimed under an ambiguously worded boundary treaty, boiled over when an American farmer shot a British-owned pig rooting in his garden. Both sides rushed troops and warships to the tiny island, and for a tense period hundreds of soldiers faced off across fortified positions, but cooler heads on both sides ensured the pig remained the conflict's only fatality. The dispute was resolved through arbitration, with Kaiser Wilhelm I awarding the island to the US in 1872.

entries.name: Siege of Vicksburg
entries.desc: Final major military action of the Vicksburg campaign, ending in a decisive Union victory in the American Civil War.
entries.tldr: Union forces under Ulysses S. Grant surrounded the Confederate stronghold of Vicksburg, Mississippi, in May 1863 after a campaign of maneuver and river crossings, settling into a siege when direct assaults failed. Trapped soldiers and civilians endured weeks of bombardment and dwindling supplies, some reportedly reduced to eating mules, until the garrison surrendered on July 4. The victory gave the Union full control of the Mississippi River, splitting the Confederacy and coinciding with the triumph at Gettysburg the day before. It ranks among the war's decisive turning points.

entries.name: Battle of Los Angeles
entries.desc: A rumored 1942 Japanese air attack on Los Angeles triggered an anti-aircraft artillery barrage over the city.
entries.tldr: Weeks after Pearl Harbor and a Japanese submarine's shelling near Santa Barbara, wartime jitters in Los Angeles boiled over when radar and visual reports suggested unidentified aircraft approaching the city at night. Anti-aircraft batteries fired over 1,400 rounds into the sky for about an hour, and the barrage itself caused deaths and property damage, though no enemy aircraft were ever confirmed present. A later investigation blamed a stray weather balloon combined with wartime nerves. The episode became a lasting piece of American UFO folklore, dramatized decades later in film.

entries.name: Battle of Rivoli
entries.desc: Napoleon's decisive defeat of Austrian forces near Rivoli, the climax of the Italian campaign of 1796–97.
entries.tldr: On 14-15 January 1797, Napoleon Bonaparte's French army defeated a larger Austrian force attempting to relieve the besieged fortress of Mantua, in the climactic battle of his 1796-97 Italian campaign. Napoleon exploited the Austrians' divided advance through mountainous terrain, defeating each column in turn rather than facing their combined strength at once. The victory forced Mantua's surrender soon after and effectively ended Austrian resistance in northern Italy. It cemented Napoleon's reputation as a rising military genius and paved the way for the favorable Treaty of Campo Formio.

entries.name: King William's War
entries.desc: North American theater of the Nine Years' War, fought between New France and New England and their Native allies.
entries.tldr: The North American extension of the Nine Years' War, it pitted the English colonies of New England and New York against New France and their Native allies, including the Iroquois and Wabanaki confederacies. Fighting consisted mostly of small frontier raids, such as the 1690 attack that destroyed Schenectady, rather than large pitched battles. It was the first of four colonial wars fought between Britain and France in North America over the following decades. The 1697 Treaty of Ryswick restored the prewar status quo, settling nothing.

entries.name: Battle of Smolensk
entries.desc: Battle of Smolensk (1812), fought during Napoleon's invasion of Russia.
entries.tldr: In mid-August 1812, advancing French forces under Napoleon caught up with the retreating Russian army near Smolensk and bombarded the ancient city into ruins before capturing it. Russian commander Barclay de Tolly chose to abandon the burning city rather than risk his army in a decisive battle, continuing the scorched-earth withdrawal that would doom Napoleon's invasion. The devastation at Smolensk foreshadowed the wider destruction Napoleon's army would leave and later suffer during the Russian campaign.

entries.name: Battle of Vaslui
entries.desc: Stephen III of Moldavia's victory over Ottoman forces near Vaslui in 1475.
entries.tldr: In January 1475, Stephen III of Moldavia, later known as Stephen the Great, used the region's marshy terrain and a scorched-earth strategy to lure and defeat a much larger Ottoman invasion force under Suleiman Pasha near Vaslui. The stunning victory, achieved against overwhelming numerical odds, prompted Pope Sixtus IV to reportedly hail Stephen as an "Athlete of Christ" for the wider defense of Christendom. The Ottomans returned in force the following year seeking revenge, but Stephen's reputation as a defender of his small principality was cemented.

entries.name: Battle of Maipú
entries.desc: Decisive Patriot victory over Spanish royalists near Santiago, completing Chile's independence.
entries.tldr: Following their earlier win at Chacabuco, Patriot forces under Bernardo O'Higgins and José de San Martín faced a renewed Spanish royalist army near Santiago that threatened Chile's fledgling independence. San Martín's infantry and cavalry broke the royalist lines after hours of fighting, inflicting heavy losses and capturing most of the surviving force. O'Higgins, still recovering from an earlier wound, arrived in time to embrace San Martín amid the victory, a moment still celebrated as the 'Embrace of Maipú.' The battle ended royalist hopes of reconquering Chile and secured its independence.

entries.name: Battle of Yamen
entries.desc: Naval battle marking the last stand of the Song dynasty against the invading Yuan dynasty forces.
entries.tldr: Fought in March 1279 off the coast of Guangdong, this naval battle marked the final destruction of the Song dynasty by the invading Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. The Song loyalist fleet, carrying the last child emperor, Zhao Bing, and the imperial court, was cornered and overwhelmed by Yuan forces under the general Zhang Hongfan. As defeat became certain, the chancellor Lu Xiufu leapt into the sea with the young emperor on his back rather than surrender, and thousands of officials reportedly followed. The battle ended Song rule and brought all of China under Mongol control.

entries.name: Battle of Neerwinden
entries.desc: Battle of Neerwinden (1793), a French defeat to Austrian forces during the War of the First Coalition.
entries.tldr: On 18 March 1793, an Austrian army under Prince Josias of Coburg defeated French Revolutionary forces led by General Charles-François Dumouriez near Neerwinden in the Austrian Netherlands. The defeat forced the French to abandon their recent conquest of Belgium and contributed to Dumouriez's subsequent defection to the Austrians. It was an early check on French revolutionary expansion during the War of the First Coalition, though French fortunes soon revived. The battle should not be confused with an earlier 1693 battle fought on nearly the same ground.

entries.name: Siege of Bursa
entries.desc: Long Ottoman siege that ended in the capture of Bursa (Prusa) in 1326, an early Ottoman conquest.
entries.tldr: Ottoman forces under Osman I began blockading the Byzantine city of Bursa in Anatolia around 1317, cutting it off from relief rather than storming its walls outright. The prolonged siege dragged on for years under Osman and then his son Orhan, who completed the conquest in 1326. Bursa's fall gave the young Ottoman beylik its first major city, which served as capital for the emerging state. It remained the Ottoman capital until Adrianople was captured later in the fourteenth century.

entries.name: Battle of Fulford
entries.desc: Harald Hardrada and Tostig Godwinson's defeat of the Northern Earls near York, days before Stamford Bridge.
entries.tldr: On 20 September 1066, the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada, allied with the exiled English earl Tostig Godwinson, defeated the English earls Edwin of Mercia and Morcar of Northumbria in a hard-fought battle near York. The victory let the invaders occupy York, but their triumph was short-lived: five days later King Harold Godwinson's army destroyed them at Stamford Bridge, killing both Hardrada and Tostig. The exhausting march and battle left Harold's army depleted just weeks before it faced William of Normandy at Hastings.

entries.name: Battle of Worcester
entries.desc: Oliver Cromwell's Parliamentarian army defeated Charles II's Royalist forces at Worcester, ending the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.
entries.tldr: On 3 September 1651, Oliver Cromwell's New Model Army decisively defeated the Royalist army of Charles II at Worcester, ending the young king's attempt to reclaim the throne with Scottish support. Cromwell called it his 'crowning mercy,' and the rout of the outnumbered Royalist force effectively ended the Wars of the Three Kingdoms. Charles himself narrowly escaped capture, famously hiding in an oak tree during his flight, and spent six weeks evading Parliamentarian forces before reaching exile in France, while England entered the republican Commonwealth period under Cromwell.

entries.name: Union of Krewo
entries.desc: Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania pledged to marry Queen Jadwiga of Poland, laying the groundwork for a Polish-Lithuanian union.

entries.name: Battle of Alcácer Quibir
entries.desc: Portuguese forces under King Sebastian were destroyed by a Moroccan army near Ksar-el-Kebir, ending Portugal's independent monarchy.
entries.tldr: In August 1578, the young King Sebastian I of Portugal led a large invasion force into Morocco to restore a deposed sultan, disregarding his own counselors' advice. Near Ksar-el-Kebir, a Moroccan army under Sultan Abd al-Malik overwhelmed the Portuguese force in a single day, killing Sebastian and most of the Portuguese nobility and army. Because Sebastian died without an heir, the resulting succession crisis let King Philip II of Spain claim the Portuguese throne, uniting the crowns for sixty years.

entries.name: Battle of Rorke's Drift
entries.desc: A small British garrison defended a mission station against a much larger Zulu force during the Anglo-Zulu War.
entries.tldr: On the night of 22-23 January 1879, a garrison of around 150 British and colonial troops defended a small mission station at Rorke's Drift in Natal against repeated assaults by roughly 3,000 to 4,000 Zulu warriors, hours after a Zulu army had annihilated a much larger British force at Isandlwana nearby. The defenders, many wounded, held their makeshift barricades through the night until the attackers withdrew at dawn. Eleven Victoria Crosses were awarded for the defense, the most ever given for a single action by the British Army, and it became a celebrated symbol of colonial military heroism.

entries.name: Battle of Mons Graupius
entries.desc: Roman forces under Agricola defeated a Caledonian army in what is now Scotland, per Tacitus's account.
entries.tldr: According to the Roman historian Tacitus, in 83 or 84 CE the Roman governor Gnaeus Julius Agricola led his legions to victory over a confederated Caledonian army under the chieftain Calgacus somewhere in northern Scotland. Tacitus, Agricola's son-in-law, put a famous anti-imperial speech in Calgacus's mouth before the battle, calling Roman conquest the making of "a desert" called peace. Roman losses were reportedly light against thousands of Caledonian dead, yet Rome never followed up by fully subduing Scotland. The battle's exact site has never been conclusively identified.

entries.name: Battle of Ad Decimum
entries.desc: Byzantine general Belisarius defeated the Vandal army near Carthage, opening the reconquest of North Africa.
entries.tldr: In 533, the Byzantine general Belisarius, commanding an expeditionary force sent by Emperor Justinian I, landed in North Africa and marched on the Vandal capital of Carthage. At a crossroads called Ad Decimum, ten miles from the city, his outnumbered troops defeated the Vandal king Gelimer's forces in a confused but decisive engagement. The victory opened the way for Belisarius to capture Carthage days later, ending nearly a century of independent Vandal rule and opening Justinian's reconquest of the West.

entries.name: Great Molasses Flood
entries.desc: A ruptured storage tank released a wave of molasses through Boston's North End, killing 21 people.
entries.tldr: On 15 January 1919, a poorly built steel tank holding over two million gallons of molasses ruptured in Boston's North End, sending a wave reportedly reaching 25 feet high through the streets at high speed. The flood killed 21 people and injured about 150, crushing buildings and sweeping horses, wagons, and people off their feet. A lengthy lawsuit later established that the company's shoddy construction, not sabotage as first suspected, caused the disaster, spurring stricter engineering regulations.

entries.name: Battle of Princeton
entries.desc: George Washington's forces defeated a British rearguard at Princeton, New Jersey, boosting American morale after Trenton.
entries.tldr: On 3 January 1777, George Washington's Continental Army struck a British rearguard at Princeton, New Jersey, just days after crossing the icy Delaware River to win at Trenton. American forces nearly broke under a British counterattack until Washington personally rode forward within yards of enemy lines to rally his men. The victory forced British troops to abandon much of New Jersey and restored American morale and enlistments after a string of earlier defeats around New York. General Hugh Mercer, mortally wounded in the fighting, became one of the campaign's notable casualties.

entries.name: Battle of the Camel
entries.desc: Caliph Ali defeated a rebel coalition led by Aisha, Talha, and Zubayr outside Basra, in the first civil war of Islam.
entries.tldr: Fought in November 656 near Basra, this battle was the first major armed conflict between Muslims during the First Fitna, pitting the fourth caliph, Ali ibn Abi Talib, against a rebel coalition led by the Prophet Muhammad's widow Aisha, with the companions Talha and Zubayr, seeking to avenge the murder of the previous caliph, Uthman. It takes its name from the fierce fighting around Aisha's camel-mounted litter, which continued until the camel was hamstrung to end it. Ali's forces prevailed, but the civil war the battle opened would divide the Muslim community for years.

entries.name: Vandalic War
entries.desc: Byzantine forces under Justinian I reconquered North Africa from the Vandal Kingdom.

entries.name: Battle of Omdurman
entries.desc: Anglo-Egyptian forces under Kitchener crushed the Mahdist army near Omdurman, Sudan, cementing British control of the region.
entries.tldr: On 2 September 1898, an Anglo-Egyptian force under Herbert Kitchener, equipped with modern artillery and Maxim machine guns, decisively defeated a much larger Mahdist army outside Omdurman in Sudan. The lopsided battle, in which a young Winston Churchill took part in one of history's last major cavalry charges, killed thousands of Sudanese fighters for minimal British losses. The victory avenged the earlier death of General Gordon at Khartoum and secured British-Egyptian control over Sudan. It became a stark symbol of the technological gap underpinning late-Victorian imperial expansion.

entries.name: Battle of Mons Lactarius
entries.desc: Byzantine forces defeated the Ostrogoths near Mount Vesuvius, ending organized Gothic resistance in Italy.
entries.tldr: In 552, the Byzantine general Narses cornered the last Ostrogothic king, Teia, on the slopes of Mons Lactarius near Mount Vesuvius, ending a two-day battle with Teia's death. The defeat broke the remaining organized Gothic resistance in Italy after nearly two decades of war under Justinian's reconquest campaign. Byzantine control of Italy that followed proved short-lived, soon challenged by Lombard invasion. The battle is often treated as the effective close of the Gothic War.

entries.name: Battle of Annual
entries.desc: Riffian Berber forces inflicted a catastrophic defeat on the Spanish Army in northeastern Morocco, triggering political crisis in Spain.
entries.tldr: In July 1921, Riffian Berber fighters led by Abd el-Krim ambushed and overwhelmed Spanish colonial forces under General Manuel Fernández Silvestre as they overextended into the Rif mountains of Morocco. Poorly supplied and scattered across isolated outposts, the Spanish army disintegrated in a rout that killed thousands, including Silvestre, and yielded huge quantities of captured weapons. The disaster, one of the worst colonial defeats a European power suffered, triggered a political crisis in Spain that fed into Miguel Primo de Rivera's 1923 coup.

entries.name: Smolensk War
entries.desc: The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth fought Muscovy over control of Smolensk.
entries.tldr: Beginning in 1632, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Tsardom of Muscovy fought over control of Smolensk, a city Russia had lost to Poland decades earlier and now sought to reclaim while Poland was weakened by the death of King Sigismund III. A Russian army besieged the city but was itself encircled and forced to surrender after a new Polish king, Władysław IV, arrived with relief forces. The resulting Peace of Polyanov confirmed Polish possession of Smolensk and other border territories. Russia's defeat exposed weaknesses that spurred later military reforms.

entries.name: Battle of Formigny
entries.desc: A decisive French victory over England near Formigny hastened the end of the Hundred Years' War in Normandy.
entries.tldr: On 15 April 1450, a French army under the Comte de Clermont, reinforced mid-battle by Arthur de Richemont's cavalry, defeated an English force near Formigny in Normandy, using mobile field artillery to disrupt the English longbowmen before they could form their usual defensive position. The English lost most of their army in the rout that followed, a rare success against forces that had dominated at Crécy and Agincourt. The victory let French forces sweep through Normandy, hastening the end of the Hundred Years' War.

entries.name: Battle of Wake Island
entries.desc: Japanese forces captured the American-held Pacific atoll of Wake Island after a fierce two-week defense.
entries.tldr: Beginning hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor, Japanese forces attempted to seize the small American-held Pacific atoll of Wake Island, defended by a garrison of Marines, sailors, and civilian contractors. An initial invasion attempt on 11 December 1941 was repelled by coastal guns and fighter aircraft, sinking a Japanese destroyer, a rare early American success. A larger Japanese force returned on 23 December and overwhelmed the defenders after fierce fighting, and the garrison surrendered that day. The prolonged defense became an early morale-boosting story for the wartime United States.

entries.name: Battles of Kawanakajima
entries.desc: Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin fought a series of inconclusive battles for control of the Kawanakajima plain in Sengoku-era Japan.
entries.tldr: Between 1553 and 1564, the rival Sengoku-era warlords Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin fought five inconclusive battles for control of the strategic Kawanakajima plain in Shinano Province, central Japan. The most famous, fought in 1561, is traditionally remembered for a dramatic single combat in which Kenshin is said to have charged into the Takeda camp and personally attacked Shingen, who parried the blows with his iron war fan. None of the battles produced a decisive victor, and the rivalry between the two, both renowned tacticians, became a celebrated episode in Japanese military legend.

entries.name: Battle of Boyacá
entries.desc: The Battle of Boyacá (1819), also known as the Battle of Boyacá Bridge was a decisive victory by a combined army of Venezuelan and New Granadan troops along with a British Legion led by General Simon Bolivar over the III Division of the Spanish Expeditionary Army of Costa Firme commanded by Spanish Colonel José Barreiro.
entries.tldr: Fought on 7 August 1819 at a bridge over the Boyacá River in present-day Colombia, the battle was the decisive engagement of Simón Bolívar's New Granada campaign in the South American wars of independence. Bolívar's combined Venezuelan and New Granadan troops, reinforced by a British Legion of foreign volunteers, intercepted and routed a Spanish royalist division under Colonel José María Barreiro as it retreated toward Bogotá. The victory opened the road to the viceregal capital, which fell within days, securing New Granada's independence and paving the way for Gran Colombia.

entries.name: First Anglo-Dutch War
entries.desc: The First Anglo-Dutch War, or First Dutch War, was a naval conflict between the Commonwealth of England and the Dutch Republic, largely caused by disputes over trade.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1652 to 1654, this was the first of several naval wars between the Commonwealth of England and the Dutch Republic, driven chiefly by commercial rivalry and England's restrictive Navigation Acts aimed at Dutch shipping. The conflict was fought almost entirely at sea, with large fleet actions in the Channel and North Sea testing new line-of-battle tactics. England's navy generally had the better of the fighting, and the 1654 Treaty of Westminster ended hostilities on favorable terms. The war set the pattern for rivalry between the two powers for the rest of the century.

entries.name: Second Ottoman–Venetian War
entries.desc: The Second Ottoman–Venetian War was fought from 1499 to 1503 between the Ottoman Empire and the Republic of Venice for control of contested lands in the Aegean, Ionian, and Adriatic seas.
entries.tldr: Fought for control of Venetian outposts in the Aegean, Ionian, and Adriatic as an increasingly powerful Ottoman navy under Sultan Bayezid II challenged Venice's long-standing maritime empire. The Ottomans won major naval victories, including at Zonchio, and captured key Venetian strongholds such as Lepanto, Modon, and Coron. Venice, unable to secure sufficient support from other Christian powers, was forced to accept a peace ceding the lost fortresses. The war marked a decisive shift of naval power in the eastern Mediterranean toward the Ottomans.

entries.name: First Ottoman–Venetian War
entries.desc: The First Ottoman–Venetian War was fought between the Republic of Venice with its allies and the Ottoman Empire from 1463 to 1479, resulting in the loss of several Venetian holdings in Albania and Greece.
entries.tldr: Sparked by disputes over Venetian holdings in the Aegean and Ottoman expansion in the Balkans, the war saw Sultan Mehmed II's forces steadily grind down Venice's fortified outposts. Venice recruited allies including Hungary and briefly Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu, but by 1479 was forced to accept a costly peace, surrendering Negroponte, Scutari, and other Aegean and Albanian possessions. The sixteen-year war marked the start of Venice's long decline as an eastern Mediterranean power.

entries.name: Battle of Edessa
entries.desc: The Battle of Edessa took place between the armies of the Roman Empire under Valerian and the Sasanian Empire under Shapur I in 260, resulting in the capture of a Roman emperor for the first time.
entries.tldr: In 260 CE, the Sasanian king Shapur I defeated a Roman army led by Emperor Valerian near Edessa in northern Mesopotamia, capturing the emperor, the only Roman emperor ever taken prisoner in battle. Valerian spent the rest of his life in Persian captivity, and hostile Roman sources later claimed he was humiliated as a human footstool, though the details are disputed. The disaster deepened Rome's Crisis of the Third Century. Shapur commemorated the victory in rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rustam that still survive.

entries.name: War of the Oranges
entries.desc: The War of the Oranges was a brief 1801 conflict in which Spanish forces, instigated and supported by France, invaded Portugal, resulting in the Treaty of Badajoz.

entries.name: Webster–Ashburton Treaty
entries.desc: The Webster–Ashburton Treaty resolved several border issues between the United States and the British North American colonies, signed in Washington, DC in 1842.

entries.name: Musket Wars
entries.desc: The Musket Wars were a series of as many as 3,000 battles and raids fought throughout New Zealand among Māori between 1806 and 1845, after Māori first obtained muskets.
entries.tldr: After Māori iwi in the north of New Zealand began acquiring European muskets through trade, most notably the Ngāpuhi chief Hongi Hika, they gained a decisive military advantage that triggered a wave of intertribal warfare as other iwi rushed to arm themselves. Estimates put the death toll at 20,000 or more across roughly 3,000 engagements, alongside mass enslavement and territorial displacement. The fighting subsided as muskets became common to all sides and exhaustion grew. The upheaval was still reshaping Māori society when the Crown negotiated the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840.

entries.name: Battle of Didgori
entries.desc: The Battle of Didgori was fought between the armies of the Kingdom of Georgia and the Seljuk Empire near Tbilisi in 1121, resulting in a devastating defeat for the Seljuk-led coalition.
entries.tldr: On 12 August 1121, King David IV 'the Builder' of Georgia led a Georgian army, reinforced by Kipchak and crusader allies, against a much larger Seljuk-led coalition near Didgori, west of Tbilisi. Using a feigned negotiation and a surprise flanking assault, David's forces routed the coalition in what Georgian chronicles remember as a near-miraculous victory. The triumph let David recapture Tbilisi the next year, ending centuries of Muslim rule there and opening Georgia's medieval Golden Age.

entries.name: Battle of Toba-Fushimi
entries.desc: The Battle of Toba–Fushimi occurred between pro-Imperial and Tokugawa shogunate forces during the Boshin War in Japan, beginning on 27 January 1868 near Kyoto.
entries.tldr: Beginning on 27 January 1868 near Kyoto, a numerically smaller Imperial force, bolstered by modern rifles and artillery and carrying a banner claimed to represent the emperor, decisively defeated the much larger army of the Tokugawa shogunate. The unexpected Tokugawa collapse triggered the wider Boshin War and accelerated the fall of the shogunate that had ruled Japan for over two and a half centuries. The victory cleared the way for the sweeping reforms of the Meiji Restoration.

entries.name: Battle of Orsha
entries.desc: The Battle of Orsha was fought on 8 September 1514 between the allied forces of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland and the army of the Grand Duchy of Moscow.
entries.tldr: On 8 September 1514, an allied Polish-Lithuanian army under Hetman Konstanty Ostrogski defeated a larger Muscovite force near Orsha, during a war over control of Smolensk. The victory, later celebrated in a famous contemporary painting, was widely publicized across Europe as a Christian check on Muscovite expansion. Despite the battlefield success, Poland-Lithuania failed to recover Smolensk, which remained under Moscow's control. The battle stands as one of the largest engagements fought in Eastern Europe in the early sixteenth century.

entries.name: Third Anglo-Burmese War
entries.desc: The Third Anglo-Burmese War was the final of three 19th-century wars between the Burmese and the British, ending in the loss of Burmese sovereignty under the Konbaung dynasty.
entries.tldr: In November 1885 British forces invaded the Konbaung kingdom of Upper Burma, citing a trade dispute and King Thibaw's dealings with the French as pretexts for a war long anticipated by British administrators in India. The campaign lasted only about two weeks before Mandalay fell and Thibaw was captured and exiled to India. Britain formally annexed all of Burma into its Indian Empire on 1 January 1886, ending the Konbaung dynasty and centuries of Burmese monarchy. Resistance continued for years afterward in a prolonged guerrilla insurgency against British rule.

entries.name: Continuation War
entries.desc: The Continuation War, also known as the Second Soviet–Finnish War, was fought by Finland and Nazi Germany against the Soviet Union from 1941 to 1944, ending with the Moscow Armistice.
entries.tldr: Finland fought alongside Nazi Germany against the Soviet Union from 1941 to 1944, seeking to reclaim territory lost in the earlier Winter War and, for some leaders, to expand further into Soviet Karelia. Finnish forces advanced deep into Soviet territory before the front stabilized, and a massive Soviet counteroffensive in summer 1944 pushed them back near the original border. Finland secured an armistice by agreeing to expel German troops from its soil, sparking the separate Lapland War. Finland preserved its independence, unlike other Axis states, though it paid heavy reparations.

entries.name: Sixth Russo-Turkish War
entries.desc: The Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774 was a major armed conflict that saw Russian armies victorious against the Ottoman Empire, bringing Crimea into the Russian sphere of influence.
entries.tldr: Fought between 1768 and 1774, this conflict pitted the Russian Empire of Catherine the Great against the Ottoman Empire over influence in the Black Sea region and the Crimean Khanate. Russian forces won a string of victories on land and destroyed the Ottoman fleet at the Battle of Chesma, forcing the Ottomans to sue for peace. The resulting Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca gave Russia its first Black Sea ports and recognized Crimea as nominally independent, paving the way for its annexation a decade later. The war marked a major shift in the balance of power, cementing Russian dominance in the region.

entries.name: Seventh Russo-Turkish War
entries.desc: The Russo-Turkish War of 1787–1792 involved an unsuccessful attempt by the Ottoman Empire to regain lands lost to Russia in the previous Russo-Turkish War, fought alongside several concurrent European wars.
entries.tldr: Fought when the Ottoman Empire, encouraged by earlier promises of British and Prussian support, declared war on Russia hoping to reverse territorial losses including Crimea from the previous war. Russian forces under commanders including Alexander Suvorov won major victories, most notably the storming of the fortress of Ismail. Austria joined Russia for much of the war, adding pressure on the Ottomans from the Balkans as well. The Treaty of Jassy confirmed Russian control of Crimea and extended its Black Sea coastline further west to the Dniester River.

entries.name: Battle of Roncevaux Pass
entries.desc: The Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778 saw a large force of Basques ambush part of Charlemagne's army in the Pyrenees, on the present border between France and Spain.
entries.tldr: On 15 August 778, as Charlemagne's army withdrew through the Pyrenees after an unsuccessful campaign in Spain, Basque forces ambushed its rearguard in the narrow Roncevaux Pass, killing several officers including Roland, prefect of the Breton March. The historical skirmish was modest in scale, but it inspired the medieval epic poem "The Song of Roland," which transformed the Basque raiders into Muslim armies and Roland into a legendary Christian martyr. That reworking made the battle one of the most famous episodes of medieval French literature, far exceeding its actual military significance.

entries.name: Battle of Loos
entries.desc: The biggest British attack of 1915, fought on the Western Front in France and marking the war's first British use of poison gas.
entries.tldr: Seeking to support a wider French offensive and use up a stockpile of newly made chlorine gas, the British army launched its largest attack of 1915 against German trench lines near the mining town of Loos. Poor wind conditions blew some of the gas back onto British troops even as the infantry advance made early gains against thin defenses. Without reserves close enough to exploit the breakthrough, the advance stalled and German counterattacks recovered most of the lost ground. The costly failure contributed to the replacement of British commander Sir John French by Douglas Haig.

entries.name: Hundred Years' War
entries.desc: A prolonged conflict between the kingdoms of England and France over rival claims to the French throne, fought intermittently from 1337 to 1453.
entries.tldr: Edward III of England claimed the French throne through his mother in 1337, launching a conflict that spanned five generations and was fought in intermittent phases rather than continuously. English longbowmen delivered stunning early victories at Crécy, Poitiers, and Agincourt, but France's fortunes turned after Joan of Arc rallied the besieged city of Orléans in 1429. By 1453, France had driven the English out of nearly all their continental holdings, leaving only Calais and cementing both nations' emerging sense of national identity.

entries.name: Spanish–American War
entries.desc: A brief 1898 war between Spain and the United States, sparked by the sinking of the USS Maine, that ended Spanish colonial rule in Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines.
entries.tldr: The 1898 war began after the battleship USS Maine exploded in Havana harbor, an incident American newspapers blamed on Spain amid sympathy for Cuban independence fighters. American forces quickly defeated Spanish forces in both the Caribbean and the Pacific, notably destroying Spanish fleets at Manila Bay and Santiago de Cuba. The brief conflict, lasting only a few months, ended Spain's centuries-old colonial empire and transferred control of Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States. It marked the emergence of the United States as a global colonial and naval power.

entries.name: Third Battle of Panipat
entries.desc: The Maratha Empire suffered a devastating defeat to the invading Durrani Empire near Panipat in 1761, reshaping the balance of power in northern India.
entries.tldr: In January 1761 the Maratha Empire, then the dominant power across much of India, suffered a catastrophic defeat near Panipat at the hands of Ahmad Shah Durrani's invading Afghan army, allied with the Rohilla Afghans and the Nawab of Awadh. Tens of thousands of Maratha soldiers were killed in the battle and its aftermath, including much of a generation of Maratha leadership. Though Durrani withdrew to Afghanistan without consolidating gains in India, the defeat crippled Maratha power, creating a vacuum that helped the British East India Company expand its influence over later decades.

entries.name: Third Anglo-Afghan War
entries.desc: A short 1919 war in which Afghanistan's new emir declared jihad against British India, ultimately securing full Afghan independence in foreign affairs.
entries.tldr: In May 1919 Afghanistan's new emir, Amanullah Khan, launched an invasion of British India and declared jihad, partly to rally domestic support after his father's assassination and to press for independence from British oversight of Afghan foreign policy. Fighting lasted only about a month before both exhausted sides agreed to a ceasefire. The resulting Treaty of Rawalpindi ended the British subsidy that had propped up earlier Afghan rulers and confirmed Afghanistan's right to its own foreign relations. Afghans still celebrate the outcome as full independence.

entries.name: Battle of Chrysopolis
entries.desc: Constantine I's decisive victory over co-emperor Licinius near Chrysopolis in 324, leaving Constantine sole ruler of the Roman Empire.
entries.tldr: Fought on 18 September 324 near Chrysopolis on the Bosphorus opposite Byzantium, the battle was the decisive final clash of the civil war between co-emperors Constantine I and Licinius, rivals for sole control of the Roman Empire. Constantine's forces, having already beaten Licinius's fleet and army earlier that year, overwhelmed his remaining army in hard fighting, after which Licinius surrendered and was spared, only to be executed the next year on suspicion of plotting a comeback. Constantine soon founded his new capital, Constantinople, near the site of his triumph.

entries.name: Battle of Callinicum
entries.desc: A hard-fought 531 clash in which Belisarius's Byzantine army was checked by a Sasanian cavalry force under Azarethes.
entries.tldr: Fought on 19 April 531 near Callinicum on the Euphrates, the battle came during a Sasanian Persian raid into Byzantine Mesopotamia, which the general Belisarius, already celebrated for his victory at Dara, moved to intercept despite his troops being outnumbered and worn from a religious fast. Belisarius's Byzantine and allied Arab forces were eventually broken by the larger Sasanian cavalry under Azarethes, though he managed an orderly retreat that limited the disaster. He kept his command and later led major Byzantine campaigns in North Africa and Italy.

entries.name: First Vienna Award
entries.desc: A 1938 arbitration following the Munich Agreement that forced Czechoslovakia to cede southern Slovakia and Carpathian Ruthenia to Hungary.
entries.tldr: Acting as arbiters under the Munich Agreement's shadow, Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy compelled Czechoslovakia to hand over southern Slovakia and Carpathian Ruthenia to Hungary in November 1938. The award redrew borders based on ethnic Hungarian population claims without a plebiscite, rewarding Hungary's alignment with the Axis powers. It further dismembered the already-weakened Czechoslovak state, a process completed months later by Germany's outright occupation of the Czech lands.

entries.name: Battle of Kolín
entries.desc: Austrian forces under Count von Daun defeated Frederick the Great's Prussian army near Kolín in 1757, the first major battle Frederick lost.
entries.tldr: Frederick the Great besieged Prague after his victory there earlier in 1757, but an Austrian relief army under Field Marshal Leopold von Daun advanced to break the siege. Frederick attacked Daun's strong defensive position near Kolín with a smaller force, and repeated Prussian infantry assaults failed to dislodge the well-entrenched Austrians. Frederick was forced to abandon the siege of Prague and retreat from Bohemia entirely, his first major defeat as a commander. The setback ended his run of early Seven Years' War victories and forced Prussia onto the defensive for years.

entries.name: Wars of the Roses
entries.desc: A series of dynastic civil wars fought between the houses of Lancaster and York for control of the English throne from 1455 to 1487.

entries.name: Battle of Neretva
entries.desc: A major 1943 Axis offensive against Yugoslav Partisan forces along the Neretva river, one of the largest confrontations of the Yugoslav theatre of World War II.
entries.tldr: Codenamed Operation Weiss by the Axis, this early 1943 offensive sent German, Italian, Croatian, and Chetnik forces against Josip Broz Tito's Yugoslav Partisans, who were encumbered by thousands of wounded and civilian refugees along the Neretva river in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Trapped against the river with bridges destroyed, the Partisans staged a daring crossing that let the main force escape encirclement and counterattack Chetnik units. The battle became a centerpiece of postwar Yugoslav national mythology, later dramatized in a major film, and let the Partisan movement survive.

entries.name: Battle of the Ebro
entries.desc: The longest and largest battle of the Spanish Civil War, fought along the Ebro River in Catalonia between July and November 1938.
entries.tldr: Fought between July and November 1938, this was the longest and largest battle of the Spanish Civil War, as Republican forces launched a surprise offensive across the Ebro River in Catalonia to relieve pressure elsewhere and reverse the war's momentum. Republican troops achieved initial gains and held territory for months under relentless Nationalist counterattacks, artillery bombardment, and air raids by the Condor Legion. The eventual Nationalist victory exhausted the Republic's last reserves and sealed the fall of Catalonia and, soon after, the end of the war.

entries.name: Battle of Akroinon
entries.desc: Byzantine forces halted a major Umayyad invasion of Anatolia near Akroinon in 740, checking Arab expansion into Byzantine territory.
entries.tldr: In 740, Byzantine emperor Leo III personally led an army that intercepted a large Umayyad invasion force near Akroinon in central Anatolia. The Byzantines inflicted a heavy defeat on the Arab army, reportedly killing most of its soldiers, in one of the most significant Byzantine victories of the ongoing Arab-Byzantine wars. It came just before the Umayyad Caliphate descended into internal crisis, and marked a turning point after which large-scale Arab invasions of Byzantine Anatolia became rarer.

entries.name: Indian Mutiny of 1857
entries.desc: A widespread uprising of sepoys and civilians against East India Company rule, beginning at Meerut in 1857 and reshaping British governance of India.
entries.tldr: Sepoys of the Bengal Army mutinied at Meerut in May 1857, sparked by rumors that new cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat, offensive to Hindu and Muslim soldiers alike, and the revolt quickly spread across northern and central India. Rebels rallied around the aged Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah II in Delhi, and fighting included prolonged sieges at Lucknow and Kanpur. British forces eventually crushed the uprising with brutal reprisals, after which the East India Company was dissolved and India came under direct British Crown rule.

entries.name: Battle of Flodden
entries.desc: An English army defeated an invading Scottish force under James IV near Flodden in 1513, part of the wider War of the League of Cambrai.
entries.tldr: On 9 September 1513, an English army under the Earl of Surrey destroyed an invading Scottish force near Flodden in Northumberland while King Henry VIII campaigned in France. King James IV of Scotland, honoring the 'Auld Alliance' with France, led the invasion personally and was killed along with much of the Scottish nobility, the last British monarch to die in battle. English bill-hooks proved devastating against the Scots' continental-style pikes on the rain-soaked ground.

entries.name: Battle of Verdun
entries.desc: The longest battle of the First World War, fought from February to December 1916 as German forces attacked French defences north of Verdun.
entries.tldr: Beginning in February 1916, German Chief of Staff Erich von Falkenhayn launched a massive offensive against the symbolically vital French fortress city of Verdun, intending to "bleed France white" through sheer attrition. French forces under General Philippe Pétain held the line via the improvised supply route known as the Voie Sacrée, under the rallying cry "Ils ne passeront pas." By the time fighting wound down in December 1916, the ten-month battle had produced roughly 700,000 combined casualties and become a lasting symbol of the war's carnage.

entries.name: Battle of Kursk
entries.desc: The largest tank battle in history, fought in the summer of 1943 as Germany's last major offensive on the Eastern Front ended in Soviet victory.
entries.tldr: Expecting a Soviet buildup around the Kursk salient, Germany launched Operation Citadel in July 1943 with massed tanks, including new Tiger and Panther models, to pinch off the bulge and destroy Soviet reserves. Soviet forces, forewarned by intelligence, had built deep, layered defenses of minefields and anti-tank guns, and the offensive stalled with heavy German losses, including in the massive armored clash at Prokhorovka. The failure marked the last major German strategic offensive on the Eastern Front. From Kursk onward, the Red Army held the strategic initiative for the rest of the war.

entries.name: La Noche Triste
entries.desc: Hernán Cortés and his Spanish and native allied forces were driven out of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan in a bloody 1520 retreat.
entries.tldr: After Hernán Cortés's Spanish expedition and its Tlaxcalan allies were besieged inside Tenochtitlan following the death of Aztec ruler Moctezuma II, the conquistadors attempted a desperate nighttime escape across the city's causeways. Aztec warriors attacked from canoes and rooftops, and hundreds of Spaniards drowned in the lake trying to carry looted gold, giving the retreat its name, 'the night of sorrows.' Cortés reportedly wept beneath a tree afterward. He regrouped with Tlaxcalan support and returned within a year to conquer the city.

entries.name: Battle of the Somme
entries.desc: One of the largest and bloodiest battles of the First World War, fought by British and French forces against Germany along the Somme in 1916.
entries.tldr: Fought from July to November 1916 along the Somme River in northern France, this joint British and French offensive against German positions became one of the bloodiest battles in human history: 1 July 1916 alone produced roughly 57,000 British casualties, the worst single day in British military history. Despite new weapons, including the tank's combat debut, and months of grinding attacks, the Allies advanced only a few miles at enormous cost before winter weather ended the offensive. It came to symbolize trench warfare's attrition, with combined casualties exceeding a million men.

entries.name: Battle of Chickamauga
entries.desc: Confederate victory over Union forces in northwest Georgia, the most significant Union defeat in the war's Western Theater.
entries.tldr: Fought over 19 and 20 September 1863 in northwestern Georgia, the battle was the culmination of the Chickamauga Campaign and, after Gettysburg, the second-costliest of the Civil War in total casualties. Confederate forces under General Braxton Bragg, reinforced from Robert E. Lee's army, exploited a gap mistakenly opened in the Union line to rout much of the Army of the Cumberland under General William Rosecrans. Only a defensive stand by General George Thomas, nicknamed the Rock of Chickamauga for it, prevented total collapse and allowed an orderly retreat to Chattanooga.

entries.name: Battle of Inab
entries.desc: Zengid forces under Nur al-Din Zengi destroyed the army of Prince Raymond of Antioch during the Second Crusade, killing Raymond.
entries.tldr: Nur al-Din Zengi lured Raymond of Antioch's army onto exposed, waterless ground near the fortress of Inab and surrounded it overnight. Raymond ignored warnings from an allied lord to withdraw, and by morning his force was cut to pieces. Raymond himself died in the fighting, and Nur al-Din is said to have sent his skull to the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad as a trophy. The defeat left the Principality of Antioch dangerously weakened and confirmed Nur al-Din as the rising champion of jihad against the Crusader states.

entries.name: Battle of Ourique
entries.desc: Portuguese forces under Afonso Henriques defeated an Almoravid army, a battle later mythologized as founding the Kingdom of Portugal.
entries.tldr: According to tradition, on 25 July 1139 Afonso Henriques, Count of Portugal, defeated a large Almoravid army near Ourique in southern Portugal, after which his soldiers proclaimed him king on the battlefield. Later legend added that Christ himself appeared to Afonso before the battle promising victory, a story that became central to Portuguese national identity. Whatever actually occurred, the battle is conventionally treated as the founding moment of the independent Kingdom of Portugal. Portugal's coat of arms is traditionally said to commemorate the five Moorish kings defeated that day.

entries.name: Indonesian National Revolution
entries.desc: Armed and diplomatic struggle between the Republic of Indonesia and the Dutch Empire following Indonesia's 1945 declaration of independence.
entries.tldr: Indonesian nationalists led by Sukarno and Hatta declared independence within days of Japan's 1945 surrender, but the Netherlands sought to reassert colonial control over its former East Indies possessions. Four years of guerrilla warfare, diplomacy, and two major Dutch military offensives followed, drawing international criticism, including pressure from the United States and the United Nations. The Netherlands formally transferred sovereignty in December 1949, ending over three centuries of Dutch colonial rule.

entries.name: Battle of Fei River
entries.desc: Heavily outnumbered Eastern Jin forces decisively defeated the Former Qin dynasty on the Fei River, ending Fu Jian's bid to unify China.
entries.tldr: In 383, the southern Eastern Jin dynasty, though vastly outnumbered, decisively defeated the northern Former Qin army of Fu Jian at the Fei River after tricking the Qin forces into retreating during a river crossing, a maneuver that spiraled into a panicked rout. The chaos gave rise to a Chinese idiom about mistaking wind and crane cries for pursuing enemies, meaning extreme panic. Fu Jian's defeat shattered his unification of northern China and triggered its rapid disintegration into rival states.

entries.name: Treaty of Brétigny
entries.desc: Treaty between Edward III of England and John II of France that ended the first phase of the Hundred Years' War.
entries.tldr: Signed in 1360, the Treaty of Brétigny concluded the first phase of the Hundred Years' War between England and France after French king John II was captured at the Battle of Poitiers four years earlier. Under its terms England renounced its claim to the French throne in exchange for full sovereignty over an enlarged territory in southwestern France, plus a massive ransom for John's release. The settlement proved unstable, as both sides struggled to fulfill its obligations. Fighting resumed within a decade, and the war ultimately dragged on for nearly a century more before ending in 1453.

entries.name: Battle of Tewkesbury
entries.desc: Decisive Yorkist victory over Lancastrian forces in the Wars of the Roses, killing the Lancastrian heir Edward of Westminster.
entries.tldr: On 4 May 1471, King Edward IV's Yorkist army crushed the Lancastrian forces of Margaret of Anjou near Tewkesbury during the Wars of the Roses. Edward of Westminster, the seventeen-year-old Lancastrian heir and Henry VI's only son, was killed in the fighting or its immediate aftermath, ending the direct Lancastrian line of succession. Henry VI himself, held prisoner in the Tower of London, died shortly after the battle, leaving Edward IV's throne effectively secure.

entries.name: Battle of Evesham
entries.desc: Future King Edward I defeated and killed rebel baron Simon de Montfort, ending the Second Barons' War.
entries.tldr: On 4 August 1265, Prince Edward, the future Edward I, led a royalist army to intercept and crush the baronial forces of Simon de Montfort near Evesham, trapping them against a bend in the River Avon during a sudden storm. De Montfort, who had effectively ruled England after capturing King Henry III the previous year, was killed and his body mutilated by the victors. The battle ended the Second Barons' War and restored royal authority, though de Montfort's parliament left a lasting mark on English governance.

entries.name: Battle of Austerlitz
entries.desc: Napoleon's decisive victory over the combined Russian and Austrian armies, among the most significant engagements of the Napoleonic Wars.
entries.tldr: Fought on 2 December 1805 in what is now the Czech Republic, the battle is often called the Battle of the Three Emperors, pitting Napoleon against the combined armies of Tsar Alexander I of Russia and Emperor Francis I of Austria. Napoleon deliberately weakened his right flank to lure the Allies into attacking, then struck their thinned center on the Pratzen Heights, splitting the army and driving much of it onto frozen lakes under artillery fire. The crushing victory forced Austria out of the war within days and is widely seen as Napoleon's tactical masterpiece.

entries.name: Battle of Lyndanisse
entries.desc: Danish forces defeated Estonian tribes during the Northern Crusades, allowing King Valdemar II to claim northern Estonia.
entries.tldr: During the Northern Crusades, King Valdemar II of Denmark led an expedition to conquer the pagan Estonians and landed near the site of modern Tallinn. Estonian tribes launched a surprise attack on the Danish camp that nearly overwhelmed it before Danish forces rallied and repelled them. According to a later legend, a red banner with a white cross fell from the sky and rallied the wavering Danes, becoming the legendary origin of the Danish flag, the Dannebrog. The victory secured northern Estonia under Danish rule for over a century, and Valdemar founded the fortress that became Tallinn.

entries.name: Battle of Aljubarrota
entries.desc: Portuguese forces under John I decisively defeated Castile, securing Portuguese independence and John's claim to the throne.
entries.tldr: Fought on 14 August 1385, the battle pitted the newly acclaimed John I of Portugal against a larger Castilian army pressing Juan I of Castile's claim to the Portuguese throne. Commander Nuno Álvares Pereira held a defensive hilltop position, backed by English longbowmen, and broke the Castilian charge with heavy losses. The victory ended Castile's bid to absorb Portugal and founded the Aviz dynasty. It also cemented the Anglo-Portuguese alliance, formalized the next year by the Treaty of Windsor, the oldest alliance still in force today.

entries.name: Third Anglo-Dutch War
entries.desc: Naval conflict between the Dutch Republic and an England allied with France, part of the wider Franco-Dutch War.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1672 to 1674, this war saw England ally with France against the Dutch Republic as part of the wider Franco-Dutch War, in which Louis XIV sought to crush Dutch power. English and French fleets fought major naval battles against the Dutch navy under Michiel de Ruyter, who repeatedly frustrated attempts at invasion or blockade. Unlike France, England gained little and grew increasingly unpopular with its own Parliament over the costly, inconclusive alliance. England withdrew via the Treaty of Westminster in 1674, ending Anglo-Dutch hostilities as France fought on alone.

entries.name: Treaty of Verdun
entries.desc: Division of the Carolingian Empire among the three surviving sons of Louis the Pious, ending the Carolingian civil war.

entries.name: Ridda Wars
entries.desc: Campaigns launched by Caliph Abu Bakr against rebellious Arabian tribes following the death of Muhammad, consolidating the Rashidun Caliphate.
entries.tldr: Fought immediately after Muhammad's death, when numerous Arabian tribes renounced Islam or refused to keep paying zakat to the new caliph, treating their earlier allegiance as personal to Muhammad rather than a lasting state. Caliph Abu Bakr sent columns under commanders including Khalid ibn al-Walid to suppress the uprisings, defeating rival prophetic claimants such as Musaylimah at the Battle of Yamama. The campaigns reunified Arabia under Rashidun rule within about a year, freeing Muslim armies for the conquests of Byzantine and Sasanian territory that followed almost immediately.

entries.name: 1920 Haiyuan earthquake
entries.desc: A catastrophic magnitude earthquake struck Haiyuan County in northwest China, one of the deadliest in history.
entries.tldr: On 16 December 1920, an earthquake estimated at magnitude 8.3 struck Haiyuan County in China's Gansu (now Ningxia) region, one of the most powerful ever recorded on the Chinese mainland. Massive landslides buried entire villages built into the region's soft loess soil, and the shaking was felt across much of northern China. Death toll estimates range from about 200,000 to over 270,000, with the following winter's famine compounding the losses. The remote epicenter means the exact scale is still debated.

entries.name: 1908 Messina earthquake
entries.desc: A devastating earthquake and tsunami struck the Strait of Messina in southern Italy, killing around 120,000 people.
entries.tldr: Just before dawn on 28 December 1908, a violent earthquake struck the Strait of Messina between Sicily and Calabria, collapsing most buildings in Messina and Reggio Calabria within seconds. A tsunami generated by the quake then swept ashore, drowning survivors who had fled to the waterfront. Estimates of the dead range as high as 120,000, one of the deadliest earthquakes in European history. International relief poured in within days, and the disaster spurred Italy's first modern seismic building codes.

entries.name: 365 Crete earthquake
entries.desc: A massive undersea earthquake near Crete caused widespread destruction and tsunamis across the eastern Mediterranean.
entries.tldr: On the morning of 21 July 365 CE, a huge undersea earthquake ruptured along the Hellenic Arc southwest of Crete, uplifting parts of the island's coastline by several meters. The quake triggered a tsunami that devastated coastal cities across the eastern Mediterranean, including Alexandria, where thousands reportedly drowned. Ancient writers such as Ammianus Marcellinus described the sea retreating before crashing back over harbors and towns. Modern seismologists rank it among the largest events ever recorded in the Mediterranean.

entries.name: Winter War
entries.desc: The Soviet Union invaded Finland, which despite being outmatched inflicted heavy losses before the Moscow Peace Treaty ended the war.

entries.name: Warsaw Convention
entries.desc: International convention regulating airline liability for international carriage of passengers, baggage, and cargo.

entries.name: Polish–Russian War of 1792
entries.desc: War between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Russian Empire under Catherine the Great, allied with the Targowica Confederation.
entries.tldr: Fought after Poland's reformist Constitution of 3 May 1791 alarmed conservative nobles and Catherine the Great, who invaded to restore the old order. A reform-minded Polish army, including Tadeusz Kościuszko, fought creditably but was heavily outnumbered, and King Stanisław August Poniatowski ultimately joined the anti-reform Targowica Confederation and surrendered. The defeat led directly to the Second Partition of Poland in 1793, stripping the Commonwealth of much of its territory. It effectively ended Poland's attempt at self-directed reform.

entries.name: Battle of Muret
entries.desc: Simon de Montfort's small force of French crusaders routed a much larger army of Aragonese and Occitan lords, the decisive battle of the Albigensian Crusade.
entries.tldr: On 12 September 1213, Simon de Montfort led a small force of French crusaders to a stunning victory over a far larger army of Aragonese and southern French lords near Muret, during the Albigensian Crusade against Cathar heresy. King Peter II of Aragon, who had come to defend his Occitan allies, was killed in the fighting. The defeat crushed the southern coalition's resistance and cleared the way for northern French domination of Languedoc. It remains one of the most lopsided victories of medieval warfare.

entries.name: Italian War of 1494–1495
entries.desc: Charles VIII of France invaded Italy to press his claim to Naples, opening decades of Italian Wars among France, Spain, and the Holy Roman Empire.
entries.tldr: Charles VIII of France marched an army into Italy in 1494 to press a dynastic claim to the Kingdom of Naples inherited through the Angevin line, exploiting the peninsula's fractured city-states. His forces swept through Italy with unprecedented speed, thanks partly to a new generation of mobile siege artillery, and briefly took Naples. An alliance of Italian states, Spain, and the Holy Roman Empire forced Charles into a costly retreat, but the invasion opened over six decades of recurring Italian Wars among Europe's major powers.

entries.name: Battle of Appomattox Court House
entries.desc: Confederate general Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Union forces, effectively ending the American Civil War.
entries.tldr: On 9 April 1865, after a week-long retreat from the fallen Confederate capital of Richmond, General Robert E. Lee's starving Army of Northern Virginia found itself surrounded by Union forces under Ulysses S. Grant near Appomattox Court House, Virginia. With escape impossible, Lee met Grant at the McLean house and surrendered his army; Grant offered generous terms, letting Confederate soldiers keep their horses and go home unmolested. Though scattered fighting continued elsewhere for weeks, the surrender is treated as the war's effective end.

entries.name: 1893 Franco-Siamese crisis
entries.desc: A French gunboat standoff and ultimatum forced Siam to cede territory east of the Mekong, cementing French colonial control of Indochina.
entries.tldr: In July 1893, French gunboats forced their way up the Chao Phraya River to Bangkok, then delivered an ultimatum demanding Siam cede all territory east of the Mekong. King Chulalongkorn's government, isolated diplomatically and unable to match French naval power, capitulated rather than risk war. The resulting treaty stripped Siam of Laos and imposed a large indemnity. The crisis marked the high point of French expansion in Indochina and left Siam a diminished buffer state.

entries.name: Battle of Talikota
entries.desc: An alliance of Deccan sultanates crushed the Vijayanagara Empire, triggering the eventual collapse of the last great Hindu empire of southern India.
entries.tldr: In January 1565, an alliance of the Deccan Sultanates of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, and Bidar united against their common rival, the Hindu Vijayanagara Empire, near the village of Talikota. The death of Vijayanagara's powerful regent Rama Raya on the battlefield triggered a collapse in the empire's army and command structure. In the aftermath, the victorious sultanates sacked and burned the magnificent capital city of Vijayanagara, ending the last great Hindu empire of southern India.

entries.name: First Anglo-Maratha War
entries.desc: The British East India Company's first war with the Maratha Empire ended inconclusively after years of fighting across western India.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1775 to 1782, this was the British East India Company's first major war against the Maratha Empire, sparked by Company interference in a succession dispute at Pune. Company forces suffered a humiliating defeat and forced surrender at Wadgaon in 1779, one of British India's worst early military setbacks. Years of further inconclusive fighting followed across western India before the 1782 Treaty of Salbai restored the prewar territorial status quo. The war exposed the limits of British power against a major Indian state for two decades.

entries.name: Battle of Köse Dağ
entries.desc: A Mongol army decisively defeated the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in eastern Anatolia, reducing the sultanate to Mongol vassalage.
entries.tldr: A Mongol army under commander Baiju invaded Anatolia and met the forces of the Seljuk Sultan of Rum, Kaykhusraw II, who had assembled a large but poorly coordinated army of Seljuk troops and foreign mercenaries. The Mongols' feigned retreat drew the Seljuk cavalry into disorganized pursuit, and Kaykhusraw fled the field early, causing his army to collapse. The defeat reduced the once-powerful Sultanate of Rum to a Mongol tributary state, fatally weakening its authority. The power vacuum let smaller Turkish principalities, including the nascent Ottoman beylik, eventually rise in its place.

entries.name: Battle of Bailén
entries.desc: Spanish forces forced the surrender of a French army corps, the first open-field defeat of a Napoleonic army and a spark for anti-French resistance.
entries.tldr: Fought over 16 to 19 July 1808 near the Andalusian town of Bailén, the battle saw Spanish forces under generals Francisco Javier Castaños and Theodor von Reding surround and force the surrender of a French army corps under General Pierre Dupont.
