It was the first time in the Napoleonic Wars a French field army had capitulated in open battle, and news of it stunned European capitals still reeling from French victories. The defeat drew Napoleon into Spain personally and became a powerful symbol that his armies were not invincible.

entries.name: Battle of Strasbourg
entries.desc: Roman forces under Julian defeated the Alamanni confederation near modern Strasbourg, securing the Rhine frontier.
entries.tldr: In 357, the Roman Caesar Julian, later emperor, led a heavily outnumbered force against a large confederation of Alamanni tribes under King Chnodomarius near modern Strasbourg. Julian's disciplined legions broke the Alamanni line and captured Chnodomarius himself, securing the Rhine frontier against further incursions for years. The victory greatly enhanced Julian's military reputation among his troops, who would later acclaim him emperor in defiance of Constantius II.

entries.name: Battle of Jerusalem
entries.desc: British Empire forces captured Jerusalem from the Ottoman Empire during World War I's Sinai and Palestine campaign.
entries.tldr: In December 1917, General Edmund Allenby's British Empire forces advanced on Jerusalem after breaking Ottoman lines further south during the Sinai and Palestine campaign. Facing encirclement, the Ottoman garrison withdrew and the city's mayor surrendered it without a fight to spare its holy sites. Allenby entered on foot out of respect for the city's sanctity, a deliberate contrast with the mounted, triumphal entry of Kaiser Wilhelm II decades earlier. The capture, the first time a Christian power had held Jerusalem since the Crusades, was a major propaganda victory for Britain.

entries.name: War of the Sixth Coalition
entries.desc: A coalition of European powers defeated Napoleonic France and forced Napoleon's abdication and exile to Elba.

entries.name: Reconquest of Constantinople
entries.desc: Nicaean forces recaptured Constantinople from the Latin Empire, restoring the Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty.
entries.tldr: Ended the 57-year Latin Empire established by the Fourth Crusade in 1204, when a Nicaean general seized a lightly defended Constantinople almost by accident while its Latin garrison was away on campaign. Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos entered the city in triumph and restored Byzantine rule, founding the Palaiologan dynasty that would govern until 1453. The empire he recovered was smaller and poorer than before the Crusade and never regained its earlier strength. Byzantine power continued to erode until the Ottoman conquest two centuries later.

entries.name: Battle of Velbazhd
entries.desc: Serbian forces defeated the Bulgarian Empire near Velbazhd, shifting the balance of power in the Balkans toward Serbia.
entries.tldr: In 1330, Serbian King Stefan Decanski defeated the Bulgarian Tsar Michael Shishman near Velbazhd, in modern North Macedonia, with Michael dying of wounds sustained in the fighting. The Bulgarian defeat marked a decisive shift in the balance of power in the Balkans away from Bulgaria and toward Serbia. It paved the way for Serbia's rapid rise under Stefan Dušan, who would go on to build the largest Serbian empire in history within a generation.

entries.name: Kashmir conflict
entries.desc: A territorial dispute between India and Pakistan over the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, ongoing since the 1947 partition of India.
entries.tldr: When British India was partitioned in 1947, Kashmir's Hindu maharaja hesitated before acceding to India after Pakistani-backed tribal raiders invaded, triggering the first Indo-Pakistani war. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 1949 split the region along the Line of Control, a division that still stands. India and Pakistan have since fought two more wars and one limited conflict over the territory, and both claim it in full. Kashmir remains one of the world's most militarized and enduring unresolved disputes.

entries.name: Battle of the Tenaru
entries.desc: Allied ground forces repelled a Japanese assault on Guadalcanal, the first major Japanese land offensive of the Pacific campaign.
entries.tldr: In August 1942, shortly after American Marines landed on Guadalcanal, a Japanese force of roughly 900 men under Colonel Kiyonao Ichiki launched a hasty night assault against the newly established Marine perimeter near the Ilu River, mistakenly recorded in American accounts as the Tenaru. The attackers, badly underestimating American strength, charged directly into prepared Marine positions backed by machine guns and artillery, and were almost entirely wiped out; Ichiki was killed. The lopsided victory was the first major American land engagement of the Pacific campaign.

entries.name: Battle of Mons
entries.desc: The British Expeditionary Force's first major engagement of World War I against the advancing German army in Belgium.
entries.tldr: On 23 August 1914, the British Expeditionary Force made its first stand of World War I along the Mons-Condé canal in Belgium, delaying the advancing German First Army with disciplined rifle fire so rapid the Germans reportedly mistook it for machine guns. Heavily outnumbered, the British were soon forced into a fighting retreat that lasted nearly two weeks. Though a tactical defeat, the stand bought time for French and British forces to regroup before the Battle of the Marne. The clash also produced the legend of the "Angels of Mons," said to have shielded the retreating troops.

entries.name: Torstenson War
entries.desc: Sweden defeated Denmark–Norway in a conflict tied to the wider Thirty Years' War, boosting Swedish power in the Baltic.
entries.tldr: In 1643, during the wider Thirty Years' War, Sweden under military commander Lennart Torstenson launched a surprise invasion of Denmark–Norway, seeking to weaken a rival power and secure Swedish trade routes free of Danish tolls. Swedish forces overran much of Jutland and won a decisive naval victory, leaving Denmark unable to continue the fight. The 1645 Treaty of Brömsebro forced Denmark to cede territory, including islands and mainland provinces, and to exempt Swedish ships from the Sound Dues. The war marked a turning point that shifted Baltic dominance decisively from Denmark to Sweden.

entries.name: Russo-Persian War of 1826–28
entries.desc: Russia's final war with Qajar Iran ended in Persian territorial losses in the South Caucasus under the Treaty of Turkmenchay.
entries.tldr: Renewed hostilities began when Iran's Qajar ruler, encouraged by clergy and hoping to reverse earlier territorial losses, invaded Russian-held land in the South Caucasus. Russian forces under General Ivan Paskevich pushed back the invasion and captured Tabriz and Erivan deep inside Persian territory. The 1828 Treaty of Turkmenchay forced Persia to cede the Erivan and Nakhchivan khanates, pay a large indemnity, and grant Russia exclusive naval rights on the Caspian Sea. It was the last of several wars that fixed the modern border between Russia and Iran.

entries.name: Battle of Abritus
entries.desc: A federation of Gothic tribes defeated the Roman army and killed Emperor Decius, the first Roman emperor to die in battle against a foreign enemy.
entries.tldr: In 251 CE, Emperor Decius led a Roman army against a coalition of Gothic and allied tribes under the Gothic king Cniva, who had been raiding the Roman province of Moesia. Lured into marshy terrain near the town of Abritus, the Roman force was ambushed and annihilated, and Decius was killed along with his son and co-emperor Herennius Etruscus. He thus became the first Roman emperor to die in battle against a foreign enemy, a shocking blow during the turbulent Crisis of the Third Century.

entries.name: Battle of Cajamarca
entries.desc: Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force ambushed and captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa, opening the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire.
entries.tldr: On 16 November 1532, a small Spanish force of fewer than 200 men under Francisco Pizarro confronted the Inca emperor Atahualpa and his vastly larger unarmed retinue in the plaza of Cajamarca in the Peruvian highlands, ostensibly for a peaceful meeting. Using surprise, cavalry, and steel weapons against an Inca force unfamiliar with such warfare, the Spanish massacred thousands of attendants within hours and captured the emperor. Atahualpa's enormous ransom in gold and silver, paid to secure his release, only led to his execution by the Spanish months later on trumped-up charges.

entries.name: Battle of Chacabuco
entries.desc: The Army of the Andes under José de San Martín defeated Spanish royalist forces near Santiago, a decisive early victory in the Chilean War of Independence.
entries.tldr: Fought on 12 February 1817 near Santiago, the battle was the decisive opening engagement of the second phase of the Chilean War of Independence, as the Army of the Andes, a combined Argentine and Chilean force led by José de San Martín and Bernardo O'Higgins, crossed the Andes in a grueling surprise march to confront Spanish royalist defenders. Caught off guard, the royalist force was routed after a coordinated pincer assault broke its lines. The win let San Martín's army occupy Santiago within days, securing Chilean independence and setting up his later campaign to liberate Peru.

entries.name: Battle of the Wilderness
entries.desc: Opening battle of Ulysses S. Grant's 1864 Overland Campaign against Robert E. Lee, fought in dense Virginia woodland during the American Civil War.
entries.tldr: Fought from 5 to 7 May 1864 in a densely wooded area of Virginia, this battle opened Union General Ulysses S. Grant's Overland Campaign against Confederate General Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia. The thick, tangled terrain limited visibility and artillery use, leading to disorganized, close-range fighting and fires that burned some wounded to death where they lay. Though tactically inconclusive, Grant, unlike his predecessors, chose to keep pressing south rather than retreat, beginning a campaign of attrition that ground down Lee's army over the following year.

entries.name: Battle of Adrianople
entries.desc: Gothic rebels under Fritigern annihilated a Roman army and killed Emperor Valens near Adrianople, a catastrophic defeat for the Eastern Roman Empire.
entries.tldr: On 9 August 378 CE, Emperor Valens led an Eastern Roman army against a large force of Gothic refugees under Fritigern who had rebelled after being mistreated by Roman officials following their admission across the Danube. Attacking before western reinforcements arrived, Valens's army was surrounded and annihilated near Adrianople, and the emperor was killed, his body never recovered. Ammianus Marcellinus compared the disaster to Rome's defeat at Cannae, and it is often cited as a turning point in Rome's decline.

entries.name: Battle of Barnet
entries.desc: Decisive Yorkist victory over Lancastrian forces in the Wars of the Roses that helped secure the English throne for Edward IV.
entries.tldr: Fought on 14 April 1471 amid thick fog just north of London, the battle was a pivotal clash of the Wars of the Roses in which the Yorkist king Edward IV, recently returned from exile, defeated the Lancastrian-aligned forces of his former ally Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, remembered as Warwick the Kingmaker. Confusion in the fog led part of Warwick's own army to attack its allies by mistake, and Warwick was killed fleeing the collapsing line. His death cleared the way for Edward's decisive win weeks later at Tewkesbury, securing the Yorkist throne for over a decade.

entries.name: War of the League of Cognac
entries.desc: Habsburg forces under Charles V fought an Italian alliance including France, the Papacy, and Venice for control of Italy from 1526 to 1530.

entries.name: Battle of Castle Itter
entries.desc: American, German, and French prisoners jointly defended an Austrian castle against the Waffen-SS in one of the final actions of World War II in Europe.
entries.tldr: Fought on 5 May 1945 in the final days of the war in Europe, the battle was one of its strangest engagements, as American tank crews, defecting Wehrmacht soldiers, and French VIP prisoners, including former prime ministers, held inside the Austrian castle of Itter, jointly fought off an attacking force of fanatical Waffen-SS troops. The improvised multinational garrison, aided by Austrian resistance fighters, held out through the day until American reinforcements arrived. It is often cited as the only battle where American and German troops fought together against a common enemy.

entries.name: Battle of Maldon
entries.desc: Viking raiders defeated an Anglo-Saxon force led by Earl Byrhtnoth near Maldon in Essex, later commemorated in an Old English poem.
entries.tldr: A Viking fleet landed near Maldon in Essex and demanded tribute from local Anglo-Saxon defenders under the elderly ealdorman Byrhtnoth. According to the Old English poem commemorating the battle, Byrhtnoth let the Vikings cross a causeway onto the mainland rather than hold the narrow crossing, an act of pride that let them fight on open ground. Byrhtnoth was killed and his forces defeated, though some retainers reportedly fought on rather than flee, embodying the heroic code the poem celebrates. The defeat contributed to England's policy of paying Danegeld to Viking raiders afterward.

entries.name: Treaty on the Creation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
entries.desc: Declaration and treaty formally establishing the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, centralising several Soviet republics under a Moscow-based federal government.

entries.name: Franco-Turkish War
entries.desc: Also known as the Cilicia Campaign, a conflict between France and Turkish nationalist forces from 1918 to 1921 in the aftermath of World War I.
entries.tldr: Also called the Cilicia Campaign, French forces occupying formerly Ottoman Cilicia after World War I clashed with Turkish nationalist militias loyal to Mustafa Kemal Atatürk from 1918 to 1921. Bitter fighting around Marash and Antep, including massacres of Armenian and Turkish civilians, wore down French resolve. France signed the 1921 Treaty of Ankara, withdrawing from Cilicia and recognizing Kemalist authority, an early diplomatic victory for the nascent Turkish republic.

entries.name: Battle of Gumbinnen
entries.desc: A hasty German offensive on the Eastern Front was repelled by the Russian Army near Gumbinnen in East Prussia, early in World War I.
entries.tldr: On 20 August 1914, a hastily organized German offensive by General Maximilian von Prittwitz's Eighth Army attacked the Russian First Army under Paul von Rennenkampf near Gumbinnen in East Prussia and was repulsed with heavy losses. The setback so unnerved Prittwitz that he considered abandoning East Prussia, prompting German command to sack him and install Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Ludendorff. Their new command team then engineered the far more famous victory at Tannenberg days later.

entries.name: Umayyad conquest of Hispania
entries.desc: Umayyad forces conquered the Visigothic Kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula, ending Christian rule across most of Iberia and establishing al-Andalus.

entries.name: Anglo-Afghan Treaty of 1919
entries.desc: Also known as the Treaty of Rawalpindi, this agreement ended the Third Anglo-Afghan War and secured Afghan control over its own foreign affairs.
entries.tldr: Signed in August 1919 at Rawalpindi, this treaty ended the brief Third Anglo-Afghan War that Emir Amanullah Khan had launched earlier that year after his father's assassination. Britain recognized Afghanistan's full independence in foreign affairs, ending restrictions from earlier Anglo-Afghan wars, and ceased its subsidy to the Afghan state. The war had been militarily inconclusive, with British air raids on Kabul shocking Afghan leaders even as ground fighting favored British India. Afghans still celebrate 19 August as Independence Day.

entries.name: Battle of Klokotnitsa
entries.desc: Bulgarian forces under Ivan Asen II crushed the Empire of Thessalonica near Klokotnitsa, restoring Bulgaria as the dominant power in southeastern Europe.
entries.tldr: Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria, provoked by the ambitions of Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Thessalonica, met and crushed the Epirote-Thessalonican army near the village of Klokotnitsa. Theodore was captured and later blinded, ending his bid to restore a Byzantine successor state as the dominant regional power. The victory let Ivan Asen annex vast territories across Macedonia, Thrace, and Albania, making the Second Bulgarian Empire the strongest state in southeastern Europe. He commemorated the triumph in an inscription boasting that he had conquered all the lands from Adrianople to Durazzo.

entries.name: Battle of Teruel
entries.desc: One of the bloodiest engagements of the Spanish Civil War, fought in brutal winter conditions as the city changed hands before falling to Nationalist forces.
entries.tldr: Fought over the winter of 1937–38 in some of the harshest conditions of the Spanish Civil War, this battle saw Republican forces capture the city of Teruel before Nationalist troops recaptured it after months of brutal urban and winter fighting. Extreme cold killed and disabled as many soldiers on both sides as combat did. The exhausting struggle drained Republican reserves and manpower just before Franco's forces launched their decisive Aragon offensive.

entries.name: Battle of the Ice
entries.desc: Alexander Nevsky's Novgorodian forces defeated the Livonian Order on the frozen Lake Peipus, halting German and Danish crusading expansion into Rus' lands.
entries.tldr: On 5 April 1242, Prince Alexander Nevsky's Novgorodian and Vladimir-Suzdal forces met the Livonian Order, a crusading military order, on the frozen surface of Lake Peipus on the border of modern Russia and Estonia. Nevsky lured the heavily armored Livonian knights onto the ice, where their formation broke down and, per tradition, portions of the ice gave way under the weight of men and horses. The defeat halted German and Danish crusading expansion into Rus' lands, and, alongside his win at the Neva, cemented Nevsky's reputation as a defender of Orthodox Rus'.

entries.name: Battle of Belleau Wood
entries.desc: American Marine and Army units, alongside French and British forces, halted the German spring offensive near the Marne River in World War I.
entries.tldr: Fought over roughly three weeks in June 1918, the battle saw United States Marine and Army units, fighting alongside the French, engage German troops in a dense forest near the Marne as part of the effort to blunt Germany's spring offensive toward Paris. Repeated frontal assaults through the woods against entrenched German machine guns produced the highest single-day casualties in Marine Corps history to that point. American forces ultimately cleared the wood, and the fight became a formative moment in Marine legend, with German reports reportedly nicknaming them devil dogs.

entries.name: Battle of Cape Esperance
entries.desc: A U.S. Navy cruiser force ambushed and defeated a Japanese squadron off Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands, part of the wider naval campaign there.
entries.tldr: Fought on the night of 11 to 12 October 1942 off Guadalcanal, the battle saw a U.S. Navy cruiser and destroyer force under Rear Admiral Norman Scott intercept a Japanese squadron attempting to bombard American positions and land reinforcements. Aided by radar and surprise, the American ships sank a Japanese cruiser and destroyer while damaging others, one of the few clear American tactical wins in the naval battles fought around Guadalcanal that year. The surrounding waters saw such intense naval combat that sailors nicknamed them Ironbottom Sound.

entries.name: Battle of Alarcos
entries.desc: Almohad forces under Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Mansur crushed the Castilian army of Alfonso VIII, forcing a Christian retreat to Toledo.
entries.tldr: In July 1195, the Almohad caliph Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Mansur crossed from North Africa with a large army to confront King Alfonso VIII of Castile, who had provoked conflict by breaking a truce. At Alarcos in central Spain, the Almohad forces crushed the Castilian army, inflicting heavy casualties and capturing the fortress town. The defeat forced Alfonso VIII to retreat to Toledo, temporarily halting the Reconquista, until Castile avenged the loss at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.

entries.name: Battle of Stallupönen
entries.desc: The opening battle of World War I's Eastern Front, in which German forces under Hermann von François defeated a larger but disorganized Russian force.
entries.tldr: On 17 August 1914, German General Hermann von François disobeyed orders to fall back and instead attacked the advancing Russian First Army under Paul von Rennenkampf near Stallupönen in East Prussia. The German forces inflicted a sharp local defeat before withdrawing as planned, and the encounter boosted German confidence in the opening days of the Eastern Front. It set the stage for the far larger German victory at Tannenberg just days later.

entries.name: Polish–Lithuanian War
entries.desc: An undeclared conflict between newly independent Lithuania and Poland fought mainly around Vilnius and Suwałki in the aftermath of World War I.
entries.tldr: Fought over Vilnius, a mostly Polish-populated city both new states claimed as their capital. Polish general Lucjan Żeligowski staged a supposed "mutiny" and seized the city in October 1920, founding the short-lived Republic of Central Lithuania that Poland soon annexed. Lithuania never recognized the loss, moved its capital to Kaunas, and froze relations with Poland for two decades. The dispute was only settled in 1939, when the Soviet Union handed Vilnius to Lithuania.

entries.name: Battle of Harran
entries.desc: A major Seljuk Turk victory over the Crusader states of Antioch and Edessa near the Mesopotamian city of Harran in 1104.
entries.tldr: In May 1104, a Seljuk Turk army decisively defeated the combined forces of the Crusader states of Antioch and Edessa near the Mesopotamian city of Harran, capturing Count Baldwin II of Edessa and his cousin Joscelin of Courtenay. The defeat shattered Crusader momentum in northern Syria and triggered a succession crisis in Antioch, which Tancred ruled as regent during Bohemond's absence. Edessa never fully recovered, and the battle marked the effective end of northern Crusader expansion.

entries.name: Ecuadorian–Peruvian War
entries.desc: A 1941 border war between Ecuador and Peru, the first of three 20th-century conflicts between the two nations.
entries.tldr: In July 1941, long-simmering border disputes between Ecuador and Peru erupted into open war after Peruvian forces invaded Ecuador's southern provinces. Peru's better-equipped military won a swift and decisive victory, occupying large stretches of Ecuadorian territory within weeks. The 1942 Rio Protocol, brokered by the United States and other American states, forced Ecuador to cede a vast swath of Amazonian territory to Peru. Ecuador long considered the settlement unjust, and the border dispute flared into renewed fighting twice more before a final peace was reached in 1998.

entries.name: Portuguese Restoration War
entries.desc: Portugal's uprising against Habsburg Spain beginning in 1640, ending the Iberian Union and restoring Portuguese independence by 1668.
entries.tldr: Began when Portuguese nobles overthrew Habsburg rule and proclaimed the Duke of Braganza King João IV, ending sixty years of dynastic union with Spain. Spain, distracted by simultaneous revolts in Catalonia and war with France, could not muster enough troops to reconquer Portugal, and fighting dragged on for decades in intermittent border campaigns. Portugal secured English and French backing along the way, and Spain finally recognized independence in the 1668 Treaty of Lisbon. The war restored Portugal's separate crown and its overseas empire.

entries.name: Battle of Bapheus
entries.desc: A decisive victory for Osman I's Ottoman forces over the Byzantines in Bithynia, marking the rise of the Ottoman state.
entries.tldr: Fought in July 1302 near Nicomedia in Bithynia, the battle pitted the small but growing forces of Turkish frontier leader Osman I against a Byzantine relief army sent by Emperor Andronikos II to shore up crumbling defenses in Anatolia. Osman's cavalry decisively defeated the Byzantines, whose line collapsed after their Alan mercenaries fled, and the victory triggered a mass exodus of Christian inhabitants from the surrounding countryside toward Byzantine-held cities. It is traditionally regarded as the founding triumph of the nascent Ottoman state, named for Osman himself.

entries.name: Battle of Leipzig
entries.desc: The largest battle of the Napoleonic Wars, in which allied Austrian, Prussian, Russian and Swedish forces decisively defeated Napoleon at Leipzig.
entries.tldr: Also called the Battle of the Nations, this four-day engagement brought together the largest armies yet assembled in the Napoleonic Wars, as Austria, Prussia, Russia, and Sweden combined against Napoleon near Leipzig. Napoleon initially held his own against the converging armies, but heavily outnumbered and low on ammunition, he was forced to withdraw. The retreat turned to disaster when a bridge over the Elster River was blown too soon, trapping thousands of French troops on the wrong bank. The defeat ended Napoleon's control of Germany, setting up the invasion of France the following year.

entries.name: Potsdam Conference
entries.desc: A meeting of Allied leaders Truman, Churchill (later Attlee), and Stalin at Potsdam to plan the postwar order after Germany's defeat.
entries.tldr: Held at a Berlin suburb in July and August 1945, bringing together Truman, Churchill (replaced mid-conference by Attlee after Labour's election win), and Stalin to decide the postwar order following Germany's defeat. The leaders agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into occupation zones, pursue denazification and demilitarization, and shift Poland's borders westward at Germany's expense. Disagreements over Eastern Europe's political future foreshadowed the coming Cold War. Truman also told Stalin, without giving details, that the US now possessed an atomic bomb.

entries.name: Battle of Moscow
entries.desc: A Soviet defensive campaign that halted the German advance on Moscow during the winter of 1941–42.
entries.tldr: Beginning in October 1941, German Army Group Center pushed to within sight of Moscow's suburbs before the onset of a brutal winter, mud, and stiffening Soviet resistance halted the advance. In December, Soviet forces under Georgy Zhukov, reinforced by fresh Siberian divisions, launched a counteroffensive that pushed German lines back and inflicted heavy losses. It was the first major strategic defeat for the Wehrmacht in the war and shattered German hopes of a quick victory over the Soviet Union. Both sides suffered enormous casualties in the freezing conditions.

entries.name: Battle of France
entries.desc: Germany's rapid invasion and defeat of France and the Low Countries in 1940, forcing the Allied evacuation at Dunkirk.
entries.tldr: Launched on 10 May 1940, Germany's invasion of France bypassed the Maginot Line by driving armored columns through the supposedly impassable Ardennes forest, splitting Allied armies and reaching the Channel within days. The rapid collapse forced the evacuation from Dunkirk and left the remaining French forces unable to mount an effective defense. France signed an armistice on 22 June 1940 in the same railway carriage used for Germany's own 1918 surrender, a deliberate humiliation ordered by Hitler.

entries.name: Great Northern War
entries.desc: A coalition led by Russia broke Swedish dominance in Northern, Central and Eastern Europe between 1700 and 1721.
entries.tldr: A coalition of Russia, Denmark-Norway, and Saxony-Poland attacked Sweden in 1700, hoping to exploit the inexperience of the teenage King Charles XII, but he won a stunning early victory at Narva against a far larger Russian force. Charles's fortunes reversed after his invasion of Russia was crushed at Poltava in 1709, and the war dragged on for over two decades. The 1721 Treaty of Nystad ended Swedish dominance in the Baltic and confirmed Russia's rise as a great European power under Peter the Great.

entries.name: Revolt of the Comuneros
entries.desc: A Castilian uprising against the rule of Charles I, at its peak controlling the cities of Valladolid, Tordesillas, and Toledo.
entries.tldr: Castilian townspeople and lesser nobles rebelled against the young King Charles I (later Emperor Charles V) over heavy taxes, foreign advisors, and fears that Castile's own interests were being subordinated to his wider Habsburg ambitions. Rebel juntas briefly governed cities including Toledo, Valladolid, and Segovia while the king was abroad. Royalist forces crushed the rebels at the Battle of Villalar in 1521, and its leaders were executed soon after. The revolt's failure cemented royal authority over Castile's cities for the rest of the Habsburg era.

entries.name: War of the Pacific
entries.desc: Chile defeated a Bolivian-Peruvian alliance over Atacama Desert resources, gaining territory from both nations.

entries.name: Operation Michael
entries.desc: The opening German offensive of the 1918 spring campaign, launched from the Hindenburg Line to break the Allied lines.
entries.tldr: Launched along the Somme front using newly developed 'stormtrooper' infiltration tactics, this was the first and largest of five German offensives in the 1918 spring campaign, aiming to break through Allied lines before American reinforcements arrived. German forces achieved the deepest advance on the Western Front since 1914, pushing the British Fifth Army back roughly 40 miles. But the advance outran its supply lines, and Allied forces stabilized the front, appointing French general Ferdinand Foch supreme Allied commander, and Germany exhausted reserves it could not replace.

entries.name: Anti-Comintern Pact
entries.desc: An anti-communist alliance between Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan, signed in Berlin and later joined by Italy and other states.
entries.tldr: Signed in Berlin in November 1936, the Anti-Comintern Pact bound Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan to cooperate against Soviet subversion, though secret protocols also pledged mutual neutrality if either fought the USSR. Fascist Italy joined a year later, and the pact eventually drew in other states aligned against communism, including Hungary and Spain. Though framed as ideological, it functioned as an early step toward the wartime Axis alliance formalized in the 1940 Tripartite Pact.

entries.name: Nine Years' War
entries.desc: A European great-power war from 1688 to 1697 pitting France against the Grand Alliance.
entries.tldr: Louis XIV's France fought a coalition known as the Grand Alliance, including England, the Dutch Republic, Spain, and the Holy Roman Empire, in a war spanning fronts from Flanders to Ireland to the Mediterranean. William of Orange's 1688 seizure of the English throne in the Glorious Revolution helped trigger the conflict by uniting England and the Dutch against French expansion under one monarch. French forces devastated the Palatinate with a scorched-earth campaign that left lasting German resentment. The 1697 Treaty of Ryswick restored prewar borders.

entries.name: Battle of Worringen
entries.desc: The decisive battle of the War of the Limburg Succession, fought near Cologne between the Archbishop of Cologne and his rivals.
entries.tldr: Fought on 5 June 1288 near Cologne, this battle was the decisive engagement of the War of the Limburg Succession, pitting the Archbishop of Cologne, Siegfried von Westerburg, and his allies against Duke John I of Brabant, who claimed the Duchy of Limburg. Brabant's forces, aided by townsmen from Cologne who resented the archbishop's rule, won a costly victory that secured Limburg for Brabant. The defeat also broke the archbishop's temporal power over Cologne, which went on to gain effective self-government as a free imperial city.

entries.name: Battle of Poltava
entries.desc: Tsar Peter I's decisive defeat of Charles XII's Swedish army, ending Sweden's status as a European great power.
entries.tldr: On 8 July 1709, Tsar Peter I's reorganized Russian army decisively defeated the invading Swedish forces of King Charles XII near Poltava in present-day Ukraine, after a failed Swedish campaign deep into Russian territory. Charles, wounded before the battle, was carried from the field and fled with the defeated remnants of his army into Ottoman exile. The catastrophic Swedish defeat ended Sweden's status as a dominant European military power and confirmed Russia's rise as a major continental force. Peter went on to found St. Petersburg and claim the title of emperor in the war's aftermath.

entries.name: Treaty of friendship and alliance between the Government of Mongolia and Tibet
entries.desc: A 1913 agreement signed at Urga between the governments of Mongolia and Tibet.

entries.name: Battle of Raseiniai
entries.desc: A major tank battle in Lithuania during the opening days of Operation Barbarossa, between German and Soviet armored forces.
entries.tldr: In the last days of June 1941, during the opening week of Operation Barbarossa, Soviet and German armored forces fought a chaotic series of engagements around Raseiniai in Lithuania, among the largest tank battles fought up to that point in the war. Soviet KV heavy tanks, whose armor German anti-tank guns could barely penetrate, caused local alarm despite the Red Army's overall disorganization. German forces ultimately encircled and destroyed the Soviet armored group, continuing their rapid advance into the Baltic states, an early sign of surprises the Wehrmacht would face later in the war.

entries.name: Locarno Treaties
entries.desc: A set of post-WWI agreements among Germany, France, Britain, Belgium, Italy, Poland and Czechoslovakia guaranteeing western European borders.
entries.tldr: Negotiated in the Swiss town of Locarno, these agreements had Germany, France, and Belgium mutually guarantee their shared borders, with Britain and Italy as guarantors, while Germany separately agreed only to arbitrate its borders with Poland and Czechoslovakia. The treaties enabled Germany's admission to the League of Nations the following year and were hailed as a new 'spirit of Locarno.' That optimism proved short-lived: Hitler repudiated the treaties in 1936 by remilitarizing the Rhineland. The asymmetric eastern borders later left Poland and Czechoslovakia exposed.

entries.name: Tripartite Pact
entries.desc: A defensive military alliance between Germany, Italy, and Japan signed in Berlin, later joined by several other Axis states.

entries.name: Battle of Crete
entries.desc: German airborne invasion of Crete in May 1941, the first major airborne invasion in military history.
entries.tldr: In May 1941, Germany launched Operation Mercury, the first large-scale airborne invasion in history, dropping paratroopers onto Crete against British, Commonwealth, and Greek defenders under General Bernard Freyberg. Ultra intercepts had given the Allies advance warning, but confusion let German forces seize the key airfield at Maleme and fly in reinforcements despite catastrophic paratrooper losses. The Allies evacuated by sea after ten days, in scenes echoing Dunkirk. German losses were so severe that Hitler later banned further large airborne operations.

entries.name: Second Battle of El Alamein
entries.desc: Allied victory in Egypt that halted the Axis advance in North Africa and marked a turning point in the desert campaign.
entries.tldr: Fought in Egypt when British Commonwealth forces under Bernard Montgomery, reinforced and resupplied after earlier setbacks, launched a set-piece offensive against Erwin Rommel's overextended Axis army. Superior numbers, artillery, and intelligence from decoded German signals let Montgomery grind through Axis defenses despite heavy casualties. Rommel, short on fuel and supplies, was forced into a long retreat across Libya that his forces never fully reversed. Churchill later called it, if not the end of the war, "the end of the beginning."

entries.name: Austro-Prussian War
entries.desc: Short war in which Prussia defeated Austria, ending Austrian dominance in Germany and paving the way for Prussian-led unification.
entries.tldr: Fought over just seven weeks in the summer of 1866, the Austro-Prussian War pitted Prussia, allied with Italy, against Austria and most other German states for supremacy within the German Confederation. Prussia's modernized army, using breech-loading rifles and railway-based mobilization devised by Helmuth von Moltke, crushed Austrian forces at the Battle of Königgrätz. Chancellor Otto von Bismarck imposed lenient peace terms to avoid lasting enmity while dissolving the Confederation and excluding Austria from German affairs.

entries.name: Battle of Tannenberg
entries.desc: Decisive German victory over the Russian army in East Prussia during the opening weeks of World War I.
entries.tldr: In late August 1914, the German Eighth Army under Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Ludendorff, aided by staff officer Max Hoffmann's use of intercepted Russian wireless signals, encircled and destroyed the Russian Second Army under Alexander Samsonov in East Prussia. Samsonov, facing the scale of the disaster, reportedly took his own life rather than report the defeat to the tsar. The German triumph, named after a nearby village to evoke an earlier medieval battle, shattered Russian offensive hopes on the Eastern Front for the rest of 1914.

entries.name: Battle of Angaur
entries.desc: U.S. Army assault on the Japanese-held island of Angaur in Palau during the Pacific War.
entries.tldr: In September 1944, U.S. Army troops of the 81st Infantry Division landed on the small island of Angaur in Palau, part of the wider campaign to secure airfields for the advance toward the Philippines. Vastly outnumbering the roughly 1,400 Japanese defenders, American forces secured most of the island within days, though a determined garrison held out in caves in the northwest for weeks longer. Nearly the entire Japanese garrison died rather than surrender, a pattern echoed in the far bloodier fighting simultaneously underway on nearby Peleliu.

entries.name: Battle of Spotsylvania Court House
entries.desc: Bloody two-week clash between Grant's and Lee's armies in Virginia during the American Civil War's Overland Campaign.
entries.tldr: Fought over nearly two weeks in May 1864 as part of Grant's Overland Campaign, this battle saw brutal, often hand-to-hand fighting between the Union and Confederate armies in Virginia, including at the notorious "Bloody Angle" salient. Neither side achieved a decisive breakthrough, but the fighting inflicted roughly 30,000 combined casualties. Rather than withdraw after the stalemate, as earlier Union commanders had, Grant continued pressing south, reflecting his strategy of relentless attrition against Lee's army.

entries.name: Hispano-Moroccan War
entries.desc: Spanish military campaign against Morocco fought around Ceuta, resulting in expanded Spanish territory in North Africa.
entries.tldr: Border clashes near the Spanish enclave of Ceuta escalated into full war in 1859 when Spain, seeking to reassert colonial prestige, invaded northern Morocco under General Leopoldo O'Donnell. Spanish forces won a costly victory at the Battle of Tetouan, occupying the city after heavy casualties from Moroccan resistance and disease. The 1860 Treaty of Wad-Ras expanded Spanish territory around Ceuta and Melilla and extracted a large indemnity, though Morocco retained its formal independence.

entries.name: Battle of Berlin
entries.desc: Final major Soviet offensive of World War II in Europe, culminating in the fall of the German capital and Hitler's suicide.
entries.tldr: Fought from mid-April to early May 1945, the Battle of Berlin was the final major offensive of World War II in Europe, as Soviet forces under Marshals Georgy Zhukov and Ivan Konev converged on the German capital from the east and south in overwhelming numbers. Fighting street by street against exhausted regulars, Volkssturm militia, and Hitler Youth, Soviet troops steadily crushed the defenders despite fierce resistance around the Reichstag. Adolf Hitler took his own life in his bunker on 30 April as Soviet troops closed in, and the garrison surrendered on 2 May.

entries.name: Munich agreement
entries.desc: Agreement by Britain, France, Germany, and Italy permitting Nazi annexation of the Sudetenland, widely seen as a failed act of appeasement.
entries.tldr: Meeting in Munich without any Czechoslovak representatives present, British prime minister Neville Chamberlain, France's Édouard Daladier, Hitler, and Mussolini agreed to let Germany annex the Sudetenland, Czechoslovakia's German-speaking border region, in exchange for Hitler's promise to seek no further territory. Chamberlain returned to London declaring he had secured 'peace for our time,' waving the signed agreement for cameras. Hitler broke the promise within six months, occupying the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939.

entries.name: Battle of Jena–Auerstedt
entries.desc: Napoleon's twin victories over Prussia that shattered the Prussian army and led to French occupation of Prussia.
entries.tldr: On 14 October 1806, Napoleon's army fought two separate engagements against Prussia on the same day, each commander unaware of the other's scale. At Jena, Napoleon personally crushed a Prussian force under Prince Hohenlohe, mistakenly believing it to be the main army. Twelve miles away at Auerstedt, Marshal Davout's single outnumbered corps unexpectedly met and shattered the true main Prussian army, mortally wounding its commander, the Duke of Brunswick. The twin disaster destroyed Prussia's military prestige and let Napoleon occupy Berlin within three weeks.

entries.name: New Zealand Wars
entries.desc: Series of conflicts between the British Crown and Māori iwi over land and sovereignty in colonial New Zealand.
entries.tldr: A series of conflicts fought across the North Island between the British Crown, supported by colonial militia, and Māori iwi resisting the sale and confiscation of their land amid rising European settlement. The wars produced the innovative Māori pā, fortified defensive works with trench and bunker systems that inflicted heavy casualties on attacking British troops, most notably at Gate Pā in 1864. Following military defeats, the colonial government confiscated millions of acres of Māori land, confiscations still contested in Treaty of Waitangi settlements today.

entries.name: Battle of Blenheim
entries.desc: Decisive Allied victory over French and Bavarian forces during the War of the Spanish Succession, fought in Bavaria.
entries.tldr: Fought on 13 August 1704 near the Bavarian village of Blindheim, anglicized as Blenheim, the battle was the decisive early clash of the War of the Spanish Succession, pitting an Allied army under John Churchill, Duke of Marlborough, and Prince Eugene of Savoy against a Franco-Bavarian force under Marshal Tallard. Marlborough's coordinated assault broke the French center after pinning its flanks, and the collapsing army suffered huge casualties and captures, including Tallard himself. Marlborough was later rewarded with the construction of Blenheim Palace, still his family's seat.

entries.name: French and Indian War
entries.desc: North American theater of the Seven Years' War, fought between Britain and France, with Native American allies, for colonial control.
entries.tldr: Fighting broke out in the Ohio Valley in 1754 when a young George Washington's Virginia militia clashed with French forces, escalating a colonial land dispute into the North American front of the global Seven Years' War. Britain's capture of Quebec in 1759 and Montreal in 1760, aided by Iroquois and other Native allies, broke French power in Canada. The 1763 Treaty of Paris ceded French Canada to Britain, reshaping North America's colonial map and setting the stage for later tensions with Britain's own colonists.

entries.name: Lapland War
entries.desc: Conflict in which Finland fought to expel German troops from Finnish Lapland after Finland's armistice with the Soviet Union.
entries.tldr: Under its 1944 armistice with the Soviet Union, Finland was obligated to expel the German troops still stationed in northern Lapland, its former co-belligerents against the USSR. The retreating Wehrmacht carried out a scorched-earth campaign, burning much of Lapland's capital, Rovaniemi, as it withdrew into occupied Norway. Fighting was intermittent and casualties far lower than in Finland's earlier wars, but the destruction left tens of thousands homeless. The war ended in April 1945 with the last German units pushed into Norway.

entries.name: Battle of Königgrätz
entries.desc: Decisive Prussian victory over Austria in Bohemia that effectively ended the Austro-Prussian War.
entries.tldr: Also known as the Battle of Sadová, this engagement pitted the Prussian army, using rapid mobilization by rail and breech-loading needle guns, against the larger Austrian army under Ludwig von Benedek in Bohemia. A late-arriving Prussian army corps struck the Austrian flank at a critical moment, turning a hard-fought battle into a rout. Austrian losses were roughly triple those of Prussia, and Vienna sued for peace within weeks. The victory confirmed Prussian military superiority and cleared the way for Prussia to unify the German states under its own leadership rather than Austria's.

entries.name: Second Schleswig War
entries.desc: War in which Prussia and Austria defeated Denmark, securing the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein for the German states.
entries.tldr: Fought after Denmark tried to fully integrate the disputed duchy of Schleswig, violating earlier international agreements and provoking Prussia and Austria, acting for the German Confederation, to invade. Prussian and Austrian forces won decisively, including at the storming of the Dybbøl fortifications, overwhelming the outnumbered Danish army. The Treaty of Vienna stripped Denmark of Schleswig, Holstein, and Lauenburg. The spoils' subsequent division between Prussia and Austria became a pretext for the Austro-Prussian War just two years later.

entries.name: Battle of Seven Pines
entries.desc: Inconclusive but bloody Civil War battle near Richmond, Virginia, notable for wounding Confederate general Joseph Johnston.
entries.tldr: Fought on 31 May and 1 June 1862 near Richmond during the Peninsula Campaign, this Civil War engagement ended inconclusively despite heavy casualties on both sides. Its lasting significance came off the battlefield: Confederate commander Joseph E. Johnston was severely wounded, and President Jefferson Davis replaced him with Robert E. Lee, who would lead the Army of Northern Virginia for the rest of the war. Also known as the Battle of Fair Oaks, it is remembered mainly as the moment that put Lee in command.

entries.name: Siege of Budapest
entries.desc: Prolonged Soviet siege that captured the Hungarian capital from German and Hungarian forces in the closing months of World War II.
entries.tldr: From late 1944 into February 1945, Soviet and Romanian forces encircled and besieged Budapest, defended by German and Hungarian troops under orders to hold at all costs. The nearly two-month siege devastated the city, destroying every bridge across the Danube and killing tens of thousands of civilians and soldiers. Fighting was especially brutal in Buda's hilltop castle district, the last pocket to fall. It ranks among the war's costliest urban battles and left Hungary under Soviet occupation for decades afterward.

entries.name: Second Battle of Kharkov
entries.desc: German victory that encircled and destroyed several Soviet armies attempting to retake Kharkiv in eastern Ukraine.
entries.tldr: Fought in eastern Ukraine when Soviet forces launched a major offensive to retake Kharkiv, only for German forces to encircle the attacking armies in a pincer movement near Barvenkovo. Hundreds of thousands of Soviet troops were killed or captured as the trap closed around them. The catastrophe left southern Soviet defenses badly weakened just as Germany launched its summer offensive toward Stalingrad and the Caucasus. It ranks among the Red Army's costliest single defeats of the war.

entries.name: Battle of Somosierra
entries.desc: Napoleon's forces broke through a Spanish mountain pass defense on the road to Madrid during the Peninsular War.
entries.tldr: On 30 November 1808, Napoleon personally ordered a squadron of his Polish light cavalry to charge directly up a narrow mountain pass into entrenched Spanish artillery batteries blocking the road to Madrid. The reckless charge, though costly, broke the Spanish defense and cleared the pass, allowing French forces to advance on the capital days later. The episode became one of the most celebrated cavalry actions of the Napoleonic Wars and cemented the reputation of Napoleon's Polish guard.

entries.name: Battle of Narva
entries.desc: Swedish victory over a much larger Russian army at the outset of the Great Northern War in Estonia.
entries.tldr: In November 1700, an outnumbered Swedish army under the young King Charles XII exploited a blinding snowstorm to rout a much larger Russian force besieging the fortress of Narva in Estonia, at the outset of the Great Northern War. Tsar Peter I, absent from the field, treated the humiliating defeat as a spur to rebuild and modernize the Russian army from the ground up. Charles's decision not to pursue the war into Russia immediately afterward is often cited as a strategic blunder. Peter's reformed forces went on to crush Charles nine years later at Poltava.

entries.name: Treaty of Rapallo
entries.desc: Agreement between Weimar Germany and Soviet Russia restoring diplomatic relations and renouncing wartime claims.
entries.tldr: Signed in April 1922 during the Genoa Economic Conference, the Treaty of Rapallo restored full diplomatic relations between Weimar Germany and Soviet Russia, both isolated by the victorious Allied powers after the First World War. Each side renounced wartime financial claims against the other and agreed to expand trade. It also opened the door to secret military collaboration, letting Germany train with arms on Soviet territory in circumvention of the disarmament limits of Versailles, which alarmed the Western Allies as a troubling alignment of two revisionist powers.

entries.name: Battle of Sedan
entries.desc: Decisive Prussian victory that captured Napoleon III and effectively ended the Franco-Prussian War.
entries.tldr: In late August and early September 1870, Prussian and allied German forces under Helmuth von Moltke encircled a French army under Marshal MacMahon, with Emperor Napoleon III present, at the fortress town of Sedan. Trapped and pounded by artillery, Napoleon III surrendered himself and roughly 100,000 troops on 2 September 1870. The humiliating capture ended the Second French Empire almost immediately, as Paris proclaimed the Third Republic within days, though the wider war dragged on.

entries.name: Jay's Treaty
entries.desc: Agreement easing lingering tensions between the United States and Great Britain after the Revolutionary War.
entries.tldr: Negotiated by Chief Justice John Jay and signed in 1794, the treaty addressed grievances lingering from the American Revolutionary War, chiefly Britain's continued occupation of forts in the Northwest Territory and disputes over wartime debts and shipping seizures. Britain agreed to withdraw from the frontier forts and grant limited American trading rights in the West Indies, though the treaty said nothing about impressment of American sailors, angering many Americans. Bitterly divisive at home, it nonetheless avoided a renewed war with Britain and bought the young republic a decade of peace.

entries.name: War of the Bavarian Succession
entries.desc: Largely bloodless conflict between Austria and Prussia over the succession to the Bavarian throne.

entries.name: Third Battle of Kharkov
entries.desc: German counteroffensive that recaptured the Ukrainian city of Kharkov after the Soviet victory at Stalingrad.
entries.tldr: In February and March 1943, following the Soviet victory at Stalingrad and a Red Army offensive that overextended its supply lines, German field marshal Erich von Manstein launched a counteroffensive that recaptured the Ukrainian city of Kharkov. The success, achieved through a mobile armored counterattack against exposed Soviet spearheads, restored a stable front and is often cited as one of the finest operational feats of the war for the German army. It cost tens of thousands of casualties on both sides. The stabilized front set the stage for the Battle of Kursk that summer.

entries.name: Northern Seven Years' War
entries.desc: Baltic conflict between Denmark-Norway and Sweden, ended by the Treaty of Stettin.
entries.tldr: Denmark-Norway and Sweden, rivals for dominance of the Baltic and its lucrative Sound tolls, fought an inconclusive war triggered partly by King Frederick II of Denmark's claim to the Swedish crown, symbolized in the 'three crowns' heraldry. Fighting ranged across southern Sweden and the Baltic Sea, with neither side able to secure a decisive advantage despite years of costly campaigning. The 1570 Treaty of Stettin restored the prewar borders essentially unchanged. The unresolved rivalry between the two Scandinavian powers erupted again within a century.

entries.name: Battle of Ulm
entries.desc: Napoleon's maneuvers forced the surrender of an Austrian army without a major battle, opening the road to Vienna.
entries.tldr: In October 1805, Napoleon's rapid and coordinated marches encircled an Austrian army under General Mack near the city of Ulm before a major battle could even develop. Cut off from supplies and reinforcement, Mack surrendered roughly 25,000 to 30,000 troops on 20 October, one of the largest bloodless capitulations of the era. The stunning maneuver opened the road to Vienna and showcased the operational brilliance that Napoleon would follow weeks later with his crushing victory at Austerlitz.

entries.name: Battle of Legnica
entries.desc: Mongol forces defeated a coalition of Polish and allied knights during the Mongol invasion of Europe.
entries.tldr: As part of the same Mongol campaign that devastated Kyiv and Hungary, a Mongol force under Baidar and Kadan swept into Poland and met a coalition of Polish, German, and allied knights led by Duke Henry II the Pious. Mongol horse archers used feigned retreats and smoke screens to disorganize the heavier European cavalry before overwhelming them. Duke Henry was killed and, according to tradition, his head was displayed on a spear outside besieged Legnica. Despite the crushing victory, the Mongols withdrew from Central Europe soon after, reportedly recalled by the death of the Great Khan Ögedei.

entries.name: Russo-Japanese War
entries.desc: Conflict between the Russian and Japanese empires over Manchuria and Korea, won decisively by Japan.
entries.tldr: Fought over rival claims to Manchuria and Korea, opening with a surprise Japanese naval attack on the Russian fleet at Port Arthur before any formal declaration of war. Japan won a string of land victories and, decisively, annihilated Russia's Baltic Fleet at Tsushima after its long voyage from Europe. The Treaty of Portsmouth, mediated by Theodore Roosevelt, recognized Japanese dominance over Korea and southern Manchuria. It was the first modern war in which an Asian power decisively defeated a European one, and the shock contributed to unrest feeding Russia's 1905 revolution.

entries.name: Treaty of Meerssen
entries.desc: Partition of the Carolingian Middle Kingdom between the East and West Frankish rulers.
entries.tldr: Signed in 870 at Meerssen, this treaty divided the Middle Kingdom of Lotharingia, the central strip of the former Carolingian Empire carved out for Emperor Lothair I's line a generation earlier, between the East and West Frankish kingdoms after Lothair II's death without a legitimate heir. West Frankish king Charles the Bald and East Frankish king Louis the German split the territory along a rough north–south line, with no claimant from Lothair II's own family receiving a share. The partition redrew borders that, in broad outline, still echo in the modern boundary between France and Germany.

entries.name: Demyansk Pocket
entries.desc: German forces encircled by the Red Army near Demyansk were resupplied by air for months during WWII.
entries.tldr: In February 1942, the Red Army encircled roughly 100,000 German troops of the II Army Corps near Demyansk in northwestern Russia, cutting them off from the main front. Rather than order a breakout, Hitler insisted the pocket hold, and the Luftwaffe sustained it for months through an unprecedented airlift of supplies. The pocket held until a land corridor was reopened in April, and the encirclement was fully relieved later that year. The apparent success wrongly convinced Hitler that airlifts could resupply a far larger encircled army at Stalingrad, with catastrophic results.

entries.name: Battle of Ramillies
entries.desc: Marlborough's victory over France secured much of the Spanish Netherlands during the War of the Spanish Succession.
entries.tldr: On 23 May 1706, the Duke of Marlborough's allied army routed French forces near the village of Ramillies in the Spanish Netherlands, exploiting superior maneuver to concentrate overwhelming strength against a weak point in the French line. The victory led to the rapid collapse of French control over most of the Spanish Netherlands, with major cities surrendering within weeks. It was among the most decisive of Marlborough's four great victories in the War of the Spanish Succession. The defeat badly damaged the prestige of Louis XIV's once-dominant army.

entries.name: First Battle of El Alamein
entries.desc: Allied forces halted the Axis advance into Egypt during the North African campaign of WWII.
entries.tldr: In July 1942, British and Commonwealth forces under General Claude Auchinleck halted the advancing Axis Panzer Army Africa, commanded by Erwin Rommel, at El Alamein in Egypt, just miles from the vital Suez Canal. Weeks of attritional fighting exhausted both sides and stopped Rommel's drive toward Alexandria and Cairo. Though inconclusive, the battle bought crucial time for the Allies to build up reinforcements and matériel in Egypt. It set the stage for the more decisive Second Battle of El Alamein months later, which turned the tide of the North African campaign.

entries.name: Battle of Kiev
entries.desc: German encirclement of Soviet forces around Kyiv produced one of the largest encirclements of WWII.
entries.tldr: In the late summer of 1941, German Army Groups South and Center converted their advance into a giant pincer around Kyiv, trapping Soviet armies that Stalin had ordered to hold the city rather than retreat. By the time the pocket collapsed in mid-September, German forces had captured over 600,000 Soviet soldiers along with vast quantities of equipment. The disaster was among the costliest encirclements in military history and devastated the Red Army's southern front. Historians still debate whether winning it cost Germany the chance to take Moscow before winter.

entries.name: Battle of Hürtgen Forest
entries.desc: Prolonged and costly Allied campaign in a forested region of Germany near the Belgian border during WWII.
entries.tldr: Fought from September to December 1944 in a dense, fortified forest near the German-Belgian border, this was one of the longest and costliest battles the US Army fought in Europe during World War II. Thick tree cover neutralized American air support and armor, while German defenders used bunkers, minefields, and artillery bursts that showered lethal wood splinters over advancing troops. Successive divisions were fed into the fighting for minimal gain, and historians have since widely criticized the campaign as unnecessary.

entries.name: Treaty of Rastatt
entries.desc: Peace agreement between France and Austria that concluded the War of the Spanish Succession.

entries.name: Potsdam Declaration
entries.desc: Allied ultimatum issued from Potsdam demanding Japan's unconditional surrender to end WWII.
entries.tldr: Issued on 26 July 1945 by the United States, Britain, and the Republic of China (the Soviet Union added its name only after later declaring war on Japan), demanding Japan's unconditional surrender. It threatened "prompt and utter destruction" if Japan refused, without revealing that an atomic bomb existed. Tokyo's ambiguous public response led the Allies to treat the ultimatum as rejected. Atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki days later, and Japan's surrender broadcast cited the declaration's terms.

entries.name: Ottoman–Safavid War
entries.desc: Conflict between the Ottoman and Safavid empires over control of Iraq and the Caucasus.
entries.tldr: The Ottoman and Safavid empires, divided by sectarian rivalry between Sunni and Shia Islam as well as territorial ambition, fought over control of Iraq and the Caucasus in the last and longest of their recurring wars. Safavid Shah Abbas I recaptured Baghdad in 1624, but the Ottomans retook it in a brutal 1638 siege under Sultan Murad IV that ended with a massacre of much of the city's Shia population. The 1639 Treaty of Zuhab that followed fixed a border still roughly tracing the modern Turkey-Iran-Iraq frontier.

entries.name: Battle of Monmouth
entries.desc: Revolutionary War battle in New Jersey where Washington's forces fought the British to a standstill, the war's last major northern engagement.
entries.tldr: Fought on 28 June 1778 in the sweltering heat of central New Jersey, this engagement pitted George Washington's Continental Army, freshly drilled at Valley Forge, against Sir Henry Clinton's withdrawing British column. General Charles Lee's confused retreat nearly turned the battle into a rout before Washington personally rallied the lines. The day ended in a tactical draw, but it proved the Continental Army could now stand toe-to-toe with British regulars in open battle. It was the last major clash of the war's northern theater.

entries.name: Battle of Mu'tah
entries.desc: Clash between an early Muslim expedition and Byzantine-allied forces near Jordan, a precursor to the Muslim conquest of the Levant.
entries.tldr: In 629, a small Muslim expeditionary force sent by Muhammad clashed with a much larger Byzantine and Ghassanid Arab army near the town of Mu'tah in modern Jordan. Three successive Muslim commanders, including Muhammad's adopted son Zayd ibn Harithah, were killed before Khalid ibn al-Walid took command and managed an orderly withdrawal. Though a military setback, the battle marked the first direct clash between the emerging Muslim state and the Byzantine Empire. It foreshadowed the far larger Muslim conquests of the Levant that followed within a decade.

entries.name: Battle of Guadalajara
entries.desc: Spanish Civil War battle in which Republican forces routed an Italian expeditionary corps sent to aid the Nationalists.
entries.tldr: Fought in March 1937 northeast of Madrid, this Spanish Civil War battle saw Republican forces, aided by International Brigades, rout an Italian expeditionary corps Mussolini had sent to help Franco's Nationalists encircle the capital. Poor coordination and determined Republican counterattacks turned the Italian advance into a chaotic retreat, with heavy losses in men and equipment. The defeat was a significant embarrassment for Fascist Italy and briefly boosted Republican morale during the defense of Madrid.

entries.name: Normandy landings
entries.desc: Allied amphibious invasion of northern France that opened the Western Front and hastened Nazi Germany's defeat.
entries.tldr: On D-Day, 6 June 1944, Allied forces under Dwight Eisenhower landed on five beaches codenamed Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword along the Normandy coast, the largest seaborne invasion in history. Elaborate deception operations had convinced German commanders the main invasion would come further north at Calais, leaving Normandy's defenses comparatively thin, though American troops still suffered heavy casualties storming Omaha Beach. Within weeks Allied forces broke out and began liberating France, opening the long-delayed Western Front.

entries.name: Swabian War
entries.desc: Conflict between the Swiss Confederacy and the Habsburgs that secured de facto Swiss independence from the Holy Roman Empire.
entries.tldr: In 1499 the Swiss Confederacy fought the Swabian League, backed by Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I, over disputed rights and long-standing tensions between the Swiss cantons and the empire. Swiss forces won a series of battles, and the brief but bloody war ended with the Peace of Basel later that year. The peace effectively released the Swiss Confederacy from imperial jurisdiction and taxation, even though full legal independence was not formally recognized until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. The war is often seen as the moment Swiss independence became a practical reality.

entries.name: Battle of the Yser
entries.desc: World War I battle in which Belgian forces flooded the Yser plain to halt the German advance along the coast.
entries.tldr: Fought from October to November 1914 along the Yser River in Belgium, this battle marked the northern end of the developing Western Front as German forces tried to break through the last stretch of unoccupied Belgian territory toward the Channel ports. Facing exhaustion and being badly outnumbered, Belgian engineers opened sluice gates to flood the low-lying Yser plain, creating a barrier that halted the German advance. The flooding froze the front line in this sector for the war, and unoccupied Belgium behind the Yser became a symbol of Belgian sovereignty.

entries.name: Battle of the Bzura
entries.desc: Largest battle of the German invasion of Poland, fought along the Bzura River as Polish forces counterattacked the advancing Wehrmacht.
entries.tldr: Fought from 9 to 19 September 1939 along the Bzura River west of Warsaw, this was the largest single battle of the German invasion of Poland, in which Polish forces under General Tadeusz Kutrzeba launched a bold counterattack against the flank of the advancing German army. The assault achieved early tactical surprise and inflicted significant casualties, but German air superiority and reinforcements gradually surrounded and crushed the Poles in the Kampinos Forest. The defeat destroyed much of the remaining Polish field army and hastened Warsaw's fall.

entries.name: Scanian War
entries.desc: War between Sweden and a coalition led by Denmark-Norway and Brandenburg over control of the Scanian provinces.
entries.tldr: Fought when Denmark-Norway, allied with Brandenburg and the Dutch Republic, tried to exploit Sweden's involvement in the wider Franco-Dutch War to reclaim the Scanian provinces lost a generation earlier. Fighting swung back and forth across southern Sweden, with the Battle of Lund among the era's bloodiest single-day engagements. French pressure on Denmark's allies eventually forced a peace that restored the prewar borders largely unchanged. Sweden kept Scania, and the province's assimilation into the Swedish state continued in the following decades.

entries.name: Battle of Lesnaya
entries.desc: Great Northern War battle in which Russian forces destroyed a Swedish relief column, weakening Charles XII ahead of Poltava.
entries.tldr: During Charles XII of Sweden's invasion of Russia, a relief column under General Lewenhaupt was bringing badly needed supplies and reinforcements to the main Swedish army when Peter the Great personally led a Russian force to intercept it near Lesnaya. After a grueling day of fighting in difficult terrain, the Swedes were routed, losing most of their supply train and thousands of men. Peter later called it the 'mother of the Poltava victory,' since the main army was left without the reinforcements it needed. That weakened force went on to suffer a decisive defeat at Poltava the following year.

entries.name: Sack of Amorium
entries.desc: Abbasid Caliphate's destruction of the Byzantine city of Amorium, one of the heaviest defeats the empire suffered.
entries.tldr: The Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim led a huge army into Byzantine Anatolia to avenge an earlier Byzantine raid and to strike at Amorium, birthplace of the reigning Byzantine dynasty. After a lengthy siege the city fell, reportedly through betrayal by a defender, and was razed with much of its population killed or enslaved. Byzantine writers treated the disaster as comparable in scale of grief to the fall of Jerusalem. Amorium never recovered its former importance, and the sack became a byword for imperial calamity.

entries.name: Act of Independence of Lithuania
entries.desc: Declaration proclaiming the restoration of an independent Lithuanian state after more than a century under Russian rule.
entries.tldr: On 16 February 1918, the Council of Lithuania signed the Act of Independence in German-occupied Vilnius, declaring the restoration of an independent Lithuanian state. The declaration came after more than a century of Russian rule, exploiting the chaos of the First World War and Tsarist collapse. German occupiers initially suppressed its publication, and Lithuania still had to fight wars of independence against Soviet, Polish, and Bermontian forces before its statehood was secured. The date is now Lithuania's Day of Restoration of the State.

entries.name: Operation Greif
entries.desc: German commando operation using English-speaking soldiers in captured American uniforms during the Battle of the Bulge.
entries.tldr: As part of the Battle of the Bulge, German commando leader Otto Skorzeny assembled English-speaking soldiers, many recruited from POW camps, and dressed them in captured American uniforms to infiltrate Allied lines, spread confusion, and seize bridges over the Meuse River. Though the unit captured few objectives, rumors of German infiltrators triggered widespread paranoia among Allied troops, who began quizzing suspected soldiers on American trivia like baseball statistics. Captured commandos were executed as spies under the laws of war for fighting out of uniform.

entries.name: Balkan Pact
entries.desc: Alliance among Greece, Romania, Turkey, and Yugoslavia intended to preserve the territorial status quo in the Balkans.
entries.tldr: Signed in Athens in February 1934, the Balkan Pact united Greece, Romania, Turkey, and Yugoslavia in a mutual guarantee of their existing Balkan frontiers against revisionist claims, particularly from Bulgaria, Hungary, and Italy. The pact reflected interwar efforts by smaller powers to build regional security as the League of Nations' collective security system weakened. It fell short of a full military alliance, and effectively dissolved once the Second World War overran the region.

entries.name: Boer Wars
entries.desc: Conflicts between the British Empire and the Boer republics over control of South Africa and its goldfields.
entries.tldr: Two conflicts, in 1880-81 and 1899-1902, pitted the British Empire against the Boer settlers of the Transvaal and Orange Free State for control of southern Africa's gold and diamond wealth. The first ended in a quick British defeat; the second was longer and bloodier, marked by guerrilla warfare and Britain's use of scorched-earth tactics and concentration camps that killed thousands of Boer civilians. British victory in 1902 absorbed the Boer republics into the empire. The wars left a legacy of Afrikaner nationalism that shaped South African politics for a century.

entries.name: Baltic Entente
entries.desc: Alliance among Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania for mutual political cooperation between the two world wars.
entries.tldr: Signed in Geneva in September 1934, the Baltic Entente formalized political cooperation among Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, states that had gained independence from the collapsing Russian Empire after the First World War. It called for regular consultation on foreign policy and mutual support in forums like the League of Nations, though it stopped short of a binding military alliance. Lithuania's territorial dispute with Poland over Vilnius limited its cohesion, and it could not stop Soviet annexation of all three states in 1940.

entries.name: Schmalkaldic War
entries.desc: War between Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and the Protestant Schmalkaldic League over religious and political control of Germany.
entries.tldr: Fought when Holy Roman Emperor Charles V moved against the Schmalkaldic League, an alliance of Protestant princes and cities that had refused to accept earlier Catholic religious settlements. Imperial and allied Catholic forces crushed the League's army at the decisive Battle of Mühlberg, capturing the Elector of Saxony in the process. Despite the victory, Charles could not permanently reverse the Reformation's spread, and Protestant princes rebelled again within a few years. The conflict ultimately led to the 1555 Peace of Augsburg, letting rulers set their own territory's religion.

entries.name: Battle of Talavera
entries.desc: Peninsular War battle in which Anglo-Spanish forces under Wellington fought Napoleon's army to a costly standstill in Spain.
entries.tldr: In late July 1809, an Anglo-Spanish army under the Duke of Wellington and General Cuesta fought two of Napoleon's marshals to a costly standstill near Talavera de la Reina in Spain. Both sides suffered heavy losses in the sweltering summer heat, and grass fires reportedly burned wounded soldiers where they lay on the field. The hard-fought stand earned Wellington his viscountcy, though supply shortages and the threat of encirclement forced the allied army to retreat into Portugal soon afterward.

entries.name: Second Sino-Japanese War
entries.desc: Major war between the Republic of China and the Empire of Japan that began in 1937 and later merged into the Pacific theatre of World War II.
entries.tldr: Erupted after the Marco Polo Bridge Incident near Beijing escalated into full-scale Japanese invasion of China, following years of tension since Japan's earlier seizure of Manchuria. Japanese forces captured major cities including Shanghai and Nanjing, where occupying troops committed mass atrocities against civilians, while China's Nationalist and Communist forces waged a costly war of attrition. The conflict merged into the wider Pacific War once Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor brought the United States into direct conflict with Japan. It was the deadliest theater of World War II in Asia.

entries.name: Armistice of 22 June 1940
entries.desc: Agreement signed at Compiègne ending the Battle of France, dividing the country into a German-occupied zone and unoccupied Vichy France.
entries.tldr: Signed on 22 June 1940 in the same railway carriage at Compiègne where Germany had accepted defeat in 1918, this armistice ended the six-week Battle of France after the rapid German blitzkrieg overran French defenses. Hitler deliberately staged the ceremony there to humiliate France and reverse the earlier armistice's symbolism. The agreement divided France into a German-occupied zone and an unoccupied southern zone run from Vichy by Marshal Philippe Pétain's collaborationist government.

entries.name: Battle of Kunersdorf
entries.desc: Decisive Austro-Russian victory over Prussia's Frederick the Great during the Seven Years' War, among his worst defeats.
entries.tldr: During the Seven Years' War, Frederick the Great attacked a combined Austrian and Russian army holding strong positions near Kunersdorf, initially breaking through and capturing enemy guns. He pressed the attack against his generals' advice, and renewed assaults against the reformed Russian center collapsed under massed artillery and cavalry counterattacks. Frederick's army disintegrated, and he reportedly considered suicide, believing Prussia's cause lost. Disagreements between the victorious commanders over how to exploit the win let Prussia survive the crisis.

entries.name: Battle of Tours
entries.desc: Frankish and Burgundian forces under Charles Martel halted an Umayyad invasion force in western France.
entries.tldr: In October 732, near the border of Frankish Aquitaine, an infantry force under Charles Martel withstood repeated cavalry charges from an Umayyad army led by Abdul Rahman Al Ghafiqi, who was killed in the fighting. The Frankish and Burgundian victory, traditionally seen as halting further large-scale Muslim expansion into western Europe, cemented Martel's power and laid the foundation for the rise of the Carolingian dynasty. Modern historians debate how decisive the battle truly was strategically, even as its symbolic importance endured for centuries.

entries.name: Battle of the Bismarck Sea
entries.desc: Allied aircraft destroyed a Japanese troop convoy bound for New Guinea, crippling Japan's ability to reinforce the Pacific front.
entries.tldr: Over 2-4 March 1943, Allied aircraft based in Australia and New Guinea attacked a Japanese convoy attempting to reinforce Lae in New Guinea, using new low-altitude 'skip bombing' tactics developed specifically to sink ships. The attacks destroyed all eight troop transports and four of the eight escorting destroyers, killing thousands of Japanese soldiers before they could reach shore. The near-total destruction of the convoy crippled Japan's ability to reinforce its forces in New Guinea by sea and marked a turning point in the Allied air campaign in the Southwest Pacific.

entries.name: Battle of Dresden
entries.desc: Napoleon's last major victory on German soil, fought against the Sixth Coalition.
entries.tldr: Fought on 26–27 August 1813 outside Dresden, this battle saw Napoleon personally command French forces to repel a much larger Allied army under Prince Karl von Schwarzenberg during the War of the Sixth Coalition. Despite being outnumbered, Napoleon exploited a cautious, poorly coordinated Allied attack to win decisively, and a stray cannonball mortally wounded the French-turned-Russian general Jean Victor Moreau as he stood beside Tsar Alexander I. It was Napoleon's last major victory of the campaign; within weeks the tide turned against him at Leipzig.

entries.name: Battle of Tinian
entries.desc: US forces captured the Mariana Islands island of Tinian from Japan; it later served as the launch site for the atomic bomb missions.
entries.tldr: In late July and early August 1944, US forces landed on Tinian in the Mariana Islands shortly after capturing neighboring Saipan, using deceptive feints and, controversially, some of the first large-scale use of napalm against Japanese defenders. The island was secured within about a week at relatively low American cost compared to other Pacific landings. Its captured airfields were later expanded to become the launch point for the B-29 bombers Enola Gay and Bockscar on their atomic bombing missions against Japan.

entries.name: Slovak–Hungarian War
entries.desc: Brief border conflict between the newly independent Slovak state and Hungary over territory in eastern Slovakia.
entries.tldr: In March 1939, days after Slovakia declared independence under German protection following the breakup of Czechoslovakia, Hungary launched an attack to seize territory in eastern Slovakia.
