The brief, roughly week-long conflict saw Hungarian forces, backed by air support, push Slovak troops back and occupy a strip of borderland. A ceasefire brokered under German pressure ended the fighting, with Hungary retaining most of the disputed territory. The episode is remembered as one of the earliest armed conflicts among the states carved from Nazi Germany's dismantling of Czechoslovakia.

entries.name: Altmark Incident
entries.desc: A British destroyer boarded the German supply ship Altmark in Norwegian waters to free Allied prisoners of war.
entries.tldr: In February 1940, the German tanker Altmark was returning to Germany through neutral Norwegian waters carrying around 300 British merchant sailors captured by the raider Admiral Graf Spee. Acting on Winston Churchill's orders, the destroyer HMS Cossack pursued the Altmark into a Norwegian fjord and boarded it, freeing the prisoners in brief hand-to-hand fighting. The incident violated Norwegian neutrality and embarrassed Norway's government, while boosting British morale during the quiet "Phoney War." It fed German suspicion that Britain might violate Norway's neutrality first.

entries.name: First Balkan War
entries.desc: Balkan League states defeated the Ottoman Empire, stripping it of nearly all its remaining European territory.
entries.tldr: In October 1912, the Balkan League, an alliance of Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, and Montenegro, launched a coordinated attack on the Ottoman Empire, exploiting its recent weakening in the Italo-Turkish War. The allies won a rapid string of victories, driving Ottoman forces out of nearly all their remaining European territory within months. The 1913 Treaty of London confirmed massive Ottoman territorial losses in the Balkans, effectively ending centuries of Ottoman rule in the region. Disputes among the victors over dividing the spoils erupted almost immediately into the Second Balkan War.

entries.name: Battle of Mohács
entries.desc: Ottoman forces crushed the Kingdom of Hungary, killing its king and opening the way for Ottoman expansion into central Europe.
entries.tldr: On 29 August 1526, Suleiman the Magnificent's Ottoman army overwhelmed the outnumbered Hungarian forces of King Louis II near the town of Mohács. Louis drowned fleeing the field, and much of the Hungarian nobility was killed, leaving the kingdom without a clear heir. The defeat led to Hungary's partition between Habsburg, Ottoman, and Transylvanian rule for over a century and a half. It remains a byword for national catastrophe in Hungarian memory.

entries.name: Treaty of Devol
entries.desc: Agreement between Bohemond I of Antioch and Byzantine Emperor Alexios I, subordinating the Principality of Antioch to Byzantium.
entries.tldr: Signed in 1108 after Byzantine forces defeated Bohemond I of Antioch's invasion of the Balkans, this treaty required Bohemond to acknowledge Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos as overlord and hold Antioch as an imperial fief. It was meant to resolve the awkward status of Antioch, a Crusader state carved from formerly Byzantine land, by subordinating it to Constantinople. In practice, Bohemond's successors ignored its terms, and Antioch kept functioning as an effectively independent crusader state.

entries.name: First Sino-Japanese War
entries.desc: War between Qing China and Meiji Japan over influence in Korea, ending in a decisive Japanese victory.
entries.tldr: Rival intervention in Korea's Donghak Peasant Rebellion pulled Qing China and Meiji Japan into open war in 1894. Japan's modernized army and navy routed Chinese forces on land and at sea, most decisively at the Battle of the Yalu River. The 1895 Treaty of Shimonoseki forced China to recognize Korean independence, cede Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula, and pay a huge indemnity, announcing Japan's arrival as a modern imperial power at China's expense.

entries.name: Battle of Shiroyama
entries.desc: Final battle of the Satsuma Rebellion in Japan, in which imperial forces crushed Saigō Takamori's samurai rebels.
entries.tldr: On 24 September 1877, the last few hundred samurai loyal to Saigō Takamori made their final stand on the hill of Shiroyama against a vastly larger imperial conscript army equipped with modern artillery. The rebels were annihilated, and Saigō himself died in the fighting, traditionally said to have been assisted to death by a retainer after being mortally wounded. The defeat crushed the Satsuma Rebellion and confirmed the supremacy of Japan's new Western-style national army over the old samurai class.

entries.name: Pontiac's War
entries.desc: A confederation of Native American tribes fought British forces across the Great Lakes region after the French and Indian War.
entries.tldr: Named for the Odawa leader Pontiac, though it was waged by an alliance of tribes angered by British policies after France's defeat, including curtailed gift-giving and settler encroachment on native land. Native forces captured most British forts west of Niagara and besieged Detroit and Fort Pitt, alarming colonial authorities. In response, London issued the Royal Proclamation of 1763, restricting colonial settlement beyond the Appalachian Mountains. That boundary later became a grievance that helped push colonists toward the American Revolution.

entries.name: French invasion of Russia
entries.desc: Napoleon's catastrophic campaign into Russia devastated the Grande Armée and marked a turning point in his downfall.
entries.tldr: Napoleon crossed into Russia in June 1812 at the head of over 400,000 troops, the largest army Europe had ever seen, intending a quick decisive battle to force Tsar Alexander I back into the Continental System. Russian forces retreated and burned Moscow rather than surrender it, and after occupying an empty, ruined city, Napoleon was forced into a disastrous winter retreat. Starvation, cold, and Cossack raids destroyed the Grande Armée, with perhaps fewer than 40,000 men returning, and the catastrophe emboldened all of Europe against him.

entries.name: Battle of Río Salado
entries.desc: Christian Castilian and Portuguese forces defeated a Marinid-Nasrid invasion, ending major Muslim offensives on the Iberian Peninsula.
entries.tldr: In October 1340, King Alfonso XI of Castile and King Afonso IV of Portugal joined forces to crush an invading army led by the Marinid sultan Abu al-Hasan Ali and the Nasrid emir of Granada near the Salado River. The Christian victory broke the last serious attempt by a North African power to reverse the Reconquista through direct invasion. Losses among the Marinid army were reportedly catastrophic, and the sultan barely escaped back to Morocco, ending large-scale African intervention in Iberian affairs.

entries.name: Battle of Kosovo
entries.desc: Clash between Serbian and Ottoman forces in Kosovo that became a foundational event in Serbian national memory.
entries.tldr: Serbian Prince Lazar led a coalition of South Slavic nobles against the invading army of Ottoman Sultan Murad I on the Field of Blackbirds. Both Lazar and Murad died in the fighting, the sultan reportedly assassinated by a Serbian knight, Miloš Obilić, who feigned surrender to reach him. The battle's outcome was militarily inconclusive, with both armies badly weakened, but it left Serbia unable to resist continued Ottoman expansion in the following decades. Kosovo became the central myth of Serbian national identity, commemorated in epic poetry and invoked in politics for centuries afterward.

entries.name: Battle of Iwo Jima
entries.desc: Brutal US Marine assault to capture the island from Japan, immortalized by the flag-raising on Mount Suribachi.
entries.tldr: American Marines invaded the fortified island in February 1945, where General Kuribayashi's garrison had abandoned beach defense for a network of tunnels and bunkers designed to bleed the attackers dry. The famous flag-raising atop Mount Suribachi came on the fifth day, but organized resistance did not end for over a month of brutal, close-quarters fighting. Nearly all 21,000 Japanese defenders died rather than surrender, while American casualties exceeded 26,000. The battle produced more Medal of Honor recipients than any other single US engagement of the war.

entries.name: Treaty of Tordesillas
entries.desc: Agreement between Spain and Portugal dividing newly discovered lands outside Europe along a meridian in the Atlantic.

entries.name: Egyptian–Wahhabi War
entries.desc: Ottoman-Egyptian campaign that crushed the First Saudi State and ended Wahhabi control of the Hejaz.
entries.tldr: Between 1811 and 1818, the Ottoman Empire's viceroy in Egypt, Muhammad Ali, dispatched armies at the sultan's request to crush the First Saudi State, whose Wahhabi forces had seized Mecca, Medina, and much of Arabia. Egyptian troops, commanded partly by his sons, eventually captured the Saudi capital of Diriyah in 1818 and razed it to the ground. The Saudi ruler was sent to Constantinople and executed, ending the first Saudi state's control of the Hejaz. The campaign marked the beginning of a cycle of Saudi state formation and collapse that repeated into the twentieth century.

entries.name: Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property
entries.desc: International treaty signed in Paris establishing the first global framework for protecting patents, trademarks, and industrial designs.
entries.tldr: Negotiated among eleven founding states meeting in Paris, this treaty established the first international framework recognizing patents, trademarks, and industrial designs across national borders, addressing inventors' growing fear of having new inventions copied abroad without recourse. Its 'right of priority' provision let an applicant who filed in one member country claim the same filing date in others within a set window. Revised several times since, the convention now has well over a hundred member states and underpins later bodies like the World Intellectual Property Organization.

entries.name: Second Balkan War
entries.desc: Bulgaria attacked its former allies over Macedonia and was defeated, losing most of its First Balkan War gains.
entries.tldr: Erupted just weeks after the First Balkan War ended, when Bulgaria, dissatisfied with its share of former Ottoman territory in Macedonia, attacked its recent allies Serbia and Greece. Romania and the Ottoman Empire joined against Bulgaria, which was rapidly overwhelmed on multiple fronts at once. The Treaty of Bucharest stripped Bulgaria of most of its earlier Balkan Wars gains and ceded Southern Dobruja to Romania. Bulgarian resentment over the loss helped shape its alliance with the Central Powers in World War I.

entries.name: Battle of Borodino
entries.desc: Bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars, fought near Moscow between Napoleon's Grande Armée and the Russian army.
entries.tldr: Fought on 7 September 1812 near Borodino, roughly 120 kilometers west of Moscow, the battle was the single bloodiest day of the Napoleonic Wars, as Napoleon's advancing Grande Armée clashed with the Russian army under General Mikhail Kutuzov in a brutal contest of massed artillery and repeated assaults on fortified positions. Neither side broke through, and combined losses ran well above 70,000 men. Kutuzov withdrew intact rather than risk annihilation, letting Napoleon occupy Moscow days later, a hollow win that failed to force Russia's surrender before the disastrous retreat.

entries.name: Ten Years' War
entries.desc: First major Cuban uprising against Spanish colonial rule, a precursor to the later Cuban War of Independence.
entries.tldr: Beginning in October 1868, Cuban planters and other rebels declared independence from Spain and launched a decade-long insurgency, the first major armed uprising against Spanish colonial rule. Guerrilla fighting spread across eastern Cuba, and rebel leaders such as Carlos Manuel de Céspedes and Máximo Gómez became early heroes of the independence movement. The war ended in 1878 with the Pact of Zanjón, which fell short of independence but promised reforms only partly kept. The conflict is remembered as the opening chapter of Cuba's struggle for independence.

entries.name: Dakota War of 1862
entries.desc: Armed conflict between the Dakota Sioux and the United States in Minnesota, ending in the mass execution of 38 Dakota men.
entries.tldr: In August 1862, facing broken treaty payments, corrupt traders, and encroaching settlement, Dakota Sioux bands in Minnesota rose up and attacked settlements and US forces along the Minnesota River. The uprising was suppressed within six weeks, and a military tribunal condemned over 300 Dakota men to death after summary trials. President Lincoln reviewed the cases and commuted most sentences, but 38 men were hanged at Mankato that December in the largest mass execution in US history. The Dakota were subsequently expelled from Minnesota entirely, their reservations abolished and lands seized.

entries.name: Georgian–Armenian War
entries.desc: Brief border war between the newly independent republics of Georgia and Armenia over disputed territories.
entries.tldr: As the Russian Empire collapsed in 1918, the newly independent republics of Georgia and Armenia went to war over the contested Lori and Borchalo districts, populated by mixed Georgian, Armenian, and other communities. Brief but sharp fighting broke out around Sadakhlo before British diplomatic pressure forced a ceasefire, since both nascent states needed to focus on graver threats from Ottoman and Bolshevik forces. A neutral zone was established, though the underlying territorial dispute went largely unresolved before both republics fell to Soviet control.

entries.name: Polish–Soviet War
entries.desc: Conflict over the borders of the newly restored Polish state, ending with Poland halting the Soviet advance at Warsaw.
entries.tldr: Fought as Poland pushed east and the Bolsheviks hoped to carry revolution into Central Europe amid the collapse of the German and Russian empires after World War I. The decisive Battle of Warsaw in August 1920, later called the "Miracle on the Vistula," saw Polish forces under Józef Piłsudski rout the advancing Red Army just outside the capital. The Soviet retreat ended hopes of exporting revolution westward and secured Poland's eastern frontier. The 1921 Treaty of Riga fixed the border until the 1939 Soviet invasion.

entries.name: Dutch Revolt
entries.desc: Revolt of the Low Countries against Spanish Habsburg rule, leading to the independence of the Dutch Republic.
entries.tldr: Beginning in 1568, the Protestant-leaning provinces of the Low Countries rose against the rule of Catholic Spain under Philip II, whose harsh religious policies and heavy taxation had provoked widespread unrest. Led initially by William the Silent, the northern provinces fought on for decades, formally declaring independence in 1581 through the Act of Abjuration. The war, later called the Eighty Years' War, dragged on until the 1648 Peace of Westphalia recognized the Dutch Republic's sovereignty. The revolt gave rise to one of early modern Europe's most prosperous and tolerant states.

entries.name: War of the First Coalition
entries.desc: First coalition of European monarchies to fight revolutionary France, ending in French territorial gains.

entries.name: Battle of Agincourt
entries.desc: Decisive English victory over a much larger French force during the Hundred Years' War.
entries.tldr: On 25 October 1415, an English army under King Henry V, exhausted and heavily outnumbered after a grueling march through Normandy, met a much larger French force near the village of Agincourt. Massed English and Welsh longbowmen, protected by narrow, muddy terrain that hampered the French knights, decimated the advancing cavalry and infantry with volleys of arrows. French casualties, including much of the nobility, vastly exceeded English losses, reviving English fortunes in the Hundred Years' War.

entries.name: Bretton Woods system
entries.desc: Post-war international monetary order agreed at a conference in New Hampshire, pegging currencies to the US dollar and gold.
entries.tldr: Delegates from 44 Allied nations met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire in July 1944 to design a postwar monetary order meant to avoid the currency chaos of the interwar years. Currencies were pegged to the US dollar, itself convertible to gold, and the conference created the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to manage the system. It underpinned two decades of stable growth in trade and reconstruction. The system collapsed in 1971 when President Nixon suspended dollar-gold convertibility, ushering in floating exchange rates.

entries.name: Battle of Halidon Hill
entries.desc: English victory over Scottish forces during the Second War of Scottish Independence.
entries.tldr: On 19 July 1333, King Edward III of England positioned his army on high ground near Halidon Hill to intercept a Scottish force under Archibald Douglas attempting to relieve his siege of Berwick-upon-Tweed. As the Scots advanced uphill through boggy ground, English and Welsh longbowmen inflicted devastating casualties before the sides even closed in melee, a tactic later refined at Crécy. The Scottish army was virtually destroyed, and Berwick surrendered soon after.

entries.name: Battles of Khalkhin Gol
entries.desc: Soviet-Mongolian victory over Japanese forces on the Mongolia-Manchuria border, ending Japanese expansion northward.
entries.tldr: In summer 1939 Japanese and Soviet-Mongolian forces clashed along the disputed Mongolia-Manchuria border, escalating from skirmishes into a full undeclared border war. Soviet commander Georgy Zhukov encircled and destroyed the Japanese 6th Army using massed tanks and artillery, a decisive Red Army victory. The defeat convinced Japan's army to abandon further expansion into Soviet Siberia and instead pursue war southward against the Western powers. A ceasefire followed within days of the fighting in Europe that opened World War II.

entries.name: First Battle of the Marne
entries.desc: Allied counteroffensive that halted the German advance into France early in the First World War.
entries.tldr: In early September 1914, French and British forces launched a desperate counteroffensive against the advancing German First and Second Armies just short of Paris, exploiting a gap that had opened between the two German forces. Paris taxi drivers famously helped ferry French reinforcements to the front, a small but symbolically potent contribution. The German advance was halted and forced into retreat to the Aisne River, ending hopes of a quick victory under the Schlieffen Plan. The battle condemned both sides to over four years of grinding trench warfare.

entries.name: First Opium War
entries.desc: Conflict between Britain and Qing China over the opium trade, ending with China ceding Hong Kong to Britain.
entries.tldr: Britain went to war after Chinese commissioner Lin Zexu confiscated and destroyed over a thousand tons of British opium at Canton to halt the drug's corrosive trade. Superior British naval firepower forced Qing China to capitulate, and the 1842 Treaty of Nanjing ceded Hong Kong to Britain, opened five treaty ports, and imposed reparations. It was the first of the 'unequal treaties' that curtailed Chinese sovereignty for a century and remains a formative grievance in modern Chinese nationalism.

entries.name: Battle of Okinawa
entries.desc: Largest amphibious assault of the Pacific War, resulting in massive casualties as Allied forces took the island of Okinawa.
entries.tldr: From April to June 1945, American forces launched the largest amphibious operation of the Pacific War against the Ryukyu island of Okinawa, a staging ground for the planned invasion of Japan. Japanese defenders fought from fortified caves and ridgelines while kamikaze aircraft struck the Allied fleet offshore, producing some of the war's heaviest naval losses. Roughly a quarter of Okinawa's civilians died alongside tens of thousands of soldiers. The staggering casualties weighed heavily on the American decision to use atomic bombs rather than invade Japan directly.

entries.name: Operation Pedestal
entries.desc: British convoy operation that fought through heavy Axis air and naval attacks to resupply besieged Malta.
entries.tldr: With Malta on the brink of starvation and surrender after two years of Axis siege and bombing, Britain assembled a heavily escorted convoy of merchant ships to force through the resupply, sailing from Gibraltar into Italian and German air and submarine attacks. Nine of fourteen merchant ships were sunk, along with an aircraft carrier and several escorts, in some of the fiercest fighting of the Mediterranean naval war. The battered tanker Ohio, kept afloat by two destroyers lashed to its sides, limped into Valletta harbor carrying vital fuel, letting Malta hold out.

entries.name: Battle of Eniwetok
entries.desc: US forces captured Eniwetok Atoll from Japanese defenders, securing a key base in the Marshall Islands.
entries.tldr: In February 1944, as part of Operation Catchpole in the Marshall Islands campaign, US Marine and Army units landed on Eniwetok Atoll to seize it from a Japanese garrison fighting from fortified bunkers and caves in close, brutal combat. The atoll fell within about a week, faster than expected after the costly earlier assault on Tarawa. Its capture gave the Navy a protected fleet anchorage closer to Japan and a staging base for further advances. Eniwetok was later used for postwar nuclear weapons testing.

entries.name: Battle of Yarmouk
entries.desc: Decisive Rashidun Caliphate victory over the Byzantine Empire that opened the Levant to Muslim conquest.
entries.tldr: Fought over six days in August 636 along the Yarmouk River on the border of modern Syria and Jordan, this battle pitted the Rashidun Caliphate's army, led by Khalid ibn al-Walid, against a much larger Byzantine force sent by Emperor Heraclius to reclaim territory lost to the early Muslim conquests. Exploiting terrain, cavalry mobility, and a sandstorm that blinded the Byzantine lines, the Muslim forces routed them, inflicting catastrophic losses. The victory permanently ended Byzantine rule over Syria and the Levant, opening the region to rapid Muslim expansion.

entries.name: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
entries.desc: Multilateral treaty signed in Geneva to reduce tariffs and promote international trade, later evolving into the WTO.
entries.tldr: Signed in Geneva in 1947 by 23 nations rebuilding a war-shattered global economy, GATT set rules to lower tariffs and curb the kind of protectionist trade wars that had deepened the Great Depression. It operated through repeated negotiating 'rounds,' most significantly the Uruguay Round, which cut tariffs dramatically over decades and extended rules to services and intellectual property. In 1995 GATT's functions were absorbed into the newly created World Trade Organization, which still administers most of its original text.

entries.name: Anglo-Nepalese War
entries.desc: Conflict between the British East India Company and the Gurkha Kingdom of Nepal that redrew the Himalayan frontier.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1814 to 1816, the Anglo-Nepalese War pitted the British East India Company against the expanding Gurkha Kingdom of Nepal over disputed lowland territory along their shared frontier. Nepalese troops, though heavily outnumbered, fought with skill that deeply impressed British officers, particularly kukri-wielding hill soldiers. The war ended with the Treaty of Sugauli, under which Nepal ceded roughly a third of its territory, including Sikkim and parts of the Terai, while keeping its independence. It began a long tradition of Gurkha service in British forces.

entries.name: Ingrian War
entries.desc: Swedish-Russian conflict over control of Ingria and northwestern Russia during Russia's Time of Troubles.
entries.tldr: Sweden intervened in Russia's chaotic Time of Troubles in 1610, initially as an ally against Polish-backed pretenders, but the alliance collapsed and Swedish forces instead seized the region of Ingria and the city of Novgorod. Fighting dragged on for years amid Russia's internal turmoil until a new tsar, Michael Romanov, was able to negotiate peace. The 1617 Treaty of Stolbovo ceded Ingria to Sweden, cutting Russia off from the Baltic Sea for nearly a century until Peter the Great reversed the loss.

entries.name: Livonian Crusade
entries.desc: Baltic campaigns by German and Danish crusaders to conquer and Christianize the pagan peoples of Livonia and Estonia.
entries.tldr: Sanctioned by successive popes, this series of campaigns by German crusading orders, chiefly the Livonian Brothers of the Sword and later the Teutonic Knights, together with Danish forces, sought to conquer and Christianize the pagan Baltic peoples of Livonia, Estonia, and Courland. Bishop Albert of Riga, who founded that city in 1201, became a central organizer, and the Sword Brothers were founded to garrison conquered land. Resistance was fierce, including the 1236 Battle of Saule, where the Sword Brothers were nearly annihilated. By 1290 the last Baltic tribes had been subdued.

entries.name: Battle of Dyrrhachium
entries.desc: Norman victory over the Byzantine Empire on the Adriatic coast that opened Robert Guiscard's campaign into the Balkans.
entries.tldr: On 18 October 1081, Norman forces under Robert Guiscard defeated a Byzantine army led by Emperor Alexios I Komnenos outside the Adriatic port of Dyrrhachium, after the elite Varangian Guard, many of them English exiles, was lured into a fatal pursuit. The emperor's daughter Anna Komnene later gave a detailed account of the battle in her Alexiad. The victory let the Normans open a campaign deep into the Byzantine Balkans, though troubles in Italy eventually forced Guiscard to abandon it.

entries.name: Akkerman Convention
entries.desc: Treaty between the Russian and Ottoman Empires settling disputes over Serbia and the Danubian Principalities.
entries.tldr: Signed in October 1826 in the Bessarabian town of Akkerman, this convention between the Russian and Ottoman empires resolved disputes left unsettled by the 1812 Treaty of Bucharest. It confirmed Serbia's autonomy under Ottoman suzerainty and expanded Russian influence over the Danubian Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia. Russia extracted the concessions under threat of renewed war while the Ottomans were busy suppressing the Greek War of Independence. It failed to prevent a fresh Russo-Turkish war two years later.

entries.name: Battle of Megiddo
entries.desc: Decisive British-led offensive in Palestine that shattered Ottoman forces and hastened the empire's collapse.
entries.tldr: In September 1918, General Edmund Allenby's Egyptian Expeditionary Force broke through Ottoman lines in Palestine near the biblical site of Megiddo (Armageddon). British cavalry exploited the breach to encircle and destroy two Ottoman armies within days. The rout opened the road to Damascus and Aleppo, effectively ending Ottoman resistance in the region. Historians view it as one of the last great cavalry victories and a major step toward the Ottoman Empire's surrender weeks later.

entries.name: Battle of Manzikert
entries.desc: Seljuk victory over the Byzantine Empire that opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement.
entries.tldr: Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes led an army into eastern Anatolia to confront the Seljuk Turks under Sultan Alp Arslan, who had raided Byzantine land for years. The premature withdrawal of key reserve units, amid rivalries in the imperial camp, left Romanos isolated and defeated, and he was captured. Alp Arslan treated him with magnanimity and released him under a peace deal, but Romanos was overthrown and blinded by rivals upon returning to Constantinople. The battle opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement, marking the start of Byzantine decline in the east.

entries.name: Battle of Jaffa
entries.desc: Richard the Lionheart's defense of Jaffa against Saladin during the Third Crusade.
entries.tldr: Late in the Third Crusade, Saladin's forces seized Jaffa by surprise, but Richard the Lionheart landed by ship with a small company and stormed the beach to retake the city almost at once. Days later Saladin counterattacked in force while most of Richard's army was unprepared; Richard arrayed his knights and crossbowmen in a tight defensive line on open ground and repelled repeated cavalry charges, reportedly riding out alone to challenge Saladin's champions. The costly stand held the city and helped push both leaders toward the truce that ended the crusade soon after.

entries.name: Battle of Vienna
entries.desc: Coalition victory that broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna and halted Ottoman expansion into Central Europe.
entries.tldr: In September 1683 a Polish-Habsburg relief army under King Jan III Sobieski broke a two-month Ottoman siege of Vienna led by Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha. Sobieski personally led a massed cavalry charge, the Polish winged hussars, down the Kahlenberg slopes into the exhausted Ottoman lines. The rout ended the last serious Ottoman attempt to conquer Central Europe and triggered the Holy League's counteroffensive that pushed the Ottomans out of Hungary in the years after. Vienna's relief is often cited as the high-water mark of Ottoman expansion into Europe.

entries.name: Armenian–Azerbaijani War
entries.desc: Territorial conflict between the newly independent Armenian and Azerbaijani republics after the Russian Empire's collapse.
entries.tldr: After the Russian Empire's collapse in 1917–1918, the newly independent Democratic Republic of Armenia and Azerbaijan Democratic Republic fought over contested, ethnically mixed territories including Nagorno-Karabakh, Nakhchivan, and Zangezur. Both fledgling states waged intermittent fighting alongside massacres of civilians on both sides between 1918 and 1920. The conflict ended only when the Soviet Red Army invaded and absorbed both republics, imposing borders that left unresolved grievances over Karabakh.

entries.name: Battle of Poitiers
entries.desc: Major English victory during the Hundred Years' War in which King John II of France was captured.
entries.tldr: On 19 September 1356, an English and Gascon army under Edward, the Black Prince, defeated a much larger French force near Poitiers during the Hundred Years' War, capturing King John II of France along with much of his nobility. English longbowmen and dismounted men-at-arms exploited the terrain to break repeated French cavalry and infantry assaults. John's costly ransom and captivity plunged France into political crisis and popular revolt, including the Jacquerie peasant uprising. The battle stands alongside Crécy and Agincourt as one of the three great English victories of the war.

entries.name: Night attack at Târgoviște
entries.desc: Surprise nighttime assault by Vlad the Impaler on the Ottoman army encamped in Wallachia.
entries.tldr: Vlad III of Wallachia, later known as Vlad the Impaler and the historical basis for Dracula, led a small force in a surprise nighttime raid on the vastly larger Ottoman army of Sultan Mehmed II encamped near his capital, Târgoviște. Vlad's men, disguised in Ottoman dress, penetrated deep into the camp seeking to kill the sultan before being repulsed with heavy losses on both sides. Though the raid failed, it inflicted serious casualties and shook Ottoman morale. Vlad later impaled thousands of captured soldiers along the road to Târgoviște, reportedly unnerving Mehmed's army into retreat.

entries.name: Operation Faustschlag
entries.desc: German offensive against Soviet Russia that forced the Bolsheviks to accept the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk.
entries.tldr: Also known as the 'Eleven Days' War,' this German and Austro-Hungarian offensive resumed hostilities against Soviet Russia after peace talks at Brest-Litovsk stalled, advancing rapidly as the demoralized, largely disbanded Russian army offered little resistance. German forces covered vast distances in days, reaching close to Petrograd before Lenin's government, fearing the capital's fall, accepted harsher terms than initially offered. The resulting Treaty of Brest-Litovsk stripped Soviet Russia of Ukraine, the Baltic states, Finland, and other populous, industrial territory.

entries.name: Battle of Chains
entries.desc: Early Rashidun victory under Khalid ibn al-Walid over Sasanian forces in Mesopotamia.
entries.tldr: Fought in 633 CE in lower Mesopotamia, the battle was among the earliest engagements of the Muslim conquest of Persia, as the Rashidun general Khalid ibn al-Walid led an Arab army against Sasanian Persian forces defending the frontier near the Euphrates. Tradition holds the battle's name comes from the Persian practice of chaining soldiers together in ranks to prevent retreat, a tactic that instead trapped many defenders when their lines broke. Khalid's decisive victory opened the path for further Muslim advances that steadily eroded Persian control of Mesopotamia.

entries.name: Battle of Stamford Bridge
entries.desc: King Harold II's victory over Norwegian invaders in England, ending Viking claims to the English throne.
entries.tldr: On 25 September 1066, King Harold II of England force-marched his army north and caught the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada, allied with Harold's exiled brother Tostig, by surprise near York. The Norwegian invaders, many without their armor, were routed and both Hardrada and Tostig were killed, effectively ending Viking claims to the English throne. The victory came at a heavy cost, though: Harold's exhausted army then had to march south to face William of Normandy's invasion at Hastings just weeks later.

entries.name: Battle of Plassey
entries.desc: British East India Company victory over the Nawab of Bengal that established British colonial control in India.
entries.tldr: On 23 June 1757, Robert Clive's East India Company force defeated the much larger army of Siraj ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal, largely because Clive had secretly bribed the Nawab's commander, Mir Jafar, to hold his troops back. The victory, achieved with relatively few casualties, delivered Bengal's vast wealth and administration into Company hands and installed the pliant Mir Jafar as puppet ruler. It marked the true beginning of British territorial rule in India, transforming a trading company into a colonial power that would soon rule much of the subcontinent.

entries.name: Battle of Hannut
entries.desc: A major tank battle in Belgium during the German invasion of the Low Countries, one of the largest armored clashes of the early war.
entries.tldr: Fought on 12–13 May 1940 in Belgium, this clash between the French Cavalry Corps under General René Prioux and two German panzer divisions was, at the time, the largest tank battle in history. French Somua and Hotchkiss tanks inflicted heavier losses on the German armor and arguably won on tactical terms, buying time for Allied forces further west. The engagement proved strategically irrelevant, though, since the main German thrust drove through the lightly defended Ardennes further south.

entries.name: Italo-Turkish War
entries.desc: Italy seized the Ottoman provinces of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, forming the colony of Libya and marking the first military use of aircraft.
entries.tldr: Italy invaded the Ottoman provinces of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica in 1911, seeking colonial territory in North Africa to match other European powers, and quickly seized the coastal cities. Fierce local resistance from Arab and Ottoman forces confined Italian control largely to the coast for much of the war, while the conflict became historically notable as the first in which aircraft were used for reconnaissance and bombing. The 1912 Treaty of Ouchy ceded the provinces to Italy, which merged them into the colony of Libya.

entries.name: Battle of Wuhan
entries.desc: One of the largest battles of the Second Sino-Japanese War, fought over the strategic tri-city area of Wuhan in central China.
entries.tldr: Fought between June and October 1938, this months-long campaign was one of the largest engagements of the Second Sino-Japanese War, as Japanese forces pushed to capture the strategic tri-city industrial and transport hub of Wuhan in central China. Chinese Nationalist forces under Chiang Kai-shek mounted a prolonged defense that inflicted heavy Japanese casualties and bought time to relocate industry and government further inland to Chongqing. Although Wuhan ultimately fell, the drawn-out fighting exhausted Japan's offensive momentum and shifted the war into a grinding stalemate.

entries.name: Battle of Tampere
entries.desc: A decisive battle of the Finnish Civil War in which White forces captured the Red stronghold of Tampere.
entries.tldr: In March and April 1918, White Guard forces under Carl Gustaf Mannerheim laid siege to Tampere, an industrial stronghold held by Finland's Red Guards during the country's brief but bloody civil war. After weeks of intense street fighting, the city fell to the Whites, breaking the back of Red resistance in western Finland. It remains one of the deadliest single engagements of the Finnish Civil War and marked a decisive turning point toward the White side's eventual victory.

entries.name: Kellogg-Briand pact
entries.desc: An international agreement, signed in Paris, in which signatory states renounced war as an instrument of national policy.
entries.tldr: Negotiated by US Secretary of State Frank Kellogg and French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand, the pact bound its signatories to renounce war as a tool of national policy and settle disputes peacefully. Sixty-two nations eventually signed, including Germany, Japan, and Italy, all of whom later broke it. It had no enforcement mechanism, and Japan's 1931 invasion of Manchuria exposed its limits within a few years. Even so, its language later underpinned the postwar prosecution of 'crimes against peace' at Nuremberg.

entries.name: Battle of Breitenfeld
entries.desc: A decisive Swedish and Saxon victory over Catholic League forces during the Thirty Years' War, marking Sweden's emergence as a major power.
entries.tldr: Fought on 17 September 1631 near Leipzig, the battle marked a turning point in the Thirty Years' War as the Protestant army of King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, allied with Saxon forces, decisively defeated the Catholic League army under Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly. Gustavus Adolphus's flexible infantry formations and mobile artillery overcame the collapse of the inexperienced Saxon wing to rout Tilly's veterans. Sweden's first major battle on German soil shattered the Catholic League's reputation for invincibility and opened much of Germany to Swedish advance.

entries.name: Battle of the Little Bighorn
entries.desc: Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho forces led by Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull annihilated Custer's 7th Cavalry detachment in Montana.
entries.tldr: On 25-26 June 1876, in Montana Territory, a coalition of Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors led by Crazy Horse, with the holy man Sitting Bull also present in the encampment, annihilated a detachment of the U.S. 7th Cavalry commanded by Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer. Custer had split his regiment and attacked the vastly larger encampment without adequate reconnaissance, and his roughly 210-man battalion was wiped out. The stunning defeat, called 'Custer's Last Stand,' shocked the public and led to a campaign that forced most Plains tribes to surrender.

entries.name: Battle of the Bridge
entries.desc: A rare early defeat for the Rashidun Caliphate's forces, routed by a Sasanian army after crossing the Euphrates on a pontoon bridge.
entries.tldr: Fought in November 634 near the Euphrates during the early Rashidun conquest of Iraq, this battle saw a Muslim army under Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi cross the river on a hastily built pontoon bridge to attack a Sasanian Persian force reinforced by war elephants. When the elephants panicked the Muslim cavalry and Abu Ubayd was killed, the retreating soldiers found the bridge cut or overwhelmed, and many drowned trying to flee back across the river. The defeat, a rare setback for the conquests, was avenged the next year at the Battle of Buwaib.

entries.name: French Revolutionary Wars
entries.desc: A series of conflicts between Revolutionary France and a coalition of European monarchies seeking to contain and reverse the Revolution.
entries.tldr: From 1792, Austria and Prussia led a coalition of monarchies seeking to crush the French Revolution and restore Louis XVI's full authority, fearing revolutionary ideas would spread across their own borders. Revolutionary France's citizen armies, mobilized through the levée en masse, held off and then reversed the invasions, carrying the war into the Low Countries, Italy, and the Rhineland. The conflict merged almost seamlessly into the Napoleonic Wars once Napoleon Bonaparte rose to power in 1799.

entries.name: Siege of Fort William Henry
entries.desc: French and Native American forces besieged and captured a British fort in colonial New York during the French and Indian War.
entries.tldr: In August 1757, during the French and Indian War, a French force under the Marquis de Montcalm, joined by allied Native American warriors, besieged the British-held Fort William Henry on Lake George. After days of bombardment the outnumbered garrison surrendered on terms allowing safe withdrawal. Despite this, Native American allies of the French attacked the retreating column, killing and capturing dozens of soldiers and civilians in an episode later notorious as a massacre. The siege and its aftermath were dramatized in James Fenimore Cooper's The Last of the Mohicans.

entries.name: Lazic War
entries.desc: A protracted conflict between the Byzantine and Sasanian empires for control of Lazica, on the eastern Black Sea coast.
entries.tldr: Also called the Roman-Persian War of 541-562, this protracted conflict pitted the Byzantine Empire against the Sasanian Empire for control of Lazica, a kingdom on the eastern Black Sea coast valued for its trade routes. Control of the region's fortresses, especially Petra, changed hands repeatedly through sieges and naval actions. Both sides courted Lazic nobility, whose loyalties shifted with the fortunes of war. The conflict ended with the 562 Fifty-Year Peace, which left Lazica under Byzantine influence in exchange for tribute to Persia.

entries.name: Battle of Dunkirk
entries.desc: German forces trapped Allied troops on the French coast, prompting a large-scale evacuation across the English Channel.
entries.tldr: In late May and early June 1940, German panzer divisions pushed British and French forces back to the Channel port of Dunkirk during the Battle of France, threatening to trap the entire British Expeditionary Force. A controversial German halt order and fierce Allied rearguard resistance bought time for Operation Dynamo, in which destroyers and civilian 'little ships' ferried roughly 338,000 troops to England. Though a military defeat with vast equipment losses, the rescue was recast in Britain as a defiant 'Dunkirk spirit' that stiffened resolve to keep fighting.

entries.name: Battle of Mactan
entries.desc: Filipino chieftain Lapu-Lapu's warriors repelled a Spanish expedition and killed explorer Ferdinand Magellan on Mactan Island.
entries.tldr: Ferdinand Magellan, having reached the Philippines during his circumnavigation voyage for Spain, allied with a local ruler and sought to compel the chieftain Lapu-Lapu of Mactan Island to submit and pay tribute. When Lapu-Lapu refused, Magellan led a small landing party ashore, but coral reefs kept his ships from close support and Lapu-Lapu's warriors vastly outnumbered them. Magellan was killed in the fighting, struck down as his men were forced to retreat. The battle is celebrated in the Philippines as an early act of resistance to colonization, and Lapu-Lapu is honored as a national hero.

entries.name: Mongol invasions and conquests
entries.desc: Beginning under Genghis Khan in Mongolia, Mongol armies built the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching across Asia and into Europe.
entries.tldr: Genghis Khan unified the Mongol and Turkic tribes of the steppe in 1206 and turned their cavalry outward, beginning campaigns his sons and grandsons continued for over a century. At its height the resulting empire stretched from Korea and China to Poland and the Middle East, the largest contiguous land empire ever assembled, moving people, goods, and ideas across Eurasia via the 'Pax Mongolica.' The conquests were also extraordinarily destructive: parts of Iran and Iraq suffered population collapse from massacre and ruined irrigation. The empire later fractured into successor khanates.

entries.name: Eighth Russo-Turkish War
entries.desc: A war between the Russian and Ottoman empires over Balkan and Black Sea territories, ending with the Treaty of Bucharest.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1806 to 1812, this war pitted the Russian Empire against the Ottomans over control of the Danubian Principalities and influence in the Balkans, complicated by the wider Napoleonic Wars raging in Europe. Russian forces under Mikhail Kutuzov eventually won a decisive campaign in 1811, forcing the Ottomans to negotiate. The 1812 Treaty of Bucharest ceded Bessarabia to Russia, just weeks before Napoleon's invasion, freeing Russian troops to face the French. The territorial gain gave Russia a lasting foothold on the lower Danube.

entries.name: Battle of Ankara
entries.desc: Timur's forces decisively defeated and captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, plunging the Ottoman Empire into a period of civil war.
entries.tldr: On 20 July 1402, the Central Asian conqueror Timur led his army against the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I near Ankara, a clash between two rival powers seeking regional dominance. Bayezid's forces, weakened by defections from resentful Anatolian vassals, were encircled and shattered, and the sultan was captured, reportedly dying in captivity within a year. The catastrophe threw the young Ottoman state into a decade-long civil war among Bayezid's sons. Timur, uninterested in permanent conquest, withdrew eastward, unintentionally giving the Ottomans time to recover.

entries.name: Battle of Kulikovo
entries.desc: A coalition of Russian principalities led by Dmitri Donskoi defeated the Golden Horde, a turning point in Russian resistance to Mongol rule.
entries.tldr: Grand Prince Dmitri of Moscow assembled a coalition of Russian princes to confront Mamai, the warlord who controlled the western Golden Horde, on the Kulikovo field near the Don. Russian forces held off repeated Mongol-Tatar assaults before a hidden reserve regiment struck the exposed flank and routed Mamai's army. Though the Golden Horde would reassert dominance within two years under a rival khan, the victory shattered the myth of Mongol invincibility. Dmitri earned the epithet 'Donskoi,' and the battle became a founding legend of Russian resistance to foreign rule.

entries.name: Montevideo Convention
entries.desc: A treaty signed in Montevideo, Uruguay, codifying the widely cited criteria for statehood in international law.
entries.tldr: Signed at the Seventh International Conference of American States in Montevideo, Uruguay, this treaty set out the four-part definition of statehood still cited today: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter relations with other states. It also codified the 'declarative theory' of recognition, holding that a state's existence does not depend on other states recognizing it, aimed partly at protecting smaller Latin American nations. Its criteria still shape debates over Taiwan, Kosovo, and Somaliland.

entries.name: Sykes–Picot Agreement
entries.desc: A secret Anglo-French agreement that divided the Ottoman Empire's Arab provinces into spheres of influence, shaping the modern Middle East.
entries.tldr: Negotiated secretly in 1916 by British diplomat Mark Sykes and French diplomat François Georges-Picot, this agreement carved the Ottoman Empire's Arab territories into future British and French zones, anticipating an Ottoman defeat in the First World War. It was drawn up even as Britain was encouraging Arab revolt with promises of independence, a contradiction that fueled resentment once terms became public after the Russian Revolution. Its borders shaped the later British and French mandates over Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, and Palestine.

entries.name: Battle of Nicopolis
entries.desc: An Ottoman army under Bayezid I crushed a large European crusading force near the Danube, ending hopes of relieving Christian rule in the Balkans.
entries.tldr: In September 1396, an Ottoman army under Sultan Bayezid I annihilated a large coalition of Hungarian, French, Burgundian, and other European crusaders besieging the Danube fortress of Nicopolis. Overconfident French knights charged prematurely against Ottoman lines, breaking the coalition's cohesion and leading to a rout; many captured knights were executed in reprisal for earlier massacres of prisoners. The disaster ended the last major crusading effort to check Ottoman expansion into the Balkans for a generation, leaving southeastern Europe increasingly exposed to Ottoman power.

entries.name: War of the Polish Succession
entries.desc: A European conflict over the Polish throne, fought mainly in Italy and the Rhineland, pitting France and Spain against Austria and Russia.

entries.name: Philippine–American War
entries.desc: An armed conflict between the First Philippine Republic and the United States following the Spanish-American War, resulting in American colonial rule of the islands.
entries.tldr: Filipino revolutionaries under Emilio Aguinaldo, who had declared independence after Spain's defeat, found themselves fighting their former ally the United States after Washington opted to annex the islands rather than recognize Philippine sovereignty. Conventional battles gave way to a brutal guerrilla insurgency, met by American tactics including forced relocation into 'zones' and reprisal campaigns such as the one on Samar following the Balangiga massacre. Aguinaldo's 1901 capture effectively ended organized resistance, though the islands stayed under US rule until 1946.

entries.name: Turkish Abductions
entries.desc: Barbary corsairs from North Africa raided Iceland, killing dozens and carrying several hundred captives into slavery in Algiers.

entries.name: Second Boer War
entries.desc: A war between the British Empire and the Boer republics of the Transvaal and Orange Free State for control of southern Africa's goldfields.
entries.tldr: Fought between Britain and the Boer republics of the Transvaal and Orange Free State after tensions over British "Uitlander" migrants and control of the region's gold mines came to a head. Early Boer successes gave way to British numerical superiority, and after occupying the Boer capitals, British forces still faced years of stubborn guerrilla resistance. Britain's response included scorched-earth tactics and concentration camps in which many Boer civilians died of disease, drawing international criticism. The 1902 Treaty of Vereeniging ended Boer independence.

entries.name: Union of Utrecht
entries.desc: An alliance of northern Dutch provinces against Spanish rule that laid the constitutional foundation for the Dutch Republic.

entries.name: Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works
entries.desc: An international agreement establishing mutual recognition of copyright between signatory nations, negotiated in Berne, Switzerland.
entries.tldr: Signed in Berne, Switzerland in 1886, the convention created the first international framework for copyright, requiring signatory nations to automatically recognize the copyrights of works from other member countries. It established minimum protection terms, most notably life of the author plus fifty years, without requiring formal registration. The United States was a notable holdout, only joining in 1989 over a century later. Administered today by the World Intellectual Property Organization, it remains the foundation of modern international copyright law.

entries.name: Marco Polo Bridge incident
entries.desc: A clash between Chinese and Japanese troops near Beijing that escalated into full-scale war between China and Japan.
entries.tldr: During night exercises near the Marco Polo Bridge outside Beijing, Japanese troops garrisoned there under a prior treaty exchanged fire with Chinese forces after a soldier went briefly missing, an incident Japanese commanders used to demand further concessions. When Chinese Nationalist forces refused to back down, skirmishing escalated within weeks into full mobilization on both sides. The clash marked the start of the Second Sino-Japanese War, which killed millions and eventually merged into the Pacific theater of World War II.

entries.name: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
entries.desc: A coalition of Christian Iberian kingdoms decisively defeated the Almohad Caliphate, a turning point in the Reconquista.
entries.tldr: Pope Innocent III proclaimed a crusade uniting the rival Christian kingdoms of Castile, Aragon, Navarre, and Portugal against the Almohad Caliphate, whose army held a strong mountain position guarding the pass into Andalusia. A local shepherd is said to have shown the Christian army a hidden route around the Almohad defenses, allowing a surprise attack that broke their lines after fierce fighting. The Almohad army's collapse opened southern Spain to Christian conquest over the following decades. The battle is remembered as the decisive turning point of the centuries-long Reconquista.

entries.name: Soviet–Japanese War
entries.desc: The Soviet Union's invasion of Japanese-held Manchuria, Korea, and the Kuril Islands in the final days of World War II.
entries.tldr: In August 1945, days after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and honoring a promise made at Yalta, the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and launched a massive offensive into Japanese-held Manchuria, Korea, and the Kuril Islands. Soviet forces rapidly overran the Japanese Kwantung Army, weakened by years of drawing troops for the Pacific war. The invasion, alongside the atomic bombings, contributed to Japan's decision to surrender within days. Soviet occupation of the Kurils and southern Sakhalin from this campaign remains a territorial dispute with Japan today.

entries.name: First Battle of Bull Run
entries.desc: The first major land battle of the American Civil War, ending in a Confederate victory near Manassas, Virginia.
entries.tldr: Fought on 21 July 1861 near Manassas, Virginia, this was the first major land battle of the American Civil War, drawing crowds of spectators from Washington who expected a quick Union victory. Union forces initially pushed Confederate lines back but were routed after Confederate reinforcements arrived and Thomas Jackson earned his nickname 'Stonewall' holding the line. The chaotic Union retreat toward Washington shattered illusions of a short war on both sides. The battle prompted the Union to begin building a much larger, better-trained army for a longer conflict.

entries.name: Treaty of the Pyrenees
entries.desc: A peace treaty ending the Franco-Spanish War and establishing the modern border between France and Spain along the Pyrenees.

entries.name: Battle of the Ardennes
entries.desc: An early clash of World War I in which French and German armies fought inconclusively in the forested Ardennes region.
entries.tldr: Fought from 21 to 23 August 1914 as part of the wider Battle of the Frontiers, French and German armies clashed in the densely forested Ardennes region in an early, chaotic engagement of the First World War. French commanders, following an aggressive doctrine of offensive a outrance, launched attacks into terrain that badly favored the entrenched, artillery-supported German defenders, resulting in heavy French casualties for little gain. The defeat, alongside setbacks elsewhere, forced a broader French retreat and hastened the war's shift toward static trench warfare.

entries.name: War of the Quadruple Alliance
entries.desc: Britain, France, Austria, and the Dutch Republic united to check Spanish expansion in Italy under Cardinal Alberoni's foreign policy.

entries.name: Brusilov Offensive
entries.desc: A massive Russian offensive against Austro-Hungarian forces on the Eastern Front, one of the most successful Allied operations of World War I.
entries.tldr: Launched in June 1916 by Russian general Aleksei Brusilov, the offensive struck Austro-Hungarian lines in Galicia using shock-troop tactics that anticipated later infiltration warfare. It broke through so completely that Austria-Hungary's army nearly collapsed, forcing Germany to divert reserves from Verdun to shore up its ally. Russian gains eventually stalled from exhausted supply lines and casualties numbering well over a million on both sides. The offensive's cost helped fuel the unrest that led to revolution in Russia the following year.

entries.name: Battle of Bosworth Field
entries.desc: Henry Tudor defeated and killed Richard III, ending the Wars of the Roses and founding the Tudor dynasty.
entries.tldr: Fought on 22 August 1485 in Leicestershire, the battle brought the Wars of the Roses to a decisive end when the Lancastrian claimant Henry Tudor, landing in Wales with a small mercenary force, defeated the Yorkist king Richard III. The battle turned when Lord Stanley and his brother, who had held back while the outcome hung in balance, intervened for Henry, and Richard was killed making a desperate cavalry charge directly at him, the last English king to die in battle. Henry was crowned on the field, founding the Tudor dynasty.

entries.name: Battle of Bannockburn
entries.desc: Robert the Bruce's Scottish forces decisively defeated the English army of Edward II, securing Scottish independence.
entries.tldr: Fought over 23 and 24 June 1314 near Stirling Castle, the battle was the decisive clash of the First War of Scottish Independence, pitting Robert the Bruce's army against a much larger English force under King Edward II sent to relieve the besieged castle. Bruce's disciplined schiltrons of spearmen, aided by ground that hampered English cavalry, broke the advance and drove Edward's army into chaotic retreat. The win did not end the war, which dragged on another fourteen years, but it secured Bruce's throne and remains Scotland's most celebrated military triumph.

entries.name: Chaco War
entries.desc: A brutal war between Bolivia and Paraguay over the arid Gran Chaco region, the deadliest interstate conflict in 20th-century South America.
entries.tldr: Bolivia and Paraguay fought from 1932 to 1935 over the sparsely populated Gran Chaco region, driven partly by mistaken hopes that it held oil reserves. Both poor, landlocked nations mobilized disproportionately large armies that suffered horrifically from disease, thirst, and the harsh terrain as much as from combat. Paraguay, fighting closer to its heartland and better led militarily, won most of the territory in dispute. The war killed some 100,000 men and remains the deadliest interstate conflict fought in South America during the twentieth century.

entries.name: Battle of Rymnik
entries.desc: A decisive Russo-Austrian victory over Ottoman forces during the Russo-Turkish War, led by Alexander Suvorov.
entries.tldr: On 22 September 1789, a Russian force under Alexander Suvorov, combined with an Austrian corps under the Prince of Coburg, decisively defeated a much larger Ottoman army near the Rymnik river in present-day Romania during the Russo-Turkish War of 1787-92. Suvorov's rapid forced march to link up with the Austrians before the Ottomans could strike first was central to the victory, part of his reputation for aggressive, unconventional tactics. The defeat further weakened Ottoman standing in the region and contributed to the later Treaty of Jassy.

entries.name: Greco-Italian War
entries.desc: Fascist Italy's invasion of Greece, which was repelled by Greek forces and drew Nazi Germany into the Balkan campaign.
entries.tldr: Mussolini ordered an invasion of Greece from occupied Albania in October 1940, expecting an easy triumph that would match Hitler's rapid conquests elsewhere in Europe. Greek forces instead halted the Italian advance and pushed deep into Albanian territory, inflicting a humiliating defeat on Fascist Italy. The reversal forced Hitler to divert German forces into the Balkans the following spring to rescue his ally, a campaign some historians argue delayed and weakened the subsequent invasion of the Soviet Union.

entries.name: Battle of Prague
entries.desc: A Prussian victory over Austrian forces early in the Seven Years' War, followed by a costly Prussian siege of the Bohemian capital.
entries.tldr: On 6 May 1757, a Prussian army under Frederick the Great defeated Austrian forces outside Prague early in the Seven Years' War, though at a heavy cost that included the death of Frederick's trusted general Kurt von Schwerin. The surviving Austrian troops retreated into Prague, which the Prussians then besieged for weeks before an Austrian relief army forced Frederick to break off and withdraw after his defeat at Kolín. Despite the tactical Prussian win, the campaign ultimately failed to knock Austria out of Bohemia, and set the pattern for a long, costly multi-front war.

entries.name: Battle of Rovine
entries.desc: Wallachian prince Mircea the Elder repelled an Ottoman invasion force, delaying the Ottoman conquest of Wallachia.
entries.tldr: On 17 May 1395, Wallachian prince Mircea the Elder faced an Ottoman invasion force, reportedly led in person by Sultan Bayezid I, at Rovine in what is now Romania. Accounts of the outcome are disputed, with some sources describing a Wallachian victory and others a costly standoff, but Mircea's forces succeeded in checking the Ottoman advance and preserving Wallachian autonomy for a time. The clash fits a broader pattern of resistance by Balkan Christian rulers against Ottoman expansion in the late fourteenth century.

entries.name: Battle of Brunanburh
entries.desc: King Æthelstan's army crushed a coalition of Scots, Vikings, and Strathclyde Britons, a defining moment in English unification.
entries.tldr: Fought in 937 at a still-disputed location in Britain, the battle saw King Æthelstan of England, grandson of Alfred the Great, lead a combined Anglo-Saxon army against an invading coalition of Scots under King Constantine II, Dublin Vikings under Olaf Guthfrithson, and Britons from Strathclyde. Æthelstan's forces crushed the alliance, killing several kings and noblemen among the invaders, in what chroniclers celebrated in verse as an unprecedented slaughter. The victory cemented Æthelstan's claim to be the first true king of a unified England.

entries.name: Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824
entries.desc: Britain and the Netherlands divided their colonial spheres of influence in the Malay Archipelago along the Strait of Malacca.
entries.tldr: Signed in London in March 1824, this treaty resolved decades of overlapping British and Dutch colonial claims in Southeast Asia by dividing the Malay Archipelago along the Strait of Malacca. Britain ceded its settlement at Bencoolen on Sumatra to the Dutch and recognized Dutch dominance south of the strait, while the Netherlands ceded Malacca and dropped claims to the Malay Peninsula and Singapore. The line it drew shaped the later border between British Malaya and the Dutch East Indies, and by extension modern Malaysia and Indonesia.

entries.name: Treaty of Batum
entries.desc: The Ottoman Empire imposed a peace settlement on the newly independent South Caucasus republics of Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan.
entries.tldr: Signed in June 1918, the Treaty of Batum was imposed by the Ottoman Empire on the newly independent republics of Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan following the collapse of Russian authority in the Caucasus during World War I. Its harsh terms ceded substantial territory to the Ottomans and left the fragile new states, especially Armenia, with little room to maneuver. The settlement was rendered largely moot within months by the Ottoman Empire's own defeat and armistice that October. It nonetheless illustrates the chaotic redrawing of Caucasus borders as empires collapsed at the war's end.

entries.name: Anglo-Zulu War
entries.desc: Britain invaded the Zulu Kingdom in southern Africa, suffering a stunning early defeat at Isandlwana before conquering Zululand.
entries.tldr: In January 1879, Britain invaded the independent Zulu Kingdom in southern Africa without authorization from London, seeking to remove it as an obstacle to a planned confederation of colonies. Zulu forces under King Cetshwayo inflicted a stunning defeat on a British column at Isandlwana, killing over a thousand soldiers in one of the worst losses in British colonial warfare. Britain rushed reinforcements and, after fighting including the defense at Rorke's Drift, crushed Zulu resistance at Ulundi in July 1879.

entries.name: Battle of Wadi al-Khaznadar
entries.desc: Mongol Ilkhanate forces under Ghazan Khan defeated the Mamluk Sultanate near Homs, Syria.
entries.tldr: Also called the Battle of Homs, this clash saw the Mongol Ilkhanate army of Ghazan Khan, reinforced by Armenian and Georgian allies, defeat the Mamluk Sultanate's forces near Homs in Syria in December 1299. The Mamluk defeat let the Mongols briefly occupy Damascus and much of Syria, one of the few times Mongol forces held Levantine territory for an extended period. Ghazan's control proved short-lived; he withdrew most of his army north soon after, and the Mamluks reclaimed Syria within about a year, culminating in victory at Marj al-Saffar in 1303.

entries.name: Battle of the Gates of Trajan
entries.desc: Bulgarian forces under Tsar Samuel ambushed and destroyed a Byzantine army in the mountains of eastern Bulgaria.
entries.tldr: In August 986, Bulgarian forces under Tsar Samuel ambushed the retreating army of Byzantine Emperor Basil II in a narrow mountain pass in eastern Bulgaria known as the Gates of Trajan, after Basil's siege of the fortress of Serdica had failed. The ambush caught the strung-out Byzantine column in difficult terrain and destroyed much of the army, with Basil narrowly escaping. The disaster forced Byzantium onto the defensive for years and is a formative humiliation for Basil II, who later waged a war that crushed Bulgaria, earning him the epithet 'Bulgar-Slayer.'

entries.name: Treaty of Craiova
entries.desc: Romania ceded Southern Dobruja to Bulgaria under pressure from Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union.
entries.tldr: Signed in August 1940 under pressure from Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, who were arbitrating Balkan territorial disputes ahead of the coming war, the Treaty of Craiova forced Romania to cede Southern Dobruja to Bulgaria. The transfer also involved a population exchange between Romanian and Bulgarian residents there. It came amid a wave of territorial losses for Romania that year, following cessions to Hungary and the Soviet Union, and helped topple King Carol II. Unlike those other losses, this cession was never reversed, and Southern Dobruja remains part of Bulgaria today.

entries.name: Battle of Hunayn
entries.desc: Muhammad's Muslim army defeated the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes near Mecca, securing control of the Arabian Peninsula's holy cities.
entries.tldr: In 630, shortly after the conquest of Mecca, the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes assembled a force to confront the growing Muslim community, ambushing Muhammad's army in the narrow Hunayn valley and initially throwing it into disorder. Muhammad and a core of steadfast companions rallied the fleeing troops, turning the battle into a decisive victory and capturing vast herds of livestock as spoils. The defeat broke Hawazin power, though the town of Ta'if held out under siege before submitting.

entries.name: Battle of Edington
entries.desc: King Alfred the Great of Wessex decisively defeated the Great Heathen Army of Danish Vikings, securing Anglo-Saxon England's survival.
entries.tldr: In May 878, King Alfred the Great of Wessex, having rallied forces from a refuge in the Somerset marshes after a surprise Viking attack, led the West Saxon army to a decisive victory over Guthrum's Great Heathen Army at Edington. The defeated Viking leader agreed to withdraw, accept baptism as Æthelstan, and honor the Treaty of Wedmore, which divided England between Wessex and the Viking-ruled Danelaw. The victory is often seen as the turning point that preserved Anglo-Saxon rule.

entries.name: Morean War
entries.desc: Venice and its Holy League allies fought the Ottoman Empire for control of the Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.
entries.tldr: Also called the Sixth Ottoman-Venetian War, this conflict saw Venice, backed by the Holy League formed after the failed 1683 Ottoman siege of Vienna, invade the Ottoman-held Peloponnese, known to Venetians as the Morea. Venetian forces under Francesco Morosini captured the region, but Morosini's 1687 bombardment of Ottoman-held Athens struck the Parthenon, then used as a gunpowder magazine, destroying much of the ancient temple. The 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz confirmed Venice's hold on the Morea, its last major gain, lost back to the Ottomans by 1715.

entries.name: Battle of Karánsebes
entries.desc: Austrian army units mistakenly attacked each other in a chaotic nighttime panic during the Austro-Turkish War, inflicting heavy self-caused casualties.
entries.tldr: During the Austro-Turkish War, an Austrian army camped near Karánsebes descended into chaos after cavalry and infantry units, some reportedly drunk, mistook each other for the enemy in the dark. Confused shouting and stray shots escalated into a firefight between regiments who believed they faced Ottoman raiders, and panic spread through the camp as artillery opened fire on the fleeing troops. The army suffered heavy casualties before dawn revealed no Turkish force had even arrived. Historians dispute the more dramatic details, but the episode remains a byword for military farce.

entries.name: Williamite War in Ireland
entries.desc: Supporters of deposed King James II fought forces loyal to William of Orange for control of Ireland and the English throne.

entries.name: Iberian War
entries.desc: The Byzantine and Sasanian Persian empires fought for control of the Caucasian kingdom of Iberia, in modern-day Georgia.
entries.tldr: The Eastern Roman Empire and Sasanian Persia fought from 526 to 532 over control of the Caucasian kingdom of Iberia, whose Christian king had appealed to Constantinople after Persia tried to impose Zoroastrianism. Byzantine general Belisarius won a notable victory at the Battle of Dara in 530, though Persia later prevailed at Callinicum. The 532 Perpetual Peace restored the prewar status quo and freed Emperor Justinian to focus resources on his ambitious reconquest campaigns in the western Mediterranean.

entries.name: Byzantine–Sassanid War of 602–628
entries.desc: The last and most devastating war between the Byzantine and Sasanian Persian empires ended in a decisive Byzantine victory that exhausted both sides before the Arab conquests.
entries.tldr: The final and most destructive of the centuries-long wars between Rome and Persia began after Emperor Maurice's murder gave Sassanid king Khosrow II a pretext to invade, and Persian armies swiftly overran Syria, Egypt, and Anatolia, even besieging Constantinople. Emperor Heraclius reversed the tide with a counter-invasion deep into Persian Mesopotamia, and Khosrow was overthrown and killed by his own son in 628. The peace restored prewar borders, but both empires were left exhausted. Within a decade Arab armies from Arabia conquered vast swaths of both crippled empires' territory.

entries.name: Mongol invasion of Central Asia
entries.desc: Genghis Khan's Mongol armies destroyed the Khwarezmian Empire, conquering Transoxiana and Persia's eastern territories.
entries.tldr: Genghis Khan launched this campaign after the Khwarezmian shah executed a Mongol trade delegation and mutilated its envoys, an insult he answered by annihilating the empire that had committed it. Cities including Bukhara, Samarkand, and Urgench were sacked in succession, with populations massacred and irrigation systems destroyed, devastation parts of Central Asia arguably never fully recovered from. Generals Jebe and Subutai then pursued the fleeing shah's son on a raid that circled the Caspian Sea and defeated Russian princes at the Kalka River, a logistical feat unmatched for centuries.

entries.name: Second Battle of Ypres
entries.desc: German forces used chlorine gas for the first time on the Western Front in an assault on Allied lines near Ypres, Belgium.
entries.tldr: Marked the first large-scale use of poison gas on the Western Front, when German troops released chlorine gas against French colonial and Canadian positions in the Ypres salient in Belgium. The gas caused panic and heavy casualties, tearing a gap in the Allied line, but German forces failed to fully exploit the breakthrough. Canadian troops earned a lasting reputation for holding their section of the line despite the attack. The battle prompted rapid development of gas masks and drew international condemnation, though chemical warfare continued through the rest of the war.

entries.name: Second Battle of Bull Run
entries.desc: Confederate forces under Robert E. Lee and Stonewall Jackson decisively defeated the Union Army of Virginia near Manassas, Virginia.
entries.tldr: Fought near Manassas, Virginia, after Robert E. Lee split his outnumbered army, sending Stonewall Jackson on a flanking march that seized the Union supply base at Manassas Junction and drew Union General John Pope into battle. Jackson's corps held a strong position along an unfinished railroad cut while Lee brought up James Longstreet's corps for a devastating flank attack. The Union army was routed back toward Washington, echoing the war's first Bull Run battle a year earlier. The victory emboldened Lee to launch his first invasion of the North, leading to Antietam weeks later.

entries.name: Second Battle of St Albans
entries.desc: The Second Battle of St Albans was fought on 17 February 1461 during the Wars of the Roses in St Albans, Hertfordshire, England.
entries.tldr: Fought during the Wars of the Roses when a Lancastrian army, marching south after victory at Wakefield, defeated Yorkist forces guarding the captive King Henry VI, freeing him from Yorkist custody. Despite winning the field, Queen Margaret's victorious but undisciplined army failed to press on and seize London, letting Edward, Earl of March, enter the city and be proclaimed King Edward IV instead. Edward reversed the setback weeks later with a decisive victory at Towton. The battle is remembered as a rare Lancastrian success amid the dynasty's eventual collapse.

entries.name: Second Anglo-Burmese War
entries.desc: The Second Anglo-Burmese War or the Second Burma War was the second of the three wars fought between the Burmese Empire and British Empire during the 19th century. The war resulted in a British victory with more Burmese territory being annexed to British India.
entries.tldr: Provoked by a dispute between British merchants and Burmese officials at Rangoon that Governor-General Lord Dalhousie used as pretext for invasion. British forces quickly seized Rangoon, Pegu, and other lower Burmese territory against limited resistance. Rather than negotiate a treaty, Britain simply annexed the province of Pegu, or Lower Burma, outright. The loss of its coastline cut the Burmese kingdom off from the sea and set the stage for the final war that ended Burmese independence in 1885.

entries.name: Second Barbary War
entries.desc: The Second Barbary War, also known as the U.S.–Algerian War and the Algerine War, was a brief military conflict between the United States and the North African state of Algiers in 1815.
entries.tldr: Fought after Algiers, taking advantage of American preoccupation with the War of 1812, resumed seizing US ships and enslaving their crews in violation of an earlier treaty. Commodore Stephen Decatur led a US naval squadron across the Atlantic and forced the Dey of Algiers to sign a treaty ending tribute payments and freeing American captives. Decatur then sailed on to extract similar concessions from Tunis and Tripoli. The brief campaign ended US payments of tribute to the Barbary states of North Africa.

entries.name: Second Anglo-Afghan War
entries.desc: The Second Anglo-Afghan War was a military conflict fought between the British Raj and the Emirate of Afghanistan from 1878 to 1880, when the latter was ruled by Sher Ali Khan of the Barakzai dynasty, the son of former Emir Dost Mohammad Khan. The war was part of the Great Game between the British and Russian empires.
entries.tldr: Triggered when Emir Sher Ali Khan received a Russian mission but turned away a British one, reviving British fears of Russian influence in Afghanistan during the era's "Great Game." British forces invaded, deposed Sher Ali, and installed his son, but a British mission was later massacred in Kabul, prompting further fighting including victory at the Battle of Kandahar. The war ended with Britain controlling Afghan foreign policy while leaving internal rule to a new emir, Abdur Rahman Khan. It left Afghanistan as a buffer state between British India and Russia.

entries.name: Second Hundred Years' War
entries.desc: The Second Hundred Years' War is a term of periodization, or a historical era designation, coined by J. R. Seeley in his work The Expansion of England (1883).
entries.tldr: Not a single continuous conflict but a historian's label for the long run of wars between Britain and France stretching from the Nine Years' War through the Napoleonic Wars, including conflicts like the Seven Years' War and the wars of the French Revolution. Coined by J.R. Seeley in 1883, the term frames over a century of intermittent Anglo-French rivalry, fought across Europe and colonial theaters worldwide, as one long contest for global empire. It ended decisively with Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo in 1815. The rivalry it describes shaped the modern British and French empires alike.

entries.name: Battle of Hattin
entries.desc: The Battle of Hattin took place on 4 July 1187, between the Crusader states of the Levant and the forces of the Ayyubid sultan Saladin. It is also known as the Battle of the Horns of Hattin, due to the shape of the nearby extinct volcano of that name.
entries.tldr: On 4 July 1187, Saladin's Ayyubid army trapped the exhausted, dehydrated forces of the Kingdom of Jerusalem near a pair of extinct volcanic hills called the Horns of Hattin, after cutting them off from water and burning the dry grass around them. The Crusader army was annihilated, King Guy of Lusignan was captured along with the relic believed to be the True Cross, and most captured Templar and Hospitaller knights were executed. Saladin swiftly overran most of the kingdom's cities, recapturing Jerusalem within three months.

entries.name: Second Anglo-Maratha War
entries.desc: Second Anglo-Maratha War was a large conflict within the Maratha Empire involving the East India Company. It resulted in a major loss of territory for the Marathas, including regions around Delhi and in present-day Gujarat falling into direct Company rule.
