entries.tldr: Fought as the East India Company, under Governor-General Lord Wellesley, intervened in a succession dispute among Maratha chiefs to expand British paramountcy in India. British forces under Arthur Wellesley, the future Duke of Wellington, and Gerard Lake won major battles including Assaye and Delhi against Maratha armies that included European-trained troops. The Marathas were forced to cede Delhi, Agra, Orissa, and other territories, bringing the Mughal emperor under British protection. The war left the Maratha Confederacy dependent on Britain until its final defeat a decade later.

entries.name: Second Anglo-Mysore War
entries.desc: The Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780–1784) saw Mysore's Hyder Ali, backed by France, fight the East India Company across southern India. Neither side gained lasting advantage, and a treaty restored prewar territory.
entries.tldr: Erupted when Hyder Ali of Mysore, alarmed by British expansion and allied with France during the American Revolutionary War, launched a surprise invasion of the Carnatic that nearly overwhelmed East India Company forces. His son Tipu Sultan continued the fight after Hyder's death in 1782. Years of costly, largely inconclusive campaigning across southern India ended with the 1784 Treaty of Mangalore, restoring each side's prewar territory. It was the only one of the four Anglo-Mysore Wars to end without a clear British victory.

entries.name: Second Silesian War
entries.desc: The Second Silesian War (1744–1745), part of the wider War of the Austrian Succession, confirmed Prussia's hold on Silesia after Frederick the Great invaded Bohemia. Austria accepted the loss at the Treaty of Dresden.
entries.tldr: Part of the broader War of the Austrian Succession, fought when Frederick the Great of Prussia, fearing Austria's recovery after early setbacks, launched a preemptive invasion of Bohemia to defend his hold on Silesia won in the first war. Despite early reverses, Prussian victories at Hohenfriedberg and Kesselsdorf forced Austria back to the negotiating table. The Treaty of Dresden confirmed Prussian possession of Silesia, a rich province that made Prussia a major European power. Austria kept seeking to reclaim it, leading to the Seven Years' War a decade later.

entries.name: First Battle of the Aisne
entries.desc: The First Battle of the Aisne was the Allied follow-up offensive against the right wing of the German First Army and the Second Army as they retreated after the First Battle of the Marne earlier in September 1914. The Advance to the Aisne consisted of the Battle of the Marne (7–10 September) and the Battle of the Aisne (12–15 September).
entries.tldr: Following their retreat after the First Battle of the Marne in September 1914, German forces dug in along the Aisne River, and pursuing Allied troops launched a follow-up offensive to try to prevent them from consolidating. The attacks failed to dislodge well-entrenched German positions on high ground above the river, and both sides began digging further defensive lines. The stalemate here is often seen as the true beginning of trench warfare on the Western Front, as fighting spread outward in the 'Race to the Sea'. It set the pattern of static warfare that defined the front for four years.

entries.name: Battle of Sekigahara
entries.desc: The Battle of Sekigahara was an important battle in Japan which occurred on October 21, 1600 in what is now Gifu Prefecture, Japan, at the end of the Sengoku period.
entries.tldr: On 21 October 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern army faced Ishida Mitsunari's Western coalition in a fog-shrouded valley in what is now Gifu Prefecture. The outcome hinged on mid-battle defections, most notably Kobayakawa Hideaki's switch to Ieyasu's side, which collapsed the Western line. Ieyasu's victory eliminated his rivals for control of Japan and led directly to his founding of the Tokugawa shogunate, closing out the chaotic Sengoku period.

entries.name: Expulsion of the Moriscos
entries.desc: King Philip III of Spain decreed the expulsion of the Moriscos, Christianized descendants of Spain's Muslim population, in 1609. Roughly 300,000 were deported to North Africa, devastating Spanish agriculture.
entries.tldr: In 1609, King Philip III of Spain ordered the expulsion of the Moriscos, Muslims of Spain who had been forcibly converted to Christianity a century earlier but were widely suspected of secretly retaining their old faith. Over roughly five years, an estimated 300,000 people, most of Spain's remaining Muslim-descended population, were deported to North Africa. The expulsion devastated agriculture in regions like Valencia where Moriscos had formed a large share of the rural workforce. It stands as one of early modern Europe's largest forced expulsions.

entries.name: Battle of Kumanovo
entries.desc: The Battle of Kumanovo, on 23–24 October 1912, was a major battle of the First Balkan War. It was an important Serbian victory over the Ottoman army in the Kosovo Vilayet, shortly after the outbreak of the war. After this defeat, the Ottoman army abandoned the major part of the region, suffering heavy losses in manpower and in war materiel.
entries.tldr: At the outbreak of the First Balkan War, the Serbian army advanced into Ottoman-held Kosovo and met the main Ottoman field army near Kumanovo. Despite Ottoman defensive advantages, Serbian artillery and infantry broke through over two days of fighting, inflicting heavy casualties and capturing large quantities of equipment. The defeated Ottoman army abandoned most of Macedonia and Kosovo in the retreat that followed, effectively ending centuries of Ottoman rule there. The victory was a foundational moment for Serbian nationalism and reshaped the map of the southern Balkans within weeks.

entries.name: Battle of the Alamo
entries.desc: The Battle of the Alamo was a pivotal event and military engagement in the Texas Revolution. Following a 13-day siege, Mexican troops under President General Antonio López de Santa Anna reclaimed the Alamo Mission near San Antonio de Béxar.
entries.tldr: In February and March 1836, during the Texas Revolution, a force of several thousand Mexican troops under President General Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna besieged a small garrison of Texian and Tejano defenders, including William Travis, Jim Bowie, and Davy Crockett, at the Alamo Mission near San Antonio de Bexar. After a thirteen-day siege, Mexican forces stormed the mission on 6 March 1836 and killed nearly all of the defenders. The defeat galvanized Texian resistance under the rallying cry 'Remember the Alamo,' contributing to Texas's decisive victory weeks later at San Jacinto.

entries.name: Malayan Emergency
entries.desc: The Malayan Emergency (1948–1960) was a guerrilla war between communist insurgents seeking independence and Commonwealth forces defending colonial Malaya. Counter-insurgency tactics eventually defeated the insurgents.
entries.tldr: Communist guerrillas of the Malayan Races' Liberation Army, drawing on anti-Japanese resistance fighters from World War II, waged a jungle insurgency against British colonial rule and the region's plantation owners. British forces pioneered counter-insurgency tactics later studied worldwide, including forced resettlement of rural Chinese communities into fortified 'New Villages' to cut off guerrilla support. The 'Emergency' label rather than 'war' was a deliberate choice, since insurers would not have covered plantation losses in a declared war. The insurgency was defeated by 1960.

entries.name: Battle of Buxar
entries.desc: The Battle of Buxar was fought between 22 and 23 October 1764, between the forces of the British East India Company, under the command of Major Hector Munro, against the combined armies of Shah Alam II, the Emperor of the Mughal Empire; Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Bengal; Balwant Singh, the Maharaja of the Benares State; Shuja-ud-daula, the Nawab of Awadh.
entries.tldr: Fought on 22 and 23 October 1764 in the eastern Indian state of Bihar, the battle pitted the British East India Company's forces under Major Hector Munro against a coalition combining Mughal emperor Shah Alam II, deposed Bengal nawab Mir Qasim, and the nawabs of Awadh and Benares. Despite being outnumbered, Munro's better-disciplined force decisively defeated the divided coalition. The win forced the Mughal emperor to grant the Company the diwani, the right to collect revenue over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, arguably the true foundation of British colonial rule in India.

entries.name: Unification Act
entries.desc: The Unification Act was an agreement signed by the Ukrainian People's Republic and the West Ukrainian People's Republic in Sophia Square in Kyiv on 22 January 1919. Since 1999, it is celebrated every year as the Day of Unity of Ukraine to commemorate the signing of the treaty; it is a state holiday in Ukraine, though not a public holiday.

entries.name: 1948 Ashgabat earthquake
entries.desc: A magnitude-7.3 earthquake struck near Ashgabat, Turkmenistan, on 6 October 1948, devastating the city. Soviet censorship suppressed reporting of the disaster's true scale for decades.
entries.tldr: Shortly after midnight on 6 October 1948, a magnitude-7.3 earthquake struck near Ashgabat, capital of the Turkmen SSR, leveling most of the city's mud-brick buildings within seconds. Casualty estimates range from the tens of thousands to over 100,000, because Soviet authorities classified the true death toll for decades. Survivors described a nighttime catastrophe with little warning, and rebuilding Ashgabat became a major Soviet postwar project. The tragedy's scope only became public after Turkmen independence in 1991.

entries.name: Battle of Arras
entries.desc: A British-led offensive near Arras, France, in 1917 that captured Vimy Ridge and made early gains before stalling into a costly stalemate, at the highest daily casualty rate of any British offensive of the war.
entries.tldr: Launched on 9 April 1917, the British-led offensive near Arras opened with Canadian Corps troops seizing the long-contested high ground of Vimy Ridge in a single coordinated attack. Elsewhere British and Australian forces made rapid early gains using new artillery tactics, but German reserves stiffened and the offensive stalled into the familiar attrition of the Western Front. British forces suffered their highest average daily casualty rate of any offensive in the war, though the battle cemented the Canadian Corps's reputation as an elite formation.

entries.name: Battle of Friedland
entries.desc: On 14 June 1807, Napoleon decisively defeated a Russian army under Levin von Bennigsen at Friedland in East Prussia. The victory forced Russia to negotiate, leading to the Treaties of Tilsit.
entries.tldr: On 14 June 1807, Napoleon lured a Russian army under Levin von Bennigsen into fighting with its back to the Alle River near Friedland in East Prussia, then used a massed artillery bombardment to shatter the Russian formations before infantry finished the rout. Thousands of Russian troops drowned or died trying to retreat across the river's few crossings. The decisive victory ended the War of the Fourth Coalition and forced Tsar Alexander I to negotiate the Treaties of Tilsit, temporarily allying Russia with France.

entries.name: Ukrainian–Soviet War
entries.desc: A war fought between 1917 and 1921 between the Ukrainian People's Republic and the Bolsheviks following the Russian Revolution.

entries.name: Battle of Caporetto
entries.desc: A major World War I battle on the Isonzo front, where German and Austro-Hungarian forces routed the Italian army.
entries.tldr: Beginning on 24 October 1917 along the Isonzo front in the Julian Alps, the battle saw a combined German and Austro-Hungarian force use new infiltration tactics, bypassing strongpoints rather than assaulting them head-on, to shatter Italy's static defensive lines near Caporetto. The surprise assault triggered a catastrophic Italian collapse and retreat of over 100 kilometers to the Piave River, with hundreds of thousands of soldiers killed, wounded, or captured. The disaster forced a change in Italian command, and the name Caporetto entered the language as a byword for total rout.

entries.name: Second Anglo-Sikh war
entries.desc: A war between the Sikh Empire and the East India Company that ended in the fall of the Sikh Empire and annexation of the Punjab.
entries.tldr: Broke out after a revolt by Sikh governors at Multan escalated into wider war against a Sikh Empire already weakened by the death of Ranjit Singh and years of internal instability. Hard-fought British victories at Chillianwala and Gujrat eventually broke Sikh military resistance. The East India Company formally annexed the Punjab, deposed the boy-king Duleep Singh, and took the Koh-i-Noor diamond as part of the settlement. It extended direct British rule to India's northwestern frontier.

entries.name: Second Vienna Award
entries.desc: A territorial arbitration by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy that transferred Northern Transylvania from Romania to Hungary.
entries.tldr: An arbitration imposed by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy on Hungary and Romania, both of whom Hitler wanted as compliant allies and sources of resources for the coming war. The award transferred Northern Transylvania, with its large Hungarian minority, from Romania to Hungary without either side's genuine consent. Romania accepted under duress rather than risk war with Germany, while Hungary celebrated the return of territory lost after World War I. The transfer was reversed after the war, restoring the region to Romania.

entries.name: Franco-Russian Alliance
entries.desc: A military alliance between France and Russia formed 1891–94 in response to the Triple Alliance, lasting until 1917.
entries.tldr: Facing isolation after Bismarck's system of alliances excluded republican France, French diplomats courted Tsarist Russia despite the ideological gulf between the two regimes. A military convention signed in 1892 and ratified through 1894 committed each power to mobilize against Germany if the other were attacked. The alliance broke French diplomatic isolation and, by locking Europe into opposing blocs alongside the Triple Alliance, became one of the underlying causes of the First World War.

entries.name: Battle of Liaoyang
entries.desc: A major land battle of the Russo-Japanese War fought near Liaoyang in present-day Liaoning Province, China.
entries.tldr: Roughly a quarter million Russian and Japanese troops clashed near Liaoyang in one of the largest battles fought anywhere up to that time, as Japan pressed its offensive in the Russo-Japanese War. Japanese armies under Marshal Oyama attacked entrenched Russian positions over a week of fighting, suffering heavy losses for limited gains. Commander Kuropatkin chose to withdraw north toward Mukden rather than risk his army's destruction, despite inflicting comparable losses. The indecisive but costly battle previewed the trench warfare that would define the First World War a decade later.

entries.name: Battle of Ain Jalut
entries.desc: A battle between the Mamluks of Egypt and the Mongol Ilkhanate near Ain Jalut, marking the first major halt to Mongol expansion.
entries.tldr: In September 1260, a Mamluk army from Egypt met a Mongol force in the Jezreel Valley near the spring of Ain Jalut, in present-day northern Israel. Using feigned retreats and superior knowledge of the terrain, the Mamluk general Baibars lured the Mongols into an ambush, decisively defeating them and killing their commander Kitbuqa. The victory halted the westward advance of the Mongol Empire, which had already destroyed Baghdad, and preserved Mamluk control of Egypt and the Levant.

entries.name: Siege of Belgrade
entries.desc: The 1456 siege in which Hungarian forces under John Hunyadi repelled an Ottoman attempt to capture Belgrade.
entries.tldr: In July 1456 an Ottoman army under Sultan Mehmed II, fresh from conquering Constantinople three years earlier, besieged the Hungarian fortress of Belgrade. A relief force led by the Hungarian noble John Hunyadi, joined by peasant crusaders rallied by the preaching of John of Capistrano, broke the siege and forced an Ottoman retreat. The victory halted the Ottoman advance into central Europe for decades. Hunyadi died of plague days later, and the relief is still marked by midday church bells rung across much of the Catholic world.

entries.name: Battle of Yamama
entries.desc: A decisive battle of the Ridda Wars in which forces of Caliph Abu Bakr defeated the self-proclaimed prophet Musaylima.
entries.tldr: Fought in 632 CE in the Yamama region of Arabia, this battle was the decisive engagement of the Ridda Wars, in which the newly formed Rashidun Caliphate under Caliph Abu Bakr crushed the forces of Musaylima, a rival who had proclaimed himself a prophet after Muhammad's death. Led by the general Khalid ibn al-Walid, Muslim forces defeated Musaylima's tribal coalition in brutal fighting, and Musaylima was killed. The heavy loss of Quran memorizers in the fighting is traditionally said to have spurred its first written compilation.

entries.name: Livonian War
entries.desc: A 1558–1583 war for control of Old Livonia between the Tsardom of Russia and a coalition of Nordic and Polish-Lithuanian powers.
entries.tldr: Ivan the Terrible's Russia invaded the crumbling Livonian Confederation in 1558 seeking Baltic ports, drawing in Sweden, Denmark, and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth as rival claimants. Poland-Lithuania's union under King Stephen Báthory eventually turned the tide, driving Russian forces back after a long siege of Pskov. The 1583 Treaty of Plussa left Russia stripped of nearly all its Baltic gains. The failure to secure a warm-water port was a setback Russia would not reverse until Peter the Great, over a century later.

entries.name: Battle of Nahrawan
entries.desc: A 658 CE battle in which Caliph Ali's forces defeated the Kharijites, former allies who had broken with him after Siffin.
entries.tldr: In 658, the forces of Caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib crushed the Kharijites, a radical faction that had broken away from Ali after denouncing his acceptance of arbitration following the Battle of Siffin. Ali's army decisively defeated the Kharijites near the Nahrawan canal in Iraq, killing most of their fighters. The surviving Kharijites nursed a lasting grievance, and one of them assassinated Ali three years later in revenge. The episode marked the emergence of Kharijism as a distinct and enduring current in early Islamic history.

entries.name: Muslim conquest of the Levant
entries.desc: The Rashidun Caliphate's conquest of Byzantine Syria between 634–638 CE, part of the wider early Muslim conquests.
entries.tldr: Following the death of the Prophet Muhammad, the Rashidun Caliphate under Caliph Umar sent armies north to conquer Byzantine-held Syria and Palestine, led in its decisive phase by general Khalid ibn al-Walid. The 636 Battle of Yarmouk, fought during a sandstorm that blinded Byzantine ranks, destroyed the main imperial army and effectively ended Byzantine rule in the region. Jerusalem surrendered in 637, reportedly to Caliph Umar in person, and Damascus and Antioch fell in quick succession, ending nearly seven centuries of Roman rule.

entries.name: War of the Third Coalition
entries.desc: The first conflict of the Napoleonic Wars, pitting Napoleon's France against a coalition led by Britain, Austria, and Russia.

entries.name: Battle of Tarawa
entries.desc: A bloody 1943 amphibious battle between the US and Japan on Tarawa Atoll in the Gilbert Islands, part of Operation Galvanic.
entries.tldr: In November 1943, US Marines launched a costly amphibious assault on the heavily fortified islet of Betio in Tarawa Atoll, part of Operation Galvanic in the Gilbert Islands. Miscalculated tides stranded landing craft on a coral reef far from shore, forcing many Marines to wade hundreds of yards under fire from entrenched Japanese defenders. The 76-hour battle killed roughly 1,000 Marines and nearly the entire Japanese garrison, and the shockingly high toll prompted major changes to American amphibious assault doctrine.

entries.name: Battle of Sarikamish
entries.desc: A disastrous World War I engagement between Russian and Ottoman forces in the Caucasus campaign, fought in winter 1914–15.
entries.tldr: In the winter of 1914–15, Ottoman War Minister Enver Pasha personally led the Third Army on an ambitious encircling offensive against Russian forces in the Caucasus near Sarikamish. Poor planning and brutal sub-zero temperatures proved as deadly as combat: tens of thousands of Ottoman troops froze to death or were lost to exposure and disease during the failed maneuver. The catastrophic defeat gutted the Ottoman Third Army and is often cited among the grievances later used to scapegoat Armenian communities in the region.

entries.name: Hungarian–Romanian War
entries.desc: A 1918–1919 war between Hungary and Romania fought amid the collapse of Austria-Hungary after World War I.
entries.tldr: As Austria-Hungary disintegrated after World War I, Romania invaded Hungary in 1919 partly in response to Béla Kun's short-lived Hungarian Soviet Republic, which Romania and the Allied powers saw as a Bolshevik threat. Romanian forces defeated the Hungarian Red Army and occupied Budapest, toppling Kun's communist government. The war helped pave the way for the 1920 Treaty of Trianon, which awarded Transylvania and other Hungarian territories to Romania and shrank Hungary to roughly a third of its former size.

entries.name: Italian War of 1551–1559
entries.desc: A war begun by Henry II of France against Charles V for control of Italy, ended by the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis.
entries.tldr: Henry II of France renewed the long Habsburg-Valois struggle for Italian dominance in 1551, contesting Charles V's control over Milan, Naples, and Siena. Fighting spread across Italy, the Low Countries, and northern France, including the decisive Spanish victory at St. Quentin in 1557. The 1559 Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis ended the war and, with it, the entire era of Italian Wars, confirming Spanish Habsburg dominance over most of Italy for the next 150 years.

entries.name: Crimean War
entries.desc: A war fought 1853–56 between Russia and an alliance of the Ottoman Empire, France, Britain, and Sardinia over the Eastern Question.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1853 to 1856, the war pitted Russia against an alliance of the Ottoman Empire, Britain, France, and Sardinia, ostensibly over Christian holy sites but really over Russian ambitions toward the declining Ottoman Empire. Much of the fighting centered on the Russian naval base at Sevastopol in Crimea, besieged for nearly a year amid infamous logistical failures. The war became notorious for disease-ridden hospitals and Florence Nightingale's pioneering nursing reforms, and for the disastrous Charge of the Light Brigade. Russia's defeat curtailed its naval power in the Black Sea.

entries.name: Battle of Shanghai
entries.desc: A major 1937 battle of the Second Sino-Japanese War fought in Shanghai, among the largest battles of the entire war.
entries.tldr: Beginning in August 1937, Chiang Kai-shek committed his best-trained divisions to defend Shanghai in a grinding, three-month urban battle against invading Japanese forces. Fighting street by street with modern weapons on both sides produced casualties that drew comparisons to World War I attrition battles. Chinese forces ultimately withdrew toward Nanjing after suffering enormous losses, but the prolonged resistance disrupted Japan's expectation of a swift victory and drew international attention to the war.

entries.name: Great stand on the Ugra river
entries.desc: An 1480 standoff on the Ugra River between Akhmat Khan of the Great Horde and Grand Prince Ivan III of Moscow, ending Mongol rule over Russia.
entries.tldr: In autumn 1480, the army of Akhmat Khan, ruler of the Great Horde, faced Grand Prince Ivan III's Muscovite forces across the Ugra River, each side unwilling to risk crossing to attack the other directly. After weeks of skirmishing and failed negotiations, an early, harsh winter and the threat of Ivan's allies attacking Akhmat's rear forced the Horde to withdraw without a decisive battle. The bloodless standoff is traditionally treated as the symbolic end of roughly two and a half centuries of Mongol-Tatar suzerainty over Russian lands.

entries.name: Battle of Baku
entries.desc: A 1918 battle for control of Baku fought between Ottoman-Azerbaijani forces and Bolshevik-Armenian Baku Commune defenders, later reinforced by British troops.
entries.tldr: Fought in the summer and autumn of 1918 amid the Russian Empire's collapse, the battle for oil-rich Baku pitted an Ottoman-led force allied with the new Azerbaijan Democratic Republic against the Bolshevik and Dashnak-led Baku Commune, briefly reinforced by a small British detachment under General Lionel Dunsterville. After the British withdrew in the face of superior numbers, Ottoman and Azerbaijani troops stormed the city on 15 September 1918, and its fall was accompanied by mass killings of Baku's Armenian population. Control of the oil fields was the central strategic prize.

entries.name: Anastasian War
entries.desc: A war fought from 502 to 506 between the Byzantine and Sasanian empires, the first major conflict between the two powers in over sixty years.
entries.tldr: Fought from 502 to 506 between the Eastern Roman emperor Anastasius I and the Sasanian shah Kavad I, this war was the first major clash between Rome and Persia in over six decades. Kavad, needing funds after Rome refused to help pay tribute to the Huns, opened the war by storming the fortress city of Amida. Fighting see-sawed across Mesopotamia until both sides, distracted by other frontiers, agreed to a truce. Anastasius then built the fortress city of Dara to guard the frontier.

entries.name: Wars of the Three Kingdoms
entries.desc: A series of conflicts from 1639 to 1653 across England, Scotland and Ireland, including the English Civil Wars and the Irish Confederate Wars.

entries.name: First Egyptian-Ottoman War
entries.desc: An 1831–1833 conflict in which Egyptian forces under Muhammad Ali Pasha seized Ottoman Syria, demanding it as reward for aiding the sultan in the Greek War of Independence.
entries.tldr: Muhammad Ali's son Ibrahim Pasha led an Egyptian army out of Egypt, crushed Ottoman forces at Homs and Konya, and drove deep into Anatolia, threatening to topple the Ottoman sultanate outright. Alarmed European powers, chiefly Russia, intervened diplomatically and militarily to prop up Istanbul. The 1833 Convention of Kütahya handed Egypt control of Syria and Adana but left Sultan Mahmud II dependent on Russian protection, a debt later paid through the Treaty of Hünkâr İskelesi. The war exposed how far Ottoman military power had decayed.

entries.name: War of Devolution
entries.desc: A 1667–1668 war in which France occupied the Spanish Netherlands and Franche-Comté, with Louis XIV claiming the territories through his wife's inheritance rights.

entries.name: Treaty of Gandamak
entries.desc: An 1879 treaty ending the first phase of the Second Anglo-Afghan War, in which Afghan emir Mohammad Yaqub Khan ceded frontier territory and control of foreign affairs to Britain.
entries.tldr: Signed in May 1879, the Treaty of Gandamak ended the first phase of the Second Anglo-Afghan War after British forces invaded Afghanistan to counter perceived Russian influence at the Afghan court. Under it, Emir Mohammad Yaqub Khan ceded frontier districts to British India and accepted a resident British envoy in Kabul, effectively ceding control of Afghan foreign policy. The arrangement collapsed within months when the envoy and his escort were massacred in an uprising, reigniting the war, a lasting lesson in the difficulty of imposing settlements on Afghanistan.

entries.name: Second Egyptian-Ottoman War
entries.desc: An 1839–1841 conflict, also called the Second Syrian War, fought mainly in Syria between Egyptian and Ottoman forces.
entries.tldr: Fought when Egypt's ambitious governor Muhammad Ali, having already won the first war, renewed conflict with the Ottoman sultan over control of Syria and effective independence for his dynasty. Egyptian forces under his son Ibrahim Pasha again defeated Ottoman armies, but European powers, alarmed at the prospect of Egyptian domination of the Levant, intervened against Egypt. Under the resulting settlement, Muhammad Ali withdrew from Syria in exchange for hereditary rule over Egypt alone. The war marked the limit of Egyptian expansion and cemented European oversight of Ottoman affairs.

entries.name: War of 1812
entries.desc: A conflict from 1812 to 1815 between the United States and Britain, fought mainly in North America and at sea amid the wider Napoleonic Wars.

entries.name: Capture of Rome
entries.desc: The 1870 seizure of Rome and the Papal States by forces of the Kingdom of Italy, completing the unification of Italy.
entries.tldr: On 20 September 1870, troops of the Kingdom of Italy breached the walls of Rome near Porta Pia and took the city from the forces of Pope Pius IX, who had ruled it as the last remnant of the Papal States. The city was annexed and made Italy's capital, completing the decades-long process of Italian unification. Pius IX refused to recognize the loss and confined himself to the Vatican, styling himself a 'prisoner', a standoff that lasted until the 1929 Lateran Treaty. The event is still commemorated in Italy as the final act of the Risorgimento.

entries.name: Battles of Rzhev
entries.desc: A series of costly Red Army offensives against the Wehrmacht around Rzhev from January 1942 to March 1943 on the Eastern Front of World War II.
entries.tldr: Around the town of Rzhev, the Red Army launched a grinding series of four major offensives against the German Ninth Army from January 1942 to March 1943, seeking to eliminate a salient threatening Moscow. Soviet losses were catastrophic, often estimated near a million casualties, for minimal territorial gain, earning it the grim nickname the 'Rzhev meat grinder'. The Germans ultimately withdrew from the salient in March 1943 to shorten their lines. Long downplayed in Soviet histories because of its cost, it is now seen as one of the war's bloodiest campaigns.

entries.name: Battle of Konotop
entries.desc: A 1659 battle in which a Cossack coalition under Hetman Ivan Vyhovsky defeated Russian Tsardom cavalry near Konotop, Ukraine, during the Russo-Polish War.
entries.tldr: Ukrainian hetman Ivan Vyhovsky, seeking to break from Russian control after allying with the Crimean Khanate and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, faced a large Russian army besieging Konotop. He lured the Russian cavalry into a pursuit across the Sosnivka River, where Crimean Tatar and Cossack forces ambushed and destroyed much of it. The defeat was one of the most severe Russia suffered against Cossack forces that century, though Vyhovsky gained little lasting advantage from it. Internal Cossack divisions soon undid his position, and Russian influence over Ukraine was later restored.

entries.name: Japanese coup d'état in French Indochina
entries.desc: A March 1945 Japanese operation that overthrew French colonial rule in Indochina as Japan faced imminent Allied invasion late in World War II.
entries.tldr: With Allied forces closing in and Vichy France no longer a reliable partner, Japan launched a surprise operation on 9 March 1945 to disarm French troops and overthrow the colonial administration it had allowed to nominally govern Indochina since 1940. French garrisons were overwhelmed within a day, and Japan installed nominally independent governments under local rulers like Emperor Bảo Đại in Vietnam. The coup shattered French colonial authority and, by removing it just before Japan's own surrender months later, opened space for Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh to seize power.

entries.name: Battle of Tolbiac
entries.desc: A battle between the Franks under Clovis I and the Alamanni, traditionally dated to 496, near what is now Zülpich, Germany.
entries.tldr: Traditionally dated to 496 near what is now Zülpich, Germany, this battle pitted the pagan Frankish king Clovis I against the Alamanni. According to a story recorded decades later by Gregory of Tours, Clovis, facing defeat, vowed to convert to the Christian God of his wife Clotilde if granted victory, and the tide of battle then turned in his favor. Whatever actually happened on the field, the tale became a foundational legend for Clovis's subsequent baptism and for Frankish Gaul's identification with Catholic Christianity.

entries.name: German invasion of the Netherlands
entries.desc: A May 1940 German military campaign that overran the Netherlands in days, part of the wider invasion of the Low Countries and France.
entries.tldr: German forces attacked the neutral Netherlands on 10 May 1940 as part of the broader assault on France and the Low Countries, using airborne troops to seize key bridges and airfields in a surprise opening move. After the Luftwaffe's devastating bombing of Rotterdam, which killed hundreds and threatened further cities with similar destruction, the Dutch government capitulated within five days. Queen Wilhelmina fled to London, and the Netherlands endured five years of occupation until Allied liberation in 1945.

entries.name: Battle of Dandanaqan
entries.desc: An 1040 battle in which the Seljuq Turks decisively defeated the Ghaznavid Empire near Merv, ending Ghaznavid dominance over Greater Khorasan.
entries.tldr: In 1040, Seljuk Turk forces led by brothers Tughril and Chaghri Beg decisively defeated the army of the Ghaznavid sultan Mas'ud I near Merv in Greater Khorasan. Mas'ud, who had underestimated the Seljuks after years of raiding, fled the field and was later killed in a subsequent coup. The victory ended Ghaznavid dominance over Khorasan and Persia and is traditionally seen as the founding moment of the Seljuk Empire, which Tughril proclaimed sultan soon after.

entries.name: Northwest Indian War
entries.desc: A conflict for control of the Northwest Territory between the United States and a confederation of Native American nations, considered the first American Indian War.
entries.tldr: The newly independent United States fought a confederation of Native American nations, including the Shawnee, Miami, and Delaware led by war chiefs Blue Jacket and Little Turtle, for control of the Northwest Territory north of the Ohio River. Native forces inflicted the worst defeat in US military history relative to force size at St. Clair's Defeat in 1791, wiping out roughly a quarter of the Army. General Anthony Wayne's campaign finally broke the confederacy at the 1794 Battle of Fallen Timbers, and the 1795 Treaty of Greenville opened most of Ohio to settlement.

entries.name: Prussian Crusade
entries.desc: A 13th-century series of campaigns by the Teutonic Knights and other Catholic crusaders to conquer and Christianize the pagan Old Prussians.
entries.tldr: A series of 13th-century campaigns invited by the Polish duke Konrad of Mazovia, who granted the Teutonic Knights land at Chełmno in exchange for subduing his pagan Baltic Prussian neighbors. Backed by papal crusading bulls and volunteers from across Catholic Europe, the Knights gradually conquered and forcibly converted the Prussian tribes, building a chain of castles to hold the new territory. Surviving Prussians were assimilated or resettled as the Knights established their own monastic state. The conquest reshaped the southeastern Baltic region for centuries.

entries.name: War of the Second Coalition
entries.desc: An 1798–1802 war between revolutionary France and a coalition of European monarchies led by Britain, Austria and Russia.

entries.name: Austro-Turkish War of 1716–1718
entries.desc: The Austro-Turkish War (1716–1718) was fought between the Habsburg monarchy and the Ottoman Empire. The 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz was not an acceptable permanent agreement for the Ottoman Empire.
entries.tldr: Seeking to reverse losses from the 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz, the Ottoman Empire went to war against Venice in 1714, prompting the Habsburg monarchy to intervene on Venice's behalf in 1716. Austrian forces led by the celebrated general Prince Eugene of Savoy won major victories at Petrovaradin and, after a lengthy siege, captured the fortress city of Belgrade in 1717. The 1718 Treaty of Passarowitz ended the war, with the Ottomans ceding Belgrade, northern Serbia, and parts of Wallachia to Austria.

entries.name: Dieppe Raid
entries.desc: Operation Jubilee or the Dieppe Raid was an Allied amphibious attack on the German-occupied port of Dieppe in northern France, during the Second World War.
entries.tldr: On 19 August 1942, Allied forces, mostly Canadian troops, staged a large amphibious raid on the German-occupied French port of Dieppe, codenamed Operation Jubilee. The assault went badly wrong from the outset, with tanks unable to cross the shingle beaches and troops pinned down by well-prepared German defenses. Of roughly 6,000 men who landed, over 3,300 were killed, wounded, or captured within hours, one of the costliest single days of the war for the Allies. Painful lessons from the disaster directly shaped the planning for the successful D-Day landings two years later.

entries.name: Vlora War
entries.desc: The Vlora War or Vlora crisis was a military conflict in the Vlorë region of Albania between the Kingdom of Italy and Albanian nationalists.

entries.name: Second Battle of Homs
entries.desc: The Second Battle of Homs was fought in western Syria on 29 October 1281, between the armies of the Mamluk dynasty of Egypt and the Ilkhanate, a division of the Mongol Empire centered on Iran.
entries.tldr: Fought in Syria between the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and an Ilkhanid Mongol army reinforced by Armenian and Georgian troops, part of continued Mongol attempts to break Mamluk power in the Levant. Mamluk Sultan Qalawun personally commanded his forces to a hard-fought victory that turned back this Mongol incursion. The win reinforced Mamluk control over Syria against renewed Ilkhanid pressure. It came a generation after the more famous Mamluk victory over the Mongols at Ain Jalut.

entries.name: Battle of Marengo
entries.desc: The Battle of Marengo was fought on 14 June 1800 between French forces under the First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte and Austrian forces near the city of Alessandria, in Piedmont, Italy.
entries.tldr: Napoleon, recently returned to power as First Consul, crossed the Alps into Italy to confront an Austrian army under General Melas that had besieged French positions across northern Italy. Melas's attack near Marengo caught the French by surprise and nearly drove them from the field, but the arrival of a division under General Desaix, who died in the fighting, turned the battle into a French win. It secured French control of northern Italy and boosted Napoleon's standing at home just months after his coup. He later had the story reshaped in official accounts to magnify his own role.

entries.name: Battle of Lechfeld
entries.desc: The Battle of Lechfeld was a series of military engagements over three days in August 955 in which the Kingdom of Germany, led by Otto I, defeated the Hungarian army.
entries.tldr: Magyar raiders had plagued Central Europe for decades when King Otto I of Germany assembled an army from across his realm to confront a large Hungarian force besieging Augsburg. Over three days near the Lech River, Otto's heavy cavalry broke the Hungarian army after hard fighting, and few of the raiders survived the retreat. The defeat ended the era of large-scale Magyar raids into Western Europe and pushed Hungary toward eventual settlement and Christianization. Otto's victory greatly boosted his prestige, foreshadowing his imperial coronation two years later.

entries.name: Battle of Karnal
entries.desc: The Battle of Karnal was a decisive victory for Nader Shah, founder of the Afsharid dynasty of Iran, during his invasion of India, defeating the army of Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah.
entries.tldr: Nader Shah, the Afsharid ruler who had recently seized the Persian throne, invaded the crumbling Mughal Empire and met Emperor Muhammad Shah's much larger army near Karnal, north of Delhi. Despite being outnumbered, Nader Shah's disciplined musketeers and cavalry outmaneuvered the unwieldy Mughal force and won a crushing victory in a matter of hours. Muhammad Shah was captured and forced to open Delhi to the Persians, who plundered the city and carried off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond. The defeat exposed Mughal weakness and hastened the empire's decline.

entries.name: Lithuanian Wars of Independence
entries.desc: The Lithuanian Wars of Independence, also known as the Freedom Struggles, refer to three wars Lithuania fought defending its independence at the end of World War I.
entries.tldr: As German occupation of Lithuania collapsed at the end of World War I, the new Lithuanian state fought off three opponents to secure independence: Soviet Russia, the Bermontians (a mixed German-Russian force), and Poland. The Polish war proved most bitter, since Polish forces seized the historic capital Vilnius in 1920, a loss Lithuania refused to accept for two decades. Despite that dispute, Lithuania secured Soviet recognition of its independence in the 1920 Treaty of Moscow, but Kaunas, not Vilnius, became its interwar capital.

entries.name: Battle of Vitoria
entries.desc: At the Battle of Vitoria, a British, Portuguese and Spanish army under the Marquess of Wellington broke the French army near Vitoria in Spain, a decisive Peninsular War victory.
entries.tldr: On 21 June 1813 an allied army of British, Portuguese, and Spanish troops under the Marquess of Wellington attacked a French force protecting King Joseph Bonaparte near Vitoria in northern Spain. Wellington's converging columns broke the French lines, and the retreat collapsed into a chaotic rout as soldiers abandoned a huge baggage train of loot, including Joseph's jewels and paintings later seized by Wellington. The defeat effectively ended Napoleonic rule in Spain and forced French forces back toward the Pyrenees, opening the way for the invasion of southern France.

entries.name: Aceh War
entries.desc: The Aceh War was an armed military conflict between the Sultanate of Aceh and the Kingdom of the Netherlands, part of the Dutch conquest of Sumatra and Indonesia.
entries.tldr: Beginning in 1873, the Netherlands invaded the independent Sultanate of Aceh in northern Sumatra to complete its control over the Indonesian archipelago. Dutch forces captured the sultan's palace early on but faced decades of tenacious guerrilla resistance led by religious and local leaders across Aceh's difficult terrain. The conflict dragged on with immense casualties until Dutch "pacification" campaigns finally suppressed organized resistance in the early twentieth century. It stands as one of the longest, costliest wars of Dutch colonial expansion.

entries.name: Battle of Crécy
entries.desc: The Battle of Crécy took place on 26 August 1346 in northern France between a French army under King Philip VI and an English army under King Edward III, an English victory in the Hundred Years' War.
entries.tldr: Fought on 26 August 1346 near Crécy in northern France, this was the first major land battle of the Hundred Years' War and a turning point in medieval warfare. King Edward III positioned English and Welsh longbowmen on a hillside, where their volleys shredded the advancing Genoese crossbowmen and repeated French cavalry charges. Edward's teenage son, later the Black Prince, held the vanguard and won his spurs in the fighting. The lopsided defeat shattered French confidence and paved the way for Edward's capture of Calais the next year.

entries.name: Siege of Constantinople
entries.desc: Constantinople, built on the land linking Europe to Asia, had strategic value for many empires and kingdoms who tried to conquer it throughout history.
entries.tldr: In 717 an Umayyad Arab army and fleet under Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik besieged Constantinople by land and sea, aiming to conquer the Byzantine capital where earlier Arab attempts had failed. Byzantine forces under Emperor Leo III used the incendiary weapon Greek fire to destroy much of the Arab navy, while a harsh winter and disease decimated the besieging army. The siege was lifted in 718, and the failure is often credited with checking further Arab expansion into southeastern Europe. It remains one of several sieges the city withstood owing to its strategic position linking Europe and Asia.

entries.name: First Battle of Gaza
entries.desc: The First Battle of Gaza was fought on 26 March 1917 during the first attempt by the Egyptian Expeditionary Force to advance through Gaza in the Sinai and Palestine Campaign of the First World War.
entries.tldr: On 26 March 1917, British and Commonwealth forces of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force made their first attempt to break through Ottoman defenses at Gaza during the Sinai and Palestine Campaign of the First World War. Early British cavalry gains were squandered by confused command decisions, and the attack was called off just as the town appeared close to falling. The failure was compounded when a second attempt weeks later also failed with heavy casualties. Commander Archibald Murray was subsequently replaced by Edmund Allenby, whose later offensive finally broke the Gaza-Beersheba line.

entries.name: Battle of Benevento
entries.desc: The Battle of Benevento was fought on 26 February 1266 near Benevento in southern Italy between the forces of Charles I of Anjou and King Manfred of Sicily, ending Hohenstaufen rule in Italy.
entries.tldr: Fought on 26 February 1266 near Benevento in southern Italy, the battle pitted Charles of Anjou, brother of the French king and papal candidate for the Sicilian crown, against King Manfred, illegitimate son of Emperor Frederick II, who had inherited Sicily's throne. Manfred's army, weakened by the defection of unreliable Italian allies, was defeated, and Manfred was killed in the fighting, his body reportedly denied Christian burial as an excommunicate. The victory installed Charles as king of Sicily and permanently ended Hohenstaufen rule over southern Italy.

entries.name: Battle of Legnano
entries.desc: The Battle of Legnano was fought between the imperial army of Frederick Barbarossa and the troops of the Lombard League on 29 May 1176, near Legnano in present-day Lombardy, Italy.
entries.tldr: Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa sought to reassert imperial authority over the wealthy cities of northern Italy, which had banded together as the Lombard League to resist him. Near Legnano, the League's infantry, rallying around a defended wagon called the Carroccio, withstood repeated charges by Barbarossa's knights until a fresh cavalry reserve broke the imperial line. Barbarossa was unhorsed and initially believed dead, and his army scattered. The defeat forced him to recognize the Lombard cities' self-governance in the Peace of Constance, a landmark win for communal independence.

entries.name: Ninth Russo-Turkish War
entries.desc: The Russo-Turkish War of 1828–1829 resulted from the Greek War of Independence; war broke out after the Ottoman Sultan closed the Dardanelles to Russian ships.
entries.tldr: Russia declared war on the Ottoman Empire after Sultan Mahmud II closed the Bosphorus and Dardanelles to Russian shipping, in response to Russian, British, and French intervention supporting Greek independence. Russian forces advanced through the Balkans and Caucasus, capturing Adrianople within striking distance of Constantinople before the Ottomans sued for peace. The 1829 Treaty of Adrianople granted Russia territorial gains, autonomy for Serbia, and confirmed Greek independence, further weakening an Ottoman Empire already reeling from losing its Janissary corps.

entries.name: Cisplatine War
entries.desc: The Cisplatine War was an armed conflict fought in the 1820s between the Empire of Brazil and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata over control of the Banda Oriental.
entries.tldr: From 1825 to 1828, the Empire of Brazil and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata fought for control of the Banda Oriental, the territory Brazil had annexed as its Cisplatine Province. Neither side achieved outright victory despite years of fighting on land and at sea, and both economies were strained by the prolonged conflict. British diplomatic mediation produced the 1828 Treaty of Montevideo, under which the disputed territory became the independent buffer state of Uruguay. The settlement satisfied British interests in keeping the Río de la Plata's two rival powers apart.

entries.name: Battle of the Zab
entries.desc: The Battle of the Zab took place on 25 January 750, on the banks of the Great Zab in what is now Iraq, spelling the end of the Umayyad Caliphate and the rise of the Abbasid Caliphate.
entries.tldr: Fought on 25 January 750 along the Great Zab River in what is now northern Iraq, this battle pitted the forces of the ruling Umayyad Caliphate, led by Caliph Marwan II, against the Abbasid revolutionary army. The larger but demoralized Umayyad force was routed, and Marwan fled westward, eventually being tracked down and killed in Egypt later that year. The Abbasid victory ended nearly a century of Umayyad rule and installed the Abbasid dynasty, which moved the caliphate's center of gravity east to Iraq and founded Baghdad, ushering in a golden age of Islamic learning and culture.

entries.name: First Anglo-Burmese War
entries.desc: The first of three wars between the British East India Company and the Konbaung dynasty of Burma, ending in a costly but decisive British victory.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1824 to 1826, the war pitted the expanding British East India Company against the Konbaung dynasty of Burma, whose earlier conquests along the Bay of Bengal had brought it into direct conflict with British India. Disease killed far more soldiers than combat on both sides during the grueling campaign. British forces eventually prevailed, and the 1826 Treaty of Yandabo forced Burma to cede Assam, Manipur, Arakan, and Tenasserim. It was the longest and most expensive war in British Indian history to that point and marked the start of Burma's absorption into the British Empire.

entries.name: Battle of Singapore
entries.desc: Japanese forces captured Singapore from the British in February 1942, one of the largest surrenders in British military history.
entries.tldr: In early 1942, Japanese forces under Tomoyuki Yamashita advanced rapidly down the Malay Peninsula on bicycles and light transport before crossing the Johor Strait onto Singapore Island. Despite outnumbering the attackers, the British and Commonwealth garrison under Arthur Percival surrendered on 15 February 1942 after Japanese troops seized the island's water supply and key positions. Winston Churchill called the loss of some 80,000 troops the worst disaster in British military history.

entries.name: Battle of Salsu
entries.desc: Goguryeo forces annihilated a vastly larger Sui Chinese army at the Salsu River, a decisive victory in the Goguryeo–Sui War.
entries.tldr: In 612, a huge Sui Chinese invasion force under Yuwen Shu pushed deep into Goguryeo territory toward Pyongyang, only to find itself overextended and short of supplies. Goguryeo general Eulji Mundeok lured the retreating Sui army into a crossing of the Salsu (Chongchon) River, then annihilated it, with only a small fraction of the original force reportedly making it back to China. The disaster crippled Emperor Yang's authority and contributed to the Sui dynasty's collapse within a few years.

entries.name: Battle of Asiago
entries.desc: Austro-Hungarian forces launched a major offensive on the Asiago plateau against Italy during World War I's Italian Front.
entries.tldr: Also called the Strafexpedition, or punitive expedition, by the Austro-Hungarian command, the offensive launched in May 1916 aimed to break the Italian front on the Asiago plateau and punish Italy for switching sides against its former ally in 1915. Austro-Hungarian troops made strong early gains against surprised defenders, advancing several kilometers, but supply trouble in the mountains and Russian pressure elsewhere stalled the attack. Italian counterattacks through June recovered much of the ground, leaving a costly, inconclusive campaign for Vienna.

entries.name: Franco-Syrian War
entries.desc: French forces defeated King Faisal's Arab Kingdom of Syria and entered Damascus, establishing the French Mandate over Syria.
entries.tldr: Following World War I, French troops moved to enforce the League of Nations mandate over Syria against the wishes of King Faisal, who had proclaimed an independent Arab Kingdom of Syria in Damascus. French forces defeated Faisal's poorly equipped army at the Battle of Maysalun in July 1920 and occupied Damascus days later. Faisal went into exile, only to be installed by Britain as king of Iraq the next year, while France began a mandate that would last until 1946.

entries.name: Battle of Brandywine
entries.desc: British forces under General Howe defeated Washington's Continental Army near Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania, during the American Revolutionary War.
entries.tldr: Fought on 11 September 1777 near Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania, the battle was the largest single-day engagement of the Revolutionary War, as British forces under General William Howe outmaneuvered George Washington's Continental Army by crossing the Brandywine Creek upstream and hitting its exposed flank. Despite resistance from units including the wounded Marquis de Lafayette, Washington's army was forced into a disorganized retreat, opening the road to Philadelphia, occupied by the British two weeks later. The army's survival let it fight on and eventually winter at Valley Forge.

entries.name: Battle of Adwa
entries.desc: Ethiopian forces under Emperor Menelik II decisively defeated an invading Italian army, securing Ethiopian independence.
entries.tldr: On 1 March 1896, a large Ethiopian army led by Emperor Menelik II overwhelmed an invading Italian colonial force near the town of Adwa in northern Ethiopia. Poor Italian intelligence and overconfidence led three separated columns into disaster against Menelik's larger, well-armed force, with thousands of Italian and colonial troops killed or captured. The defeat forced Italy to recognize Ethiopian sovereignty, making Ethiopia the only African state to repel a European colonial conquest during the Scramble for Africa.

entries.name: Alaska Purchase
entries.desc: The United States purchased Alaska from the Russian Empire for $7.2 million, extending American territory into the Arctic.
entries.tldr: In 1867, US Secretary of State William Seward negotiated the purchase of Alaska from the Russian Empire for $7.2 million, roughly two cents per acre. Russia sold the territory partly for fear of losing it without compensation in a future war, particularly to Britain, and because the fur trade that justified the colony was in decline. American critics mocked the deal as "Seward's Folly," doubting the value of the remote territory. The later discovery of gold and oil proved it enormously valuable.

entries.name: Battle of the Plains of Abraham
entries.desc: British forces defeated the French outside Quebec City in a turning point of the Seven Years' War that led to British control of Canada.
entries.tldr: On 13 September 1759, outside Quebec City, a British army under General James Wolfe defeated a French and colonial force under the Marquis de Montcalm on a plateau known as the Plains of Abraham, after Wolfe's troops scaled a poorly guarded cliff path to reach the field undetected overnight. Both commanders were mortally wounded during the roughly fifteen-minute battle, but the British held the field, and Quebec surrendered days later. The victory was a turning point of the Seven Years' War in North America, leading to the British conquest of New France, ceded formally in 1763.

entries.name: Battle of Nördlingen
entries.desc: Catholic Habsburg forces crushed the Protestant Swedish army at Nördlingen, a major turning point of the Thirty Years' War.
entries.tldr: On 6 September 1634, combined Habsburg Spanish and Imperial armies crushed the Protestant Swedish and German army near Nördlingen in Swabia, inflicting catastrophic losses that broke Sweden's military dominance in the Thirty Years' War. The defeat pushed Sweden's German Protestant allies to make peace with the Emperor at Prague the following year. It also drew Catholic France, alarmed by growing Habsburg strength, into open war against Spain and the Empire. The battle marked a major turning point that prolonged the war for another fourteen years.

entries.name: Battle of Leuthen
entries.desc: Frederick the Great's Prussian army used maneuver and terrain to rout a much larger Austrian force, securing control of Silesia.
entries.tldr: Facing a much larger Austrian army occupying Silesia after Frederick the Great's defeat at Kolín, the Prussian king used the terrain around Leuthen to conceal an oblique attack against one end of the overextended Austrian line. Prussian infantry, drilled to maneuver with precision, rolled up the flank before the rest of the Austrian army could react, turning a hopeless numerical situation into a decisive victory. The win is still studied as a model of tactical maneuver against superior numbers, and it secured Frederick's hold on Silesia.

entries.name: Battle of the Dnieper
entries.desc: One of the largest operations of World War II, Soviet forces crossed the Dnieper River and drove German forces from Ukraine's eastern bank.
entries.tldr: Fought from August to December 1943, this vast Soviet campaign aimed to force the Dnieper River, which German forces had fortified as part of the 'Eastern Wall' defensive line meant to halt the Red Army's advance after Kursk. Soviet troops crossed the wide river using improvised rafts and pontoons under heavy fire, established bridgeheads on the western bank, and eventually recaptured Kyiv in November 1943. Involving over four million men, its success shattered German hopes of stabilizing the Eastern Front and confirmed the Red Army's strategic initiative.

entries.name: First English Civil War
entries.desc: War between Royalists and Parliamentarians in England and Wales, part of the Wars of the Three Kingdoms, that reshaped English governance.
entries.tldr: Fighting broke out in 1642 after years of conflict between Charles I and Parliament over taxation, religion, and the limits of royal authority. Parliamentarian forces, eventually reorganized into the New Model Army under Oliver Cromwell and Thomas Fairfax, defeated the Royalists decisively at Naseby in 1645. Charles surrendered to the Scots in 1646, ending the first phase of fighting, though he was later tried and executed in 1649 after a second civil war reignited the conflict.

entries.name: Burgundian Wars
entries.desc: Conflict between the Duchy of Burgundy and the Swiss Confederacy in which Charles the Bold was defeated repeatedly and killed at Nancy.
entries.tldr: From 1474 to 1477, the ambitious Duke Charles the Bold of Burgundy fought the Swiss Confederacy and its allies in a bid to expand his territories along the Rhine. Swiss pikemen inflicted crushing defeats on Charles's army at Grandson and Morat, shattering the myth of Burgundian invincibility. Charles was killed at the final Battle of Nancy in January 1477, and his death without a male heir triggered the breakup of Burgundy between France and the Habsburgs. The wars cemented the Swiss pikeman's reputation as Europe's premier mercenary infantry.

entries.name: Thirteen Years' War
entries.desc: War between the Prussian Confederation, backed by Poland, and the Teutonic Order, ending Teutonic dominance over western Prussia.
entries.tldr: Beginning in 1454, the Prussian Confederation, an alliance of cities and nobles resentful of the Teutonic Order's rule, rose in revolt and sought protection from the Kingdom of Poland, triggering more than a decade of warfare. Fighting was costly and inconclusive for long stretches, straining both sides financially, until the war ended with the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466. The treaty split Prussia, granting western Prussia directly to Poland while the Order retained eastern Prussia as a Polish fief. The settlement marked the start of the Order's long decline as an independent power.

entries.name: Battle of Oudenarde
entries.desc: Anglo-Dutch forces under Marlborough and Prince Eugene defeated the French army during the War of the Spanish Succession.
entries.tldr: On 11 July 1708, allied British, Dutch, and Austrian forces under the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy caught a French army in the open and inflicted a sharp defeat near Oudenarde in Flanders during the War of the Spanish Succession. Marlborough's rapid forced march to intercept the French, followed by a fluid encirclement of their flank, is considered one of his finest tactical achievements. The victory let the allies besiege and capture Lille later that year, pushing deep into French territory. It further damaged the reputation of Louis XIV's once-dominant army.

entries.name: Battle of Nancy
entries.desc: René II of Lorraine and the Swiss Confederacy defeated and killed Charles the Bold, ending Burgundian power in Lorraine.
entries.tldr: In the harsh winter of 1476-77, Duke Charles the Bold of Burgundy laid siege to Nancy only to be caught outside its walls by a relief army of Lorrainers and Swiss Confederate pikemen under René II. Charles's mercenary-heavy force was overwhelmed, and his body was found days later, stripped and half-frozen in a nearby pond. His death without a male heir ended Burgundy's bid to become an independent great power, triggering a partition of his lands between France and the Habsburgs. The battle marked the high point of Swiss infantry's reputation in European warfare.

entries.name: Battle of Malplaquet
entries.desc: One of the bloodiest battles of the 18th century; the Grand Alliance under Marlborough won a costly victory over the French in the War of the Spanish Succession.
entries.tldr: During the War of the Spanish Succession, the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy led a Grand Alliance army against a strongly entrenched French force under Marshal Villars near Malplaquet. Repeated allied assaults eventually forced the French from their lines, but at a staggering cost, with allied casualties roughly double the retreating French. The battle is often cited as a Pyrrhic victory that fueled war weariness in Britain and the Netherlands. Villars reportedly told Louis XIV that another such defeat for the allies would ruin them.

entries.name: Hindenburg disaster
entries.desc: The German airship Hindenburg caught fire and was destroyed while attempting to dock in New Jersey, killing 36 people and ending the airship era.
entries.tldr: The German passenger airship LZ 129 Hindenburg, the largest aircraft ever built, was attempting to dock at Naval Air Station Lakehurst in New Jersey on 6 May 1937 after a transatlantic crossing when its hydrogen envelope caught fire. The airship was engulfed in flames and crashed to the ground within roughly 30 seconds, killing 36 people aboard and on the ground, though remarkably many passengers and crew survived. Captured on newsreel film and radio, the disaster shattered public confidence in hydrogen airships and effectively ended the era of passenger airship travel.

entries.name: Mahdist War
entries.desc: Muhammad Ahmad's Mahdist Sudanese forces overthrew Ottoman-Egyptian rule and later fought the British, establishing an independent Mahdist state in Sudan.
entries.tldr: Muhammad Ahmad, a religious leader who declared himself the Mahdi, led a Sudanese uprising that destroyed an Egyptian army under British general William Hicks and, in 1885, captured Khartoum after a long siege, killing governor-general Charles Gordon. Gordon's death made him a martyr in Britain and delayed reconquest for over a decade. The Mahdist state that followed ruled most of Sudan until an Anglo-Egyptian force under Herbert Kitchener crushed it at the 1898 Battle of Omdurman, using Maxim guns against Mahdist cavalry to devastating effect.

entries.name: Battle of Almansa
entries.desc: Decisive Bourbon victory over Habsburg forces during the War of the Spanish Succession, securing Philip V's hold on Spain.
entries.tldr: Fought on 25 April 1707 during the War of the Spanish Succession, the battle saw a Bourbon army under the exiled English general the Duke of Berwick crush a smaller Habsburg force under the Earl of Galway near Almansa in southeastern Spain. Poor coordination among the Allies' Portuguese, English, and Dutch contingents let their cavalry collapse. The defeat effectively ended Habsburg hopes of putting Archduke Charles on the Spanish throne, letting Philip V overrun Valencia and Aragon and abolish their historic local liberties, centralizing Spain under Bourbon rule.

entries.name: Battle of Solferino
entries.desc: Franco-Piedmontese victory over Austria that was the climactic battle of the Second Italian War of Independence.
entries.tldr: On 24 June 1859, French and Piedmontese forces under Napoleon III and Victor Emmanuel II defeated the Austrian army commanded by Emperor Franz Joseph in the largest battle fought in Europe since Leipzig. The engagement, marked by chaotic close-quarters fighting and roughly 30,000 casualties, was the decisive clash of the Second Italian War of Independence. Swiss businessman Henry Dunant witnessed the aftermath and was so shaken by the suffering of wounded soldiers that he was inspired to found the Red Cross.

entries.name: Siege of Acre
entries.desc: Mamluk capture of the last Crusader stronghold in the Holy Land, ending nearly two centuries of Crusader presence in the Levant.
entries.tldr: Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil besieged the last major Crusader stronghold in the Holy Land with a massive army and siege engines after his father had already captured most other Crusader towns. Acre's defenders, including military orders like the Templars and Hospitallers, resisted for weeks but were eventually overwhelmed once the walls were breached. Much of the population was killed or enslaved, and survivors fled by sea to Cyprus. The fall of Acre ended nearly two centuries of Crusader presence on the Levantine mainland.

entries.name: Battle of Marston Moor
entries.desc: Parliamentarian and Scottish Covenanter victory over Royalist forces, the largest battle of the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.
entries.tldr: During the English Civil War, Parliamentarian forces allied with a Scottish Covenanter army to besiege Royalist-held York, prompting Prince Rupert of the Rhine to march to its relief. The two sides met on Marston Moor, where an evening cavalry charge led by Oliver Cromwell's troopers broke the Royalist horse and turned a wavering battle into a decisive Parliamentarian win. The defeat cost the Royalists control of northern England and ended their hopes of winning the war outright. Cromwell's performance established his reputation as a formidable cavalry commander.

entries.name: Nakba
entries.desc: Mass displacement and dispossession of Palestinian Arabs accompanying the establishment of Israel in 1948.
entries.tldr: Arabic for 'catastrophe,' the term describes the mass flight and expulsion of roughly 700,000 Palestinian Arabs from their homes during the 1947-49 war surrounding the creation of the state of Israel. Around 400 Palestinian villages were depopulated and largely destroyed or repopulated, and most of the displaced were never permitted to return, becoming refugees in neighboring Arab states. Israel disputes aspects of the causes and scale, but the event, commemorated each May, remains central to Palestinian national identity and the unresolved refugee question.

entries.name: Battle of Morgarten
entries.desc: Swiss Confederate ambush that destroyed an invading Austrian army, a founding victory of the Old Swiss Confederacy.
entries.tldr: On 15 November 1315, warriors of the newly formed Swiss Confederacy ambushed an invading Habsburg army in a narrow pass beside Lake Ägeri, rolling logs and boulders down onto the trapped knights before closing in with halberds. The Austrian cavalry, unable to maneuver in the confined terrain, suffered a crushing defeat. The victory secured the young alliance of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden and is remembered as a founding triumph of Swiss independence. It also showed how disciplined infantry could defeat mounted knights on the right terrain.

entries.name: Battle of Gazala
entries.desc: Axis victory over British Commonwealth forces in the Western Desert Campaign that led to the fall of Tobruk.
entries.tldr: Fought from late May to mid-June 1942 in the Libyan desert west of Tobruk, this battle saw Field Marshal Erwin Rommel's Axis forces outmaneuver a numerically superior British Eighth Army despite becoming briefly trapped in a defensive pocket nicknamed 'the Cauldron.' Rommel resupplied his encircled units through a gap in British minefields and broke out to shatter the Allied defensive 'boxes' one by one, forcing a British retreat. The victory led directly to the fall of Tobruk days later.

entries.name: Operation Nordwind
entries.desc: Last major German offensive on the Western Front, launched to relieve pressure from the Battle of the Bulge.
entries.tldr: With the Battle of the Bulge stalling in the Ardennes, German forces launched this second, simultaneous offensive further south in Alsace, aiming to destroy the US Seventh Army and retake Strasbourg, recently liberated by Free French forces. Fierce fighting around Hatten-Rittershoffen and the Colmar Pocket produced heavy casualties on both sides before the German advance was halted. Hitler ordered the operation partly to relieve pressure on the Ardennes offensive, spreading thin German reserves across two fronts. Its failure marked the last major German offensive in the west.

entries.name: Battle of Aachen
entries.desc: Bitter urban battle in which American forces captured the first major German city of World War II.
entries.tldr: In October 1944, American forces of the US First Army fought their way into Aachen, the first major German city to fall to the Allies in the Second World War and symbolically significant as Charlemagne's historic seat. Hitler ordered the city defended to the last man, leading to nearly three weeks of brutal house-to-house urban combat. American troops eventually reduced German strongpoints with tanks and artillery firing point-blank through city streets, forcing a garrison surrender on 21 October.

entries.name: Battle of Białystok–Minsk
entries.desc: German encirclement that destroyed two Soviet armies in the opening days of Operation Barbarossa.
entries.tldr: Fought over the last week of June 1941, the battle came in the opening days of Operation Barbarossa, Nazi Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union, as Army Group Centre's panzer pincers raced ahead of the infantry to encircle Soviet forces around Białystok and Minsk. Two entire Soviet armies, plus parts of several others, were trapped in the resulting pockets and largely destroyed, with several hundred thousand soldiers killed, captured, or missing. The encirclement exposed the Red Army's disorganization after Stalin's prewar purges and opened the road toward Smolensk and Moscow.

entries.name: Battle of Uman
entries.desc: German offensive that encircled and annihilated two Soviet armies near Uman, Ukraine, in 1941.
entries.tldr: In late July and early August 1941, German and allied Axis forces encircled the Soviet Sixth and Twelfth Armies near Uman in Ukraine during the opening months of Operation Barbarossa. The resulting "Uman pocket" trapped over 100,000 Soviet soldiers, most of whom were killed or captured as the encirclement closed. It was one of several catastrophic Soviet defeats in the summer of 1941 that nearly destroyed the Red Army's forces in Ukraine before the front stabilized later that year.

entries.name: Machtergreifung
entries.desc: Adolf Hitler's rise to the German chancellorship and the Nazi Party's subsequent consolidation of dictatorial power.
entries.tldr: Meaning 'seizure of power,' this term covers the weeks after Adolf Hitler's January 1933 appointment as German chancellor by President Hindenburg, during which the Nazi Party rapidly dismantled Weimar democracy. The Reichstag fire that February was used to justify emergency decrees suspending civil liberties, and the Enabling Act let Hitler's cabinet legislate without parliament. Rival parties and unions were banned within months, and by Hindenburg's 1934 death Hitler had merged the presidency and chancellorship into the Führer title.

entries.name: Battle of Varna
entries.desc: Ottoman victory over a Crusader army led by Władysław III of Poland and Hungary, ending the Crusade of Varna.
entries.tldr: In November 1444, a Crusader army led by the young Polish-Hungarian king Wladyslaw III and the Hungarian commander John Hunyadi marched into the Balkans to expel the Ottomans from Europe, but was crushed by Sultan Murad II's forces near the Black Sea port of Varna. Wladyslaw was killed in the fighting, reportedly beheaded with his head displayed on a pike as proof of the Ottoman victory. The disastrous defeat ended the Crusade of Varna and secured Ottoman dominance in the Balkans for generations.

entries.name: First Boer War
entries.desc: Boer victory over British forces in the Transvaal that restored South African Republic independence.
entries.tldr: Fought from December 1880 to March 1881, this brief conflict saw Boer settlers of the Transvaal rise against British annexation of their republic, imposed just three years earlier. Boer commandos, skilled marksmen on familiar terrain, inflicted sharp defeats on British forces, most notably at Majuba Hill where the British commander was killed. The humiliated British government chose to negotiate, restoring Transvaal self-government under nominal oversight. Tensions over gold-rich Transvaal territory erupted into the far larger Second Boer War eighteen years later.

entries.name: War of the Austrian Succession
entries.desc: Multi-power European conflict sparked by Maria Theresa's succession to the Habsburg throne.

entries.name: Battle of Marignano
entries.desc: French and Venetian victory over the Old Swiss Confederacy that ended the War of the League of Cambrai.
entries.tldr: Newly crowned French king Francis I invaded Italy to reclaim the Duchy of Milan, and his army, reinforced by Venetian allies, met the renowned pikemen of the Old Swiss Confederacy, defending the city for a rival claimant. Two days of fierce fighting, including artillery bombardment that neutralized the Swiss pike formations' usual advantage, ended in a costly French and Venetian win. Swiss losses were severe enough that the battle marked the end of the Confederacy's era as Europe's dominant land power. The victory secured French control of Milan and ended the War of the League of Cambrai.

entries.name: Battle of Gettysburg
entries.desc: Union victory over Confederate forces widely regarded as the turning point of the American Civil War.
entries.tldr: Fought over three days, 1–3 July 1863, near the Pennsylvania town of Gettysburg, this was the largest and bloodiest battle ever fought in North America, with roughly 50,000 combined casualties. Confederate General Robert E. Lee's second invasion of the North culminated on the final day in Pickett's Charge, a doomed frontal assault on entrenched Union positions repulsed with devastating losses. The Union victory marked the strategic high-water mark of the Confederacy, which never again invaded the North.

entries.name: Battle of Eylau
entries.desc: Bloody, inconclusive clash between Napoleon's Grande Armée and Russian forces in East Prussia.
entries.tldr: Fought in a blinding snowstorm on 7–8 February 1807 near the East Prussian town of Eylau, this battle pitted Napoleon's Grande Armée against a Russian army under Levin von Bennigsen, reinforced by Prussian troops. When Russian artillery shattered a French corps, Marshal Joachim Murat led one of history's largest cavalry charges to stabilize the French line. Both sides suffered appalling casualties, and neither achieved a clear victory. The battle's cost shocked French opinion and foreshadowed the bloodier stalemates of later campaigns.

entries.name: Seven Years' War
entries.desc: Global conflict pitting Britain and Prussia against France, Austria, and their allies across Europe, the Americas, and India.
entries.tldr: A genuinely global conflict fought on multiple continents as Britain and Prussia faced France, Austria, Russia, and other allies in a struggle over the European balance of power and colonial supremacy. Fighting ranged from Frederick the Great's campaigns in Central Europe to British-French battles in North America, India, and West Africa, with Britain emerging as the dominant global colonial power. The 1763 Treaty of Paris gave Britain most of French North America, while Prussia retained Silesia. Winston Churchill later called it the first true "world war."

entries.name: Battle of the Pyramids
entries.desc: Napoleon's victory over Ottoman Egyptian forces near Cairo during the French invasion of Egypt.
entries.tldr: On 21 July 1798, near Cairo, Napoleon Bonaparte's invading French army defeated the Egyptian Mamluk forces defending the region, using disciplined infantry squares to repel repeated Mamluk cavalry charges with devastating effect. The battle, named for the pyramids of Giza visible on the horizon, opened Egypt to French occupation, though French naval power was crippled days later when Admiral Nelson destroyed the fleet at the Battle of the Nile. The campaign brought a wave of French scholars to Egypt whose studies helped launch the modern discipline of Egyptology.

entries.name: Battle of Bunker Hill
entries.desc: On 17 June 1775, British troops took the Charlestown peninsula near Boston from American militia in a costly frontal assault. Britain's heavy casualties in the technical victory showed the war would not be quickly won.
entries.tldr: Fought on 17 June 1775 during the early siege of Boston, the battle takes its name from Bunker Hill though most fighting occurred on adjacent Breed's Hill, where colonial militia had hastily fortified a position overlooking the city. British troops under General William Howe launched repeated frontal assaults up the hill against entrenched Americans, who inflicted devastating casualties before running low on ammunition and withdrawing. Though a technical British victory, the huge cost stunned London and showed the rebellion would not be swiftly crushed.

entries.name: Battle of Monte Cassino
entries.desc: Fought across four Allied assaults between January and May 1944, this battle broke the German Gustav Line defenses south of Rome, at the cost of the historic abbey's destruction, and opened the road to Rome.
entries.tldr: Allied forces launched four successive assaults between January and May 1944 to break through the German Gustav Line anchored on the hilltop abbey of Monte Cassino, south of Rome. Believing German troops occupied the ancient monastery, Allied bombers reduced it to rubble in February, though German paratroopers had in fact stayed clear of the building until after its destruction.
