Polish, British, American, and French troops suffered enormous casualties before Polish forces finally took the ruins in May. The abbey has since been rebuilt.

entries.name: Battle of Grunwald
entries.desc: On 15 July 1410, a Polish–Lithuanian–Ruthenian army decisively defeated the Teutonic Knights near Grunwald, killing the order's Grand Master. The defeat broke the Teutonic Order's military dominance in the region.
entries.tldr: On 15 July 1410, a Polish–Lithuanian–Ruthenian army led by King Władysław II Jagiełło and Grand Duke Vytautas annihilated the Teutonic Knights near the villages of Grunwald and Tannenberg, killing Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen along with most of the order's senior leadership. It ranks among the largest battles of medieval Europe and one of the most decisive defeats the order ever suffered. Although the order survived a siege of its capital at Marienburg, the battle permanently broke its military dominance.

entries.name: Battle of Großbeeren
entries.desc: On 23 August 1813, Prussian forces under Friedrich von Bülow defeated a Franco-Saxon corps south of Berlin. The victory blocked a French advance on the city during the War of the Sixth Coalition.
entries.tldr: On 23 August 1813, Prussian troops under General Friedrich von Bülow intercepted a Franco-Saxon corps under Marshal Nicolas Oudinot as it advanced on Berlin as part of Napoleon's plan to seize the Prussian capital. Despite rain-soaked terrain, Bülow's forces broke the advancing columns and forced Oudinot into a disorganized retreat, abandoning the offensive. The victory, largely won by Prussian Landwehr militia, preserved Berlin during the War of the Sixth Coalition.

entries.name: Battle of the Milvian Bridge
entries.desc: The Battle of the Milvian Bridge took place between the Roman Emperors Constantine I and Maxentius on 28 October AD 312. It takes its name from the Milvian Bridge, an important route over the Tiber.
entries.tldr: On 28 October 312, near Rome, the emperor Constantine I defeated his rival Maxentius for control of the Western Roman Empire at a crossing of the Tiber called the Milvian Bridge. According to later Christian tradition, Constantine saw a vision before the battle, often described as a cross of light with the words 'in this sign, conquer,' and had his soldiers mark their shields with a Christian symbol. Maxentius drowned in the Tiber retreating across a pontoon bridge that collapsed under fleeing troops. The victory secured Constantine's rule and is linked to his embrace of Christianity.

entries.name: transition from Ming to Qing
entries.desc: The transition from Ming to Qing was a decades-long conquest of China by the Manchu-led Qing dynasty, beginning with Nurhaci's unification of the Jurchen tribes in 1616. It ended Ming rule over China.

entries.name: Battle of Okehazama
entries.desc: On 12 June 1560, Oda Nobunaga's greatly outnumbered forces ambushed and killed rival warlord Imagawa Yoshimoto, an upset victory that launched Nobunaga's rise toward unifying Japan.
entries.tldr: On 12 June 1560, Oda Nobunaga led a small force through a surprise flanking march and, aided by a sudden thunderstorm that masked his approach, launched a devastating ambush on the resting army of the powerful warlord Imagawa Yoshimoto. Imagawa was killed by Nobunaga's samurai, and his leaderless invasion force collapsed. The stunning upset transformed Nobunaga from a minor regional lord into a rising power and set him on the path toward unifying most of Japan. The battle is still studied as a classic example of a smaller force defeating a much larger one through surprise.

entries.name: Adams–Onís Treaty
entries.desc: Signed in 1819 by John Quincy Adams and Luis de Onís, this treaty ceded Spanish Florida to the United States and fixed the western border between the US and New Spain along a line to the Pacific.
entries.tldr: Negotiated by US Secretary of State John Quincy Adams and Spanish minister Luis de Onís, this treaty, signed in 1819 and ratified in 1821, ceded all of Spanish Florida to the United States in exchange for the US assuming $5 million in claims by American citizens against Spain. It also drew a definitive boundary between Louisiana Territory and Spain's remaining possessions, running to the Pacific and confirming US claims to Oregon. It followed years of tension over Florida, including Andrew Jackson's unauthorized incursions there.

entries.name: Partitio terrarum imperii Romaniae
entries.desc: The Partitio terrarum imperii Romaniae was the 1204 treaty dividing the conquered Byzantine Empire among the crusaders after they sacked Constantinople. It created a patchwork of Latin states on former Byzantine soil.
entries.tldr: After the knights of the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204, diverting from their original goal of Jerusalem, the crusade's Venetian and Frankish leaders drew up this treaty dividing the conquered Byzantine Empire among themselves. Venice secured coastal ports and islands that built its Mediterranean trading empire for centuries, while Frankish nobles carved out feudal states including the Latin Empire of Constantinople. The partition proved hard to enforce, since Byzantine successor states resisted and retook Constantinople in 1261, but it permanently fragmented Byzantine territory.

entries.name: Arab conquest of Armenia
entries.desc: A series of Rashidun Caliphate campaigns from 639 to 661 against Byzantine-held Armenia. The fighting brought Armenia under Arab suzerainty while its local nakharar princes retained considerable autonomy.
entries.tldr: Between 639 and 661, armies of the Rashidun Caliphate launched repeated campaigns into Armenia, then contested between Byzantine and Sasanian influence, eventually bringing the region under Arab suzerainty. Rather than direct rule, the caliphate let Armenia's local nakharar noble families keep considerable autonomy over their hereditary territories in exchange for tribute and nominal submission. This let Armenian Christian culture and church institutions survive largely intact under Muslim overlordship for centuries.

entries.name: Battle of Khotyn
entries.desc:
Battle of Khotyn can refer to several battles that took place near Khotyn:Battle of Khotyn (1509)
Battle of Khotyn (1530)
Battle of Khotyn (1621)
Battle of Khotyn (1673)
Siege of Khotyn (1788)
entries.tldr: This entry covers the 1673 clash at Khotyn, where Polish-Lithuanian forces under hetman Jan Sobieski stormed the Ottoman fortress and routed its garrison. Sobieski's artillery and cavalry broke the Ottoman lines in a single day, inflicting heavy losses as defenders fled across the Dniester River, many drowning when a bridge collapsed under the retreat. News of the victory reached Warsaw just as King Michael I died, and Sobieski's triumph helped secure his own election as king of Poland soon after. The win briefly checked Ottoman expansion into eastern Europe.

entries.name: Anglo-Spanish War
entries.desc: A conflict from 1654 to 1660 in which Oliver Cromwell's England attacked Spain's American and European possessions as part of the "Western Design." England seized Jamaica from Spain during the fighting.
entries.tldr: Launched in 1654 as part of Oliver Cromwell's "Western Design" to weaken Catholic Spain's American empire, this war saw an English fleet fail to capture Santo Domingo but succeed in seizing the lightly defended island of Jamaica in 1655. Fighting spread to European waters, where English admirals like Robert Blake intercepted Spanish treasure convoys and won a notable victory at Santa Cruz de Tenerife. Spain, weakened by its parallel war with France, could not recapture Jamaica. The war ended in 1660 with English possession of Jamaica confirmed.

entries.name: Siege of Baghdad
entries.desc: The 1258 Siege of Baghdad saw a Mongol army under Hulegu Khan capture and sack the city, killing the last Abbasid caliph and ending the Abbasid Caliphate's five centuries of rule.
entries.tldr: In February 1258 a Mongol army led by Hulegu Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, surrounded and stormed Baghdad, then the intellectual capital of the Islamic world. The city's libraries, including the House of Wisdom, were destroyed and much of the population massacred over days of sack. Caliph al-Musta'sim was executed, ending the Abbasid Caliphate's five-century rule and shattering the political unity of the Islamic heartland. The destruction is often cited as a lasting blow to Mesopotamia's irrigation-based agriculture and scholarly culture.

entries.name: Battle of Tippecanoe
entries.desc: On 7 November 1811, American forces under William Henry Harrison defeated Tecumseh's Native confederacy while Tecumseh was away, dispersing the alliance and giving Harrison a reputation he later rode to the presidency.
entries.tldr: On 7 November 1811, Governor William Henry Harrison led a preemptive expedition against Prophetstown, the settlement built by Tecumseh and his brother Tenskwatawa to unite Native American resistance to US expansion. With Tecumseh away recruiting allies, Tenskwatawa's warriors launched a dawn attack on Harrison's camp instead of waiting to be struck, and both sides took heavy losses before the Americans burned the village. The battle badly weakened Tecumseh's confederacy and gave Harrison the nickname he later rode to the presidency in his 1840 "Tippecanoe and Tyler Too" campaign.

entries.name: Caucasian War
entries.desc: A prolonged conflict in which the Russian Empire subdued the peoples of the North Caucasus who resisted subjugation during the Russian conquest of the region, ending in annexation and the mass expulsion of Circassians.
entries.tldr: Over roughly a century, Russian imperial forces waged a grinding campaign to subjugate the mountain peoples of the North Caucasus, most notably the Chechens, Dagestanis, and Circassians. Resistance was led for decades by the Avar imam Shamil, whose Islamic mountain state held off Russian armies until his capture in 1859. The war's final and most brutal phase targeted the Circassians, culminating in a mass expulsion in 1864 that killed or displaced hundreds of thousands, an event many now describe as ethnic cleansing. Its legacy still shapes tensions in the North Caucasus today.

entries.name: Siege of Damascus
entries.desc: The 1148 Siege of Damascus was the main campaign of the Second Crusade: crusader forces besieged the Muslim-ruled city before abandoning the effort after only four days, effectively ending the crusade.
entries.tldr: In July 1148 the leaders of the Second Crusade, newly arrived in the Holy Land, chose to besiege the Muslim-ruled city of Damascus rather than pursue their original goal of retaking Edessa. The crusader army camped in orchards outside the city but was forced onto more exposed ground after only four days, and Muslim relief forces compelled a full withdrawal. The failed siege effectively ended the Second Crusade in humiliation and pushed Damascus toward closer alliance with other Muslim powers. It is often cited as a turning point that hardened Muslim unity against the Crusades.

entries.name: Battle of Saragarhi
entries.desc: On 12 September 1897, 21 soldiers of the 36th Sikhs held a signalling post against thousands of Afghan tribesmen, fighting to the last man; the stand is remembered as one of history's celebrated last stands.
entries.tldr: On 12 September 1897, twenty-one soldiers of the 36th Sikh Regiment held an isolated signalling post on the Samana Range against an assault by thousands of Orakzai and Afridi tribesmen. Every defender fought to the death, but their resistance delayed the attackers long enough for nearby forts to be reinforced and held. The stand is commemorated annually by Sikh regiments and is often ranked among history's most celebrated last stands for its extreme disparity in numbers.

entries.name: Battle of Kohima
entries.desc: Fought from April to June 1944, this battle halted Japan's invasion of British India; combined with the victory at Imphal, it forced a costly Japanese retreat and marked the turning point of the Burma campaign.
entries.tldr: Japanese forces besieged the small hill station of Kohima, a lightly defended British supply depot in northeast India, hoping to cut off Allied forces at Imphal and open the road into India. British and Indian troops held a shrinking perimeter for weeks, at one point fighting Japanese soldiers across a district commissioner's tennis court. Relief columns broke the siege in June 1944, and the starving Japanese army was forced into a disastrous retreat through the monsoon. Combined with Imphal, Kohima ended Japan's last major offensive of the war and is often called the 'Stalingrad of the East.'

entries.name: Battle of Mukden
entries.desc: Fought from February to March 1905, this was the largest land battle fought before World War I; Japan's victory over the Russian army effectively ended Russian land resistance in the Russo-Japanese War.
entries.tldr: Fought over three weeks from February to March 1905 around the Manchurian city of Mukden, this was the largest land battle the world had yet seen, involving hundreds of thousands of troops on fronts stretching over fifty miles. Japanese forces under Ōyama Iwao outmaneuvered the Russian army, forcing a costly retreat despite failing to achieve full encirclement. The defeat, following the earlier fall of Port Arthur, effectively ended organized Russian land resistance in the war. Combined with the naval disaster at Tsushima soon after, it pushed Russia toward a negotiated peace.

entries.name: Battle of the Yalu River
entries.desc: On 17 September 1894, Japan's navy decisively defeated China's Beiyang Fleet at the mouth of the Yalu River, establishing Japanese naval supremacy for the remainder of the First Sino-Japanese War.
entries.tldr: On 17 September 1894, during the First Sino-Japanese War, the Imperial Japanese Navy engaged China's Beiyang Fleet near the mouth of the Yalu River, in one of the largest naval battles since the age of sail. Japan's faster, more modern cruisers outmaneuvered and outgunned the Chinese fleet, sinking several ships while suffering no losses of their own. The engagement established Japanese naval dominance for the rest of the war, letting Japan control the sea lanes needed to invade Korea and Manchuria, and contributed to the Treaty of Shimonoseki.

entries.name: Battle of Dara
entries.desc: The Battle of Dara was fought between the Eastern Roman Empire and the Sasanians in 530 AD. It was one of the battles of the Iberian War.
entries.tldr: Fought in 530 near the fortress city of Dara on the Byzantine-Persian frontier, this battle pitted a Sasanian army under the general Perozes against a smaller East Roman force commanded by the young general Belisarius. Using field fortifications and disciplined cavalry reserves, Belisarius routed the larger Persian force. It was Belisarius's first major victory and established his reputation as Emperor Justinian I's leading general, during the Iberian War over control of the Caucasus.

entries.name: Ōnin War
entries.desc: The Ōnin War (1467–1477) was a civil war among rival samurai clans over succession disputes during Japan's Muromachi period. Its devastation of Kyoto and the shogunate's weakened authority ushered in the Sengoku era.

entries.name: Treaty of Hadiach
entries.desc: The Treaty of Hadiach was a treaty signed on 16 September 1658 in Hadiach, Cossack Hetmanate between representatives of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and Zaporozhian Cossacks.
entries.tldr: Signed in September 1658, this treaty between the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and Cossack hetman Ivan Vyhovsky sought to reincorporate Cossack Ukraine as an autonomous third component, styled the Grand Duchy of Rus'. Its terms promised Cossack self-governance, religious rights for the Orthodox Church, and elevated status for the Cossack elite. Opposition among rank-and-file Cossacks favoring closer ties with Muscovy, plus Polish resistance to its generous terms, left it only partly ratified. Renewed warfare and Vyhovsky's downfall soon left Ukraine divided among rival powers.

entries.name: Battle of Arnhem
entries.desc: The Battle of Arnhem was fought during the Second World War, as part of the Allied Operation Market Garden. It took place around the Dutch city of Arnhem from 17 to 26 September 1944.
entries.tldr: Fought from 17 to 26 September 1944, the battle was the disastrous climax of Operation Market Garden, an Allied plan to seize a chain of bridges across the Netherlands and outflank German defenses. British and Polish airborne troops landed near Arnhem to capture the Rhine road bridge, but ground forces advancing overland were delayed, and the paratroopers met unexpectedly strong German armor. A small force under Lieutenant Colonel John Frost held the bridge four days before being overwhelmed, and the failed effort ended Allied hopes of finishing the war in 1944.

entries.name: Battle of Stalingrad
entries.desc: Fought from August 1942 to February 1943, Soviet forces encircled and destroyed Germany's Sixth Army in the deadliest battle in history, marking the turning point of World War II on the Eastern Front.
entries.tldr: From August 1942 to February 1943, German and Soviet forces fought a grinding, house-by-house battle for the city of Stalingrad that became the deadliest single battle in history. Soviet commanders launched Operation Uranus in November 1942, encircling Germany's Sixth Army under Friedrich Paulus, who surrendered against Hitler's explicit orders once relief and resupply proved impossible. The German defeat, with roughly two million combined casualties, is widely seen as the psychological and strategic turning point of World War II on the Eastern Front.

entries.name: Battle of Yamazaki
entries.desc: The Battle of Yamazaki  was fought in 1582 in Yamazaki, Japan, located in current-day Kyoto Prefecture. This battle is sometimes referred to as the Battle of Mt.
entries.tldr: Fought on 2 July 1582 near Kyoto, this battle pitted Toyotomi Hideyoshi against Akechi Mitsuhide, the samurai general who had just forced his lord Oda Nobunaga to commit suicide in the Honno-ji Incident. Hideyoshi rushed his army back from western Japan in a famously swift march to confront Mitsuhide before he could consolidate power. Mitsuhide's outnumbered forces were routed, and he was killed while fleeing, having ruled only thirteen days, earning him the epithet 'the Thirteen-Day Shogun.'

entries.name: Battle of Soissons
entries.desc: In 486, Frankish king Clovis I defeated the Roman general Syagrius near Soissons, ending the last vestige of Roman rule in northern Gaul and opening the region to Frankish control.
entries.tldr: In 486, the Frankish king Clovis I defeated Syagrius, the last Roman military governor still holding territory in northern Gaul, near Soissons. The victory ended organized Roman rule in the region and opened the way for Frankish consolidation of what would become France. A famous later anecdote, the Vase of Soissons, in which Clovis executed a soldier who defied him over looted treasure, is often cited as an early demonstration of his growing royal authority over his warband.

entries.name: Siege of Orléans
entries.desc: The Siege of Orléans (1428–1429) was the turning point of the Hundred Years' War: English forces besieged the city until Joan of Arc rallied French troops to break the siege, reviving French morale.
entries.tldr: English forces besieged the strategically vital city of Orléans in October 1428, and its fall would have opened the way to conquer the rest of unoccupied France during the Hundred Years' War. In 1429 a young woman named Joan of Arc arrived claiming divine guidance, rallied dispirited French troops, and led an assault that forced the English to lift the siege within days. The victory reversed the war's momentum and led directly to the coronation of Charles VII at Reims. Joan's role at Orléans made her a national symbol, though she was captured and executed only two years later.

entries.name: Battle of Sagrajas
entries.desc: In 1086, Almoravid forces under Yusuf ibn Tashfin defeated Alfonso VI of Castile at Sagrajas, checking the Christian reconquest of Iberia and opening al-Andalus to decades of Almoravid rule.
entries.tldr: Yusuf ibn Tashfin, founder of the Almoravid dynasty, crossed from North Africa at the invitation of Iberia's Muslim rulers to help stem the Christian advance, and on 23 October 1086 his combined forces crushed Alfonso VI of Castile near Sagrajas. The defeat, one of the worst suffered by a Christian king during the Reconquista, cost Alfonso most of his army and stalled his expansion for years. The victory also gave the Almoravids the pretext to depose the fractious taifa kings and absorb al-Andalus directly into their empire.

entries.name: Battle of Vimy Ridge
entries.desc: In April 1917, the four divisions of the Canadian Corps captured German-held Vimy Ridge in a costly, coordinated assault that is remembered in Canada as a defining moment of national identity.
entries.tldr: In April 1917 the four divisions of the Canadian Corps, fighting together for the first time, assaulted German-held Vimy Ridge in northern France as part of the wider Battle of Arras. Careful rehearsal, a creeping artillery barrage, and improved infantry tactics let the Canadians seize the heavily fortified ridge within days, at a cost of over 10,000 casualties. The ridge had resisted earlier French assaults for years. The victory is commemorated in Canada as a founding moment of national identity, and a memorial now stands atop the ridge.

entries.name: Treaty of Paris
entries.desc: Treaty of Paris may refer to one of many treaties signed in Paris, France:
entries.tldr: The Treaty of Paris signed in 1259 settled a long-running dispute between King Henry III of England and King Louis IX of France dating back to the loss of the Angevin lands earlier in the century. Henry formally renounced his claims to Normandy, Anjou, Maine, and Poitou. In return Louis recognized Henry's continued possession of Gascony, now held as a vassal fief of the French crown rather than outright sovereign territory. That awkward feudal relationship, with an English king owing homage to a French one, later fed renewed conflict, including the Hundred Years' War.

entries.name: Third Geneva Convention
entries.desc: The Third Geneva Convention of 1949 set standards for the humane treatment of prisoners of war. It expanded protections established after the mistreatment of POWs during the Second World War.
entries.tldr: Adopted in 1949 alongside three companion conventions, this convention established detailed legal protections for prisoners of war, building on earlier agreements that proved inadequate during the mass captivity and abuse of POWs in the Second World War. It sets standards covering humane treatment, food and medical care, and protection from violence and intimidation, while prohibiting coercive interrogation. It applies to international armed conflicts and binds nearly every country, remaining the core legal framework invoked in disputes over treatment of captured combatants.

entries.name: Battle of Coronel
entries.desc: On 1 November 1914, a German East Asia Squadron under Maximilian von Spee defeated a British squadron under Christopher Cradock off Chile, sinking two cruisers. It was the Royal Navy's first defeat at sea in a century.
entries.tldr: On 1 November 1914 off central Chile, Vice Admiral Maximilian von Spee's German East Asia Squadron intercepted a weaker British force under Sir Christopher Cradock. German gunnery sank the armored cruisers HMS Good Hope and HMS Monmouth with the loss of all hands, including Cradock, while the German ships suffered barely a scratch. It was the Royal Navy's first defeat at sea in over a century. London responded by dispatching battlecruisers that annihilated von Spee's squadron five weeks later at the Falkland Islands.

entries.name: Battle of Dettingen
entries.desc: Fought on 27 June 1743 near Dettingen in Bavaria during the War of the Austrian Succession, an allied army defeated the French. It was the last time a reigning British monarch personally led troops into battle.
entries.tldr: On 27 June 1743, the 'Pragmatic Army' of British, Hanoverian, and Austrian troops, personally led by King George II, defeated a French force under the Duc de Noailles near Dettingen in Bavaria during the War of the Austrian Succession. The French had nearly trapped the allies against the Main River, but a premature cavalry charge let the allied infantry escape and drive the French back. George II fought on foot after his horse bolted, the last reigning British monarch to lead troops personally in battle.

entries.name: Battle of Pliska
entries.desc: In July 811, Bulgarian forces under Khan Krum ambushed and destroyed the Byzantine army in the Balkan passes, killing Emperor Nicephorus I, whose skull Krum reportedly had made into a drinking cup.
entries.tldr: In late July 811, the Bulgarian Khan Krum lured the invading army of Byzantine Emperor Nicephorus I into the mountain passes near the Bulgarian capital of Pliska and annihilated it in a night ambush. Nicephorus himself was killed, the first Byzantine emperor to die fighting a foreign enemy in centuries, and Krum reportedly had his skull lined with silver and used as a drinking cup. The catastrophic defeat shocked Byzantium and emboldened Bulgaria to expand deep into the Balkans in the following years.

entries.name: Attack of the Dead Men
entries.desc: The Attack of the Dead Men, or the Battle of Osowiec Fortress, was a battle of World War I that took place at Osowiec Fortress, at 4:00 AM on August 6, 1915.
entries.tldr: During the German siege of the Russian-held Osowiec Fortress in present-day Poland, German forces released chlorine gas before attacking at 4 a.m. on 6 August 1915, expecting the garrison wiped out. Instead, surviving Russian defenders of the 226th Zemlyansky Regiment, badly burned and coughing blood from the gas, mounted a desperate bayonet counterattack. The horrifying sight of these disfigured, dying soldiers reportedly panicked the German attackers into a chaotic retreat, a legend of Russian wartime endurance.

entries.name: Battle of Denain
entries.desc: On 24 July 1712, French forces under Marshal Villars defeated a Dutch and Austrian army near Denain during the War of the Spanish Succession, reversing France's decline and easing peace terms at Utrecht.
entries.tldr: On 24 July 1712, Marshal Claude de Villars led a surprise French assault across the Scheldt to storm the fortified camp at Denain, overwhelming the Dutch garrison before Prince Eugene of Savoy's main allied army could intervene. The victory, achieved when France's fortunes in the War of the Spanish Succession looked hopeless, let Villars roll up allied supply depots and fortresses along the frontier. It restored French bargaining power and eased the terms France secured in the 1713 Treaty of Utrecht.

entries.name: Second Opium War
entries.desc: The Second Opium War (1856–1860) was fought by Britain and France against Qing China to expand trading rights, including the legalization of opium. China's defeat forced further concessions, including more treaty ports.
entries.tldr: Fought by Britain, joined by France, against Qing China after an incident involving the Arrow, a Chinese-owned but British-registered ship, gave pretext to force wider trading and diplomatic access than the first war had won. Anglo-French forces captured Guangzhou and later Beijing, burning the Emperor's Summer Palace in retaliation for the torture and killing of European envoys. The Treaties of Tientsin and Beijing opened further ports, legalized the opium trade, and permitted foreign legations to reside in Beijing. The defeat deepened Qing China's growing era of foreign encroachment.

entries.name: Battle of New Orleans
entries.desc: On 8 January 1815, Andrew Jackson's American forces decisively defeated the British army outside New Orleans, fought after the war-ending Treaty of Ghent had already been signed, and made Jackson a national hero.
entries.tldr: Unaware that peace commissioners had already signed the Treaty of Ghent weeks earlier, British veterans of the Napoleonic Wars assaulted Andrew Jackson's fortified lines below New Orleans and suffered devastating losses from American artillery and rifle fire. The lopsided victory cost Jackson's mixed force of regulars, militia, and privateers led by Jean Lafitte only a fraction of British casualties. News of the win reached Washington around the same time as the peace treaty, letting Americans celebrate the war as a triumph. The battle made Jackson a national hero.

entries.name: Philippine Revolution
entries.desc: The Philippine Revolution (1896–1898) was an independence war waged by the Katipunan movement against Spanish colonial rule. It ended over 300 years of Spanish rule but was soon followed by American annexation.
entries.tldr: The Katipunan, a secret society founded by Andrés Bonifacio, launched an armed uprising against Spanish colonial rule after its existence was discovered, forcing an early revolt rather than the planned rising. Emilio Aguinaldo emerged as the movement's leading general, eventually displacing and executing Bonifacio before declaring a short-lived Philippine Republic. Fighting stalled into a truce in 1897, but revolution reignited in 1898 alongside the Spanish-American War, with American naval support helping revolutionaries defeat Spain, only for the islands to pass to American control.

entries.name: Gunboat War
entries.desc: Naval conflict between Denmark–Norway and Britain, supported by Sweden, during the Napoleonic Wars.
entries.tldr: Britain, wary that Denmark-Norway's fleet might fall into Napoleon's hands, bombarded Copenhagen in 1807 and seized the entire Danish-Norwegian navy without a formal declaration of war. Stripped of its major warships, Denmark-Norway waged the rest of the conflict with small, agile gunboats harassing British and allied shipping in Danish and Norwegian waters. The prolonged war, allied with a British blockade, crippled the twin kingdom's economy and contributed to Norway's separation from Denmark in 1814.

entries.name: Third Battle of Ypres
entries.desc: Also known as Passchendaele, a WWI campaign fought by the Allies against Germany near Ypres, Belgium.
entries.tldr: Fought from July to November 1917 near Ypres, Belgium, this British-led offensive, commonly known by the name of its final objective, Passchendaele, aimed to break through German lines and reach the coast. Heavy rain turned the battlefield into a notorious quagmire that bogged down tanks, artillery, and infantry alike. Allied forces eventually captured the ruined village of Passchendaele after months of attrition, advancing only a few miles at a cost of hundreds of thousands of casualties on each side. The battle became emblematic of the horror of First World War trench warfare.

entries.name: Battle of Nagashino
entries.desc: Allied forces of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu decisively defeated the Takeda clan.
entries.tldr: On 28 June 1575, the allied armies of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated the Takeda clan's famed cavalry near Nagashino Castle in central Japan. Nobunaga's forces used long wooden palisades and coordinated volleys from thousands of arquebusiers to break the Takeda cavalry charges, a tactic later celebrated as an early example of massed firearm use in Japan. Many senior Takeda generals died in the defeat, badly weakening the clan. The battle marked a turning point in Nobunaga's drive to unify Japan under his rule.

entries.name: Great Sioux War of 1876
entries.desc: War between the US and allied Lakota Sioux and Northern Cheyenne forces over the Black Hills.
entries.tldr: The US government demanded that Lakota and Cheyenne bands leave unceded hunting grounds in the Black Hills after gold was discovered there, and moved to force them onto reservations by military campaign in 1876. Combined Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho forces under leaders including Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull annihilated Lieutenant Colonel George Custer's detachment at the Battle of the Little Bighorn. Despite that stunning defeat, sustained US military pressure over the following year forced most bands onto reservations and stripped the Black Hills from Sioux control.

entries.name: Arauco War
entries.desc: Long conflict between Spanish colonizers and the Mapuche people in Chile's Araucanía region.
entries.tldr: Beginning in 1546 and lasting, with intermittent truces, into the nineteenth century, the Arauco War pitted Spanish colonial forces against the Mapuche people of southern Chile, who fiercely resisted conquest of their Araucanía homeland. Mapuche warriors adapted quickly to European tactics and horses, inflicting notable defeats on the Spanish, including the death of conquistador Pedro de Valdivia in 1553. Unable to achieve lasting conquest, Spain eventually recognized the Bío-Bío River as a de facto frontier for centuries.

entries.name: Battle of White Mountain
entries.desc: Early Thirty Years' War battle near Prague where forces backing Ferdinand II defeated Frederick V's army.
entries.tldr: On 8 November 1620, near Prague, the Catholic League army, commanded by Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, decisively defeated the Protestant army of Frederick V, the self-styled 'Winter King' of Bohemia, in barely an hour of fighting. Frederick fled into exile and Bohemia lost its independence, becoming a hereditary Habsburg possession subjected to forced re-Catholicization and the suppression of the Czech nobility. The battle ended the Bohemian phase of the Thirty Years' War and set the stage for the conflict's much longer, bloodier continuation.

entries.name: Battle of Valmy
entries.desc: France's first major Revolutionary War victory, halting a Prussian advance on Paris.
entries.tldr: On 20 September 1792, a French revolutionary army, many of its soldiers raw volunteers, stood its ground against an invading Prussian force near Valmy in an engagement decided largely by an extended artillery duel rather than close combat. The Prussians, weakened by disease and logistical strain, unexpectedly withdrew rather than press the attack. The unlikely French stand, witnessed by the writer Goethe among the Prussian entourage, boosted revolutionary confidence and is often cited as marking a new era in European history.

entries.name: Battle of the Golden Spurs
entries.desc: Flemish rebels won a surprise victory over the French royal army near Kortrijk in 1302.
entries.tldr: On 11 July 1302, near Kortrijk in Flanders, an army of Flemish townsmen, fighting largely on foot with pikes and goedendags, inflicted a shocking defeat on a heavily armored French royal army sent to crush a Flemish revolt against French overlordship. The French cavalry, bogged down in marshy ground crossed by streams, was cut down in large numbers, and the battle takes its name from the hundreds of golden spurs stripped from dead French knights afterward. The victory of commoners over noble cavalry shocked Europe and is commemorated in Flanders as a symbol of regional identity.

entries.name: Siege of Yorktown
entries.desc: Final major land battle of the American Revolutionary War, won by American and French forces.
entries.tldr: In autumn 1781, American forces under George Washington and French troops under the Comte de Rochambeau trapped a British army led by Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia. A French fleet under the Comte de Grasse blocked British reinforcement or evacuation by sea, sealing the garrison's fate. After weeks of bombardment Cornwallis surrendered his roughly 8,000 troops on October 19, effectively ending major fighting in the Revolutionary War. News of the defeat helped bring down the British government and led to peace talks recognizing American independence.

entries.name: Franco-Prussian War
entries.desc: Conflict between France and the Prussian-led North German Confederation, 1870–71.
entries.tldr: Provoked partly by the Ems Dispatch, a doctored account of a diplomatic exchange over the Spanish succession, France declared war on Prussia in July 1870. Prussia's superior mobilization and artillery crushed French armies at Sedan, where Napoleon III himself was captured, and besieged Paris into surrender. The 1871 peace ceded Alsace-Lorraine to the new German Empire, proclaimed at Versailles, and left France thirsting for revenge for the next four decades.

entries.name: Svalbard Treaty
entries.desc: Recognized Norwegian sovereignty over the Svalbard archipelago while restricting its military use.
entries.tldr: Signed in 1920 after the First World War, the Svalbard Treaty recognized Norwegian sovereignty over the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard, previously no one's territory despite competing mining and fishing interests. In exchange, it guaranteed citizens of signatory nations equal rights to economic activity there, such as coal mining, and required Norway to keep the islands demilitarized. Dozens of countries, including Russia, have since acceded to its terms. It still shapes Svalbard's governance, allowing a Russian mining settlement to operate on Norwegian soil.

entries.name: November Uprising
entries.desc: Armed rebellion by Polish officers in Warsaw against Russian imperial rule, 1830–31.
entries.tldr: Polish army cadets in Warsaw rose up against Russian imperial rule after learning their forces might be used to suppress revolutions elsewhere in Europe, quickly drawing in much of Congress Poland's population and army. The rebels declared the dethronement of Tsar Nicholas I as King of Poland, but divisions between conservative and radical factions slowed effective military organization. Russian forces under Ivan Paskevich crushed the uprising after a year, capturing Warsaw in September 1831, and harsh Russification followed alongside the 'Great Emigration' of Polish exiles.

entries.name: Entente Cordiale
entries.desc: Agreements signed in 1904 that markedly improved relations between the UK and France.
entries.tldr: Signed in April 1904, the Entente Cordiale was a set of agreements between Britain and France resolving longstanding colonial disputes, notably over Egypt and Morocco, rather than a formal military alliance. It ended centuries of intermittent Anglo-French rivalry and signaled a new diplomatic alignment against a rising Germany. The entente was tested and strengthened by the Moroccan Crises, and laid the groundwork for British and French military cooperation once the First World War broke out. It remains a byword for the broader Franco-British partnership of the twentieth century.

entries.name: Battle of Balaclava
entries.desc: Crimean War battle near Sevastopol between British, French, and Ottoman allies and Russian forces.
entries.tldr: Fought on 25 October 1854 during the Crimean War, the battle near the British port of Balaclava is best remembered for the disastrous Charge of the Light Brigade, in which a garbled order sent British cavalry directly into well-defended Russian guns. Earlier in the same fight, Scottish infantry famously formed a thin red line and repelled a Russian cavalry charge. Tactically inconclusive, the battle left the ongoing siege of nearby Sevastopol largely unaffected, but the Light Brigade's charge became legend, memorialized soon after in Tennyson's poem.

entries.name: Battle of Wagram
entries.desc: Napoleon's costly but decisive victory over Austria that broke up the Fifth Coalition.
entries.tldr: Fought over 5-6 July 1809 near Vienna, Napoleon's Grande Armee engaged the Austrian army of Archduke Charles in one of the largest battles of the Napoleonic Wars, involving some 300,000 men. After a costly first day, Napoleon massed a huge artillery battery and a decisive infantry assault under Marshal MacDonald broke the Austrian center on the second day. Austrian casualties and exhaustion forced Charles to retreat, and the defeat led to the Treaty of Schoenbrunn, which dissolved the Fifth Coalition and stripped Austria of territory and population.

entries.name: First Barbary War
entries.desc: The US fought Ottoman Tripolitania over tribute demands for safe passage of American shipping.
entries.tldr: From 1801 to 1805, the young United States fought its first war overseas against Tripolitania, one of the North African Barbary states, after refusing continued tribute payments demanded for safe passage of American shipping. The conflict featured the dramatic burning of the captured frigate USS Philadelphia by Stephen Decatur and an overland march by US Marines and mercenaries to capture the city of Derna. A negotiated peace in 1805 ended Tripoli's demands, though full Barbary tribute payments only ended after a second war a decade later.

entries.name: Battle of Suomussalmi
entries.desc: Finnish forces defeated a much larger Soviet army during the Winter War of 1939–40.
entries.tldr: Over December 1939 and January 1940, Finnish ski troops under Colonel Hjalmar Siilasvuo used mobility and knowledge of the terrain to encircle and destroy two invading Soviet divisions in the forests around Suomussalmi. Fighting in temperatures far below freezing, the Finns broke the larger Soviet force into isolated pockets, or "mottis," and picked them off piecemeal. The lopsided victory, achieved against a vastly larger enemy, became one of the most celebrated episodes of Finnish resistance during the Winter War.

entries.name: Battle of Kulm
entries.desc: The Battle of Kulm was fought near the town Kulm and the village Přestanov in northern Bohemia. It was fought on 29–30 August 1813, during the War of the Sixth Coalition.
entries.tldr: During the War of the Sixth Coalition, a French corps under General Vandamme pursued retreating allied forces into Bohemia, hoping to cut off their line of retreat after the allied defeat at Dresden. Russian, Austrian, and Prussian troops rallied near the villages of Kulm and Přestanov and, reinforced by a Prussian corps arriving unexpectedly on Vandamme's rear, surrounded and crushed the French force. Vandamme himself was captured along with thousands of his men. The victory restored allied morale after Dresden and helped set up the decisive campaign that culminated at Leipzig weeks later.

entries.name: Battle of Waterloo
entries.desc: On 18 June 1815, Anglo-allied forces under Wellington and Prussian forces under Blücher defeated Napoleon near Waterloo, ending his rule permanently and bringing the Napoleonic Wars to a close.
entries.tldr: On 18 June 1815, near the village of Waterloo south of Brussels, an Anglo-allied army under the Duke of Wellington held off repeated French assaults, including a massed cavalry charge and the final advance of the Imperial Guard, while awaiting a Prussian army under Field Marshal Bluecher. When the Prussians reached the field in the evening, the combined Allied counterattack broke the French army and forced a general retreat. Napoleon abdicated for the second time days later and was exiled to Saint Helena, and Waterloo permanently ended his rule and the Napoleonic Wars.

entries.name: Battle of Badr
entries.desc: Fought on 13 March 624 CE near Badr in the Hejaz, this battle saw a small Muslim force under Muhammad defeat a larger Meccan army. The unexpected victory established Muhammad's authority and is commemorated in the Quran.
entries.tldr: Fought on 13 March 624 CE near Badr in the Hejaz, the battle saw a Muslim force of roughly 300 men led by the Prophet Muhammad ambush and rout a much larger Meccan caravan-guard army. Despite being heavily outnumbered, the Muslims used disciplined tactics and surprise to kill or capture many of Mecca's leading men, including the prominent opponent Abu Jahl. The unexpected victory sharply boosted Muhammad's authority in Medina and is referenced directly in the Quran as a sign of divine support, setting the stage for years of conflict with Mecca that followed.

entries.name: Battle of Uhud
entries.desc: The Battle of Uhud was fought between the early Muslims and the Quraysh during the Muslim–Quraysh wars in a valley north of Medina near Mount Uhud on Saturday, 23 March 625 AD.
entries.tldr: Fought on 23 March 625 in a valley near Mount Uhud north of Medina, this battle initially favored the outnumbered Muslim forces under Muhammad until a group of archers left their post to seize plunder, abandoning a key defensive position. Meccan Quraysh cavalry under Khalid ibn al-Walid exploited the gap to encircle and rout the Muslims, wounding Muhammad and killing his uncle Hamza. The defeat, a stark contrast to the earlier victory at Badr, became a lasting lesson on discipline and obedience referenced in the Quran.

entries.name: 1948 Arab–Israeli War
entries.desc: The interstate phase of the 1948 Palestine war, fought between Israel and neighboring Arab states after Israel declared independence. Israel won, gaining more land than the UN partition plan had proposed.
entries.tldr: When Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, armies from Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq, and Lebanon invaded, opening the interstate phase of the wider 1948 Palestine war. Israeli forces, better organized despite an international arms embargo, halted the invasions and went on the offensive. Armistice agreements in 1949 left Israel controlling more territory than the 1947 UN partition plan had allotted, while Jordan and Egypt held the West Bank and Gaza. The war produced hundreds of thousands of Palestinian refugees.

entries.name: 1948 Palestine war
entries.desc: Civil war between Palestine's Arab and Jewish communities after the UN partition vote, ending with British withdrawal and Israeli independence. It caused Palestinian displacement and led into the wider Arab–Israeli war.
entries.tldr: Following the UN's November 1947 vote to partition Mandatory Palestine, fighting broke out between Arab and Jewish communities even before British forces completed their withdrawal. Jewish militias gradually gained the upper hand over Palestinian Arab irregulars and allied volunteers, capturing key cities as British administration collapsed. The war culminated in Israel's 14 May 1948 declaration of independence, which triggered invasion by Arab states. Roughly 700,000 Palestinians were displaced, an event Palestinians call the Nakba.

entries.name: Seven Days Battles
entries.desc: The Seven Days Battles were a series of seven battles over seven days from June 25 to July 1, 1862, near Richmond, Virginia, during the American Civil War. Confederate General Robert E.
entries.tldr: Fought southeast of Richmond as Confederate General Robert E. Lee, newly given command of the Army of Northern Virginia, launched attacks to drive Union General George McClellan's larger army from the Confederate capital during the Peninsula Campaign. Despite tactical missteps and heavy Confederate casualties in battles like Gaines's Mill and Malvern Hill, Lee forced McClellan into a fighting retreat to the James River. The campaign ended the immediate threat to Richmond and established Lee's aggressive reputation. It set the stage for his invasion of Maryland later that summer.

entries.name: Battle of Talas
entries.desc: In July 751, Abbasid and allied forces defeated Tang China's army near the Talas River, halting Chinese expansion into Central Asia and, by tradition, helping papermaking technology spread to the Islamic world.
entries.tldr: In July 751, an Abbasid army under Ziyad ibn Salih clashed with a Tang Chinese force under Gao Xianzhi near the Talas River in Central Asia, with the battle's outcome decided when Karluk mercenaries fighting for the Chinese defected mid-fight. The Abbasid victory halted further Tang expansion westward and secured Central Asia for Islamic influence for centuries. According to tradition, though the details are debated, Chinese prisoners taken after the battle helped transmit papermaking technology to the Islamic world.

entries.name: Treaty of Shimoda
entries.desc: The Treaty of Shimoda (1855) was the first treaty between Russia and Japan, establishing diplomatic relations and dividing the Kuril Islands between them. It followed Japan's opening to foreign trade.

entries.name: Battle of Cold Harbor
entries.desc: Fought near Mechanicsville, Virginia, from 31 May to 12 June 1864, Union assaults on entrenched Confederate lines were repulsed with heavy losses. It is remembered as one of Grant's costliest failures of the war.
entries.tldr: Part of Grant's 1864 Overland Campaign against Robert E. Lee, this Virginia battle culminated in a Union frontal assault on 3 June that was shattered within about an hour, producing thousands of casualties for almost no ground gained. Grant later called it the attack he most regretted ordering in the entire war. The stalemate pushed Grant to abandon direct assaults on Lee's lines and instead swing south toward Petersburg. It remains a byword for the futility of massed infantry charges against entrenched positions.

entries.name: Battle of Stirling Bridge
entries.desc: On 11 September 1297, Scottish forces under William Wallace and Andrew Moray defeated a larger English army by exploiting a narrow river crossing, a decisive early victory in the Wars of Scottish Independence.
entries.tldr: On 11 September 1297, Scottish forces under William Wallace and Andrew Moray watched as a much larger English army under the Earl of Surrey began crossing a narrow wooden bridge over the River Forth. The Scots attacked once enough English troops had crossed, trapping and slaughtering them while the rest of the army could only watch helplessly from the far bank. The decisive victory, one of the few times medieval infantry defeated mounted knights so completely, made Wallace's reputation and led to his appointment as Guardian of Scotland.

entries.name: Saxon Wars
entries.desc: The Saxon Wars (772–804) were Charlemagne's campaigns to conquer and Christianize the independent Saxon tribes. After decades of revolts and reprisals, Saxony was subdued and absorbed into the Frankish Empire.
entries.tldr: A three-decade series of campaigns in which Charlemagne sought to conquer the independent, still-pagan Saxon tribes east of the Frankish kingdom and forcibly convert them to Christianity. Saxon resistance under leaders like Widukind included repeated revolts, met with brutal reprisals such as the mass execution at Verden. Charlemagne eventually broke Saxon resistance through a mix of warfare, forced resettlement, and harsh conversion laws imposed on the population. Saxony's incorporation extended Frankish power to the edge of Scandinavia and the Slavic lands.

entries.name: Halifax explosion
entries.desc: On 6 December 1917 the explosives-laden SS Mont-Blanc collided with another ship in Halifax harbour and detonated, devastating the city and killing or injuring thousands in one of history's largest accidental explosions.
entries.tldr: On 6 December 1917, the French cargo ship SS Mont-Blanc, loaded with high explosives for the war effort, collided with the Norwegian vessel Imo in Halifax's harbor and caught fire. Crowds gathered on shore and at windows to watch the burning ship, unaware of its cargo, when it detonated in one of the largest artificial explosions before the nuclear age. The blast flattened much of Halifax's Richmond district and killed around 2,000 people, prompting a major relief effort from Boston that helped seed the tradition of Nova Scotia's annual Christmas tree gift to that city.

entries.name: Battle of Guadalete
entries.desc: Fought in July 711 in southern Spain, Umayyad forces under Tariq ibn Ziyad defeated the Visigothic army of King Roderic, who was killed. The victory opened the way for the swift Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula.
entries.tldr: Traditionally dated to July 711, this battle in southern Spain saw an Umayyad invasion force under Tariq ibn Ziyad defeat the Visigothic army of King Roderic, whose fate afterward is uncertain since his body was never conclusively identified. Ancient and medieval accounts of the battle's exact location and circumstances vary considerably. The Visigothic kingdom's sudden collapse let Umayyad forces overrun most of the Iberian Peninsula within a few years, establishing what became Al-Andalus.

entries.name: Battle of Dobro Pole
entries.desc: An Allied offensive on the Macedonian front from 15 to 18 September 1918 broke through Bulgarian lines at Dobro Pole. The breakthrough led directly to Bulgaria's surrender that month, the first Central Power to fall.
entries.tldr: From 15 to 18 September 1918, a combined Serbian and French force launched a surprise offensive against fortified Bulgarian positions at Dobro Pole on the Macedonian front, breaking through after heavy artillery bombardment. The collapse of the Bulgarian line triggered a general retreat and mutinies within an army already exhausted by years of static warfare. Within two weeks Bulgaria requested an armistice, the first Central Power to surrender in World War I, exposing the southern flank of its allies.

entries.name: Battle of the Korsun–Cherkassy Pocket
entries.desc: Fought from January to February 1944, Soviet forces encircled two German army corps near Korsun, destroying much of the trapped force and marking a major Red Army victory of the Dnieper–Carpathian offensive.
entries.tldr: Fought from January to February 1944 as part of the Soviet Dnieper–Carpathian offensive, Red Army forces encircled roughly two German army corps, some 56,000 men, in a pocket near the towns of Korsun and Cherkasy in Ukraine. German relief attempts and a desperate breakout by the trapped forces in mid-February resulted in heavy losses, with many encircled troops killed or captured trying to escape through Soviet lines in freezing, muddy conditions. The pocket's destruction was a major Soviet victory, sometimes compared to a smaller Stalingrad.

entries.name: Battle of Cherbourg
entries.desc: The Battle of Cherbourg was part of the Battle of Normandy during World War II. It was fought immediately after the successful Allied landings on 6 June 1944.
entries.tldr: Fought between 6 and 30 June 1944, the battle for the Norman port of Cherbourg came right after the Allied D-Day landings, as American forces of the U.S. VII Corps pushed across the Cotentin Peninsula to seize a deep-water harbor essential for supplying the invasion. German defenders, ordered by Hitler to hold at all costs, fought a stubborn delaying action before the garrison surrendered on 26 June, though isolated resistance continued for days. Retreating engineers had thoroughly demolished the port, and it took Allied engineers weeks to make it usable.

entries.name: People's Crusade
entries.desc: The People's Crusade of 1096 was a popular, poorly organized march to the Holy Land that preceded the main armies of the First Crusade. Most participants were killed by Seljuk forces after crossing into Anatolia.
entries.tldr: Inspired by the preaching of Peter the Hermit, this loosely organized mass of peasants, minor knights, and pilgrims set out for the Holy Land months ahead of the main armies later gathered by the great lords of the First Crusade. Poorly supplied and undisciplined, bands within the movement carried out massacres of Jewish communities in the Rhineland en route, among the first large-scale pogroms in European history. After crossing into Anatolia, most crusaders were ambushed and slaughtered by Seljuk forces near Nicaea, with only a small remnant surviving to join the main crusade later.

entries.name: Battle of Zenta
entries.desc: On 11 September 1697, Habsburg forces under Prince Eugene of Savoy destroyed an Ottoman army crossing the Tisza River, a victory that led to the Treaty of Karlowitz and ended Ottoman expansion into Central Europe.
entries.tldr: On 11 September 1697, a Habsburg imperial army under Prince Eugene of Savoy caught the Ottoman army of Sultan Mustafa II while it was crossing the Tisza River near Zenta and inflicted a devastating defeat, destroying much of the Ottoman force as it was pinned against the riverbank. The Ottoman Grand Vizier was among the thousands killed, and the sultan himself narrowly escaped. The rout forced the empire to the negotiating table, leading to the 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz, which ceded large territories to the Habsburgs and ended Ottoman expansion into Central Europe.

entries.name: King George's War
entries.desc: King George's War (1744–1748) was the North American theatre of the War of the Austrian Succession, fought between British and French colonists and their Native allies. Peace restored prewar borders, settling little.
entries.tldr: Fought as the North American theater of the War of the Austrian Succession, this conflict pitted British colonists, chiefly from New England, against New France and its Native allies. Its most celebrated episode was the 1745 New England militia capture of the supposedly impregnable French fortress of Louisbourg on Cape Breton Island. The 1748 Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle handed captured Louisbourg back to France, infuriating New Englanders who felt their sacrifice had been wasted. The unresolved rivalry set the stage for the French and Indian War a few years later.

entries.name: Battle of the Neva
entries.desc: In 1240, Novgorod forces under Prince Alexander defeated an invading Swedish force on the Neva River, a victory that earned him the epithet 'Nevsky' and became a lasting symbol of Russian resistance to Western incursion.
entries.tldr: In July 1240, a Novgorodian force led by the young Prince Alexander launched a surprise attack on an invading Swedish army that had landed at the confluence of the Neva and Izhora rivers, part of a broader pattern of Catholic Scandinavian and German incursions into Orthodox Rus' territory. Alexander's smaller force struck before the Swedes could organize a defense and drove them back to their ships with heavy losses. The victory earned him the epithet 'Nevsky,' 'of the Neva,' and, alongside his later win at the Battle of the Ice, became a lasting symbol of resistance to Western incursion.

entries.name: Attack on Pearl Harbor
entries.desc: Japan launched a surprise strike on the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on 7 December 1941, sinking or damaging much of the battle fleet. The attack brought the United States into the Second World War.
entries.tldr: On the morning of 7 December 1941, hundreds of Japanese carrier-based aircraft struck the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, in a surprise attack meant to cripple American naval power before Japan expanded into Southeast Asia. The raid sank or damaged eight battleships and killed over 2,400 Americans, though the fleet's carriers were at sea and escaped destruction. President Roosevelt called it "a date which will live in infamy" the next day, and Congress declared war on Japan almost unanimously, bringing the US into the war.

entries.name: Cologne War
entries.desc: From 1583 to 1588, Catholic forces led by Bavaria's Duke Ernest defeated Protestant claimant Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg for control of the Electorate of Cologne, reasserting Catholic rule in the region.
entries.tldr: Beginning in 1583, the Archbishop-Elector of Cologne, Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg, converted to Protestantism and refused to resign his office, upending the religious balance guaranteed by the Peace of Augsburg. Catholic forces backed by Bavaria and Spain, led by Ernest of Bavaria, drove Gebhard out and secured the electorate for the church by 1588. The conflict devastated the Rhineland and helped keep the region firmly Catholic into the modern era. It is often seen as an early rehearsal for the far larger Thirty Years' War three decades later.

entries.name: Persian Expedition of 1796
entries.desc: The Persian Expedition of 1796, ordered by Catherine the Great, was a Russian campaign against Persia following the sack of Tbilisi. Catherine's death soon after led her successor Paul I to abandon its gains.
entries.tldr: Catherine the Great ordered this Russian campaign into the Caucasus and northern Persia in retaliation for the Persian ruler Agha Mohammad Khan's brutal 1795 sack of Tbilisi, capital of Russia's Georgian ally. Russian forces under General Valerian Zubov advanced rapidly, capturing Derbent and Baku and occupying much of the eastern Caucasus with little resistance. Catherine's death in November 1796, however, brought her son Paul I to the throne, and he reversed her expansionist policy, ordering Zubov's forces to withdraw entirely, leaving Russian control of the Caucasus to wait for later tsars.

entries.name: Treaty of Pereyaslav
entries.desc: The Treaty of Pereyaslav (1654) was an agreement in which Zaporozhian Cossacks pledged allegiance to the Russian tsar. It brought Cossack Ukraine under Russian protection, away from Polish-Lithuanian rule.
entries.tldr: Signed in January 1654, the Treaty of Pereyaslav recorded the allegiance sworn by Zaporozhian Cossack hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky and his officers to Tsar Alexis of Russia, seeking protection after years of revolt against Polish–Lithuanian rule. In return, the Cossacks retained substantial autonomy over their own administration, courts, and military structure. The treaty's exact meaning remains disputed, variously read as a personal union, a military alliance, or a fuller incorporation of Ukraine into Russia. It is seen by many as a foundational moment in that long, contested relationship.

entries.name: Treaty of Georgievsk
entries.desc: The Treaty of Georgievsk (1783) made the eastern Georgian kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti a protectorate of the Russian Empire. It marked the start of Russian expansion into the Caucasus.
entries.tldr: Signed in 1783 at Georgievsk in the North Caucasus, this treaty placed the eastern Georgian kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti under Russian protection in exchange for military guarantees against Persian and Ottoman threats. King Erekle II sought the arrangement to shield his kingdom from stronger regional powers, but Russia failed to intervene when Persian forces devastated Tbilisi in 1795. The treaty nonetheless became the legal basis Russia later used to formally annex the Georgian kingdom in 1801. It marked an early step in Russia's long expansion into the Caucasus.

entries.name: Battle of Westerplatte
entries.desc: On 1 September 1939, German forces attacked the small Polish garrison at Westerplatte, the opening engagement of the invasion of Poland and the start of World War II in Europe.
entries.tldr: At dawn on 1 September 1939 the German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on the small Polish military depot at Westerplatte in the Free City of Danzig, marking the opening engagement of the invasion of Poland and the start of the Second World War in Europe. A garrison of roughly 200 Polish soldiers under Major Henryk Sucharski held out against repeated infantry and naval assaults for seven days before surrendering on 7 September, far longer than either side had expected. The stubborn defense became an enduring symbol of Polish resistance under overwhelming odds.

entries.name: Treaty of Saadabad
entries.desc: The Treaty of Saadabad (1937) was a non-aggression pact signed by Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Afghanistan in Tehran. It aimed to secure regional stability among the four states in the interwar period.

entries.name: Anglo-Japanese Alliance
entries.desc: A mutual-defense pact between Britain and Japan signed in 1902, aimed chiefly at containing Russian expansion in East Asia. It underpinned Japan's rise as a great power until it lapsed in 1923.
entries.tldr: Signed in London in January 1902, the Anglo-Japanese Alliance committed each power to aid the other if attacked by more than one enemy, primarily to check Russian expansion into Manchuria and Korea. It gave Japan diplomatic cover to fight the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905 without fear of French intervention on Russia's behalf, a war Japan won decisively. Renewed and broadened twice, it helped bring Japan into the First World War on the Allied side. Rising unease over Japan's power led it to lapse in 1923.

entries.name: Battle of Prokhorovka
entries.desc: Fought on 12 July 1943 as part of the Battle of Kursk, this was one of the largest tank engagements of World War II; it checked the German southern advance and helped end Germany's last major offensive in the East.
entries.tldr: On 12 July 1943, Soviet and German armored forces clashed near the village of Prokhorovka in one of the largest tank engagements of World War II, part of the broader Battle of Kursk. Soviet counterattacks, though suffering heavy tank losses of their own, blunted the advance of German SS panzer divisions attempting to break through the southern shoulder of the Kursk salient. The battle helped end Germany's last major strategic offensive in the east, after which the Red Army held the initiative for the rest of the war.

entries.name: Battle of Aspern-Essling
entries.desc: In May 1809, Austrian forces under Archduke Charles drove Napoleon's army back across the Danube near Vienna. It was Napoleon's first major defeat in the field, though he recovered and won at Wagram weeks later.
entries.tldr: Fought over 21 and 22 May 1809 in villages east of Vienna, the battle came as Napoleon tried to cross the Danube and confront the Austrian army under Archduke Charles. Repeated Austrian attacks on the bridgehead villages, combined with the collapse of Napoleon's pontoon bridges under fire, forced the French back across the river with heavy losses, including the death of Marshal Jean Lannes. It was Napoleon's first major personal defeat in the field, though he rebuilt his army and beat Charles decisively six weeks later at Wagram.

entries.name: Battle of Alam el Halfa
entries.desc: In late August and early September 1942, Britain's Eighth Army under Montgomery repelled Rommel's attempt to break through south of El Alamein. The failed offensive left the Axis unable to threaten Egypt again.
entries.tldr: In early September 1942, German field marshal Erwin Rommel launched an offensive to outflank the British Eighth Army's Alamein line and break through to the Suez Canal. British commander Bernard Montgomery, newly arrived and forewarned by Ultra intelligence, had fortified the Alam el Halfa ridge and let Rommel's tanks exhaust themselves against strong defenses. Short on fuel, Rommel withdrew, ending Axis hopes of reaching Egypt and setting the stage for Montgomery's later offensive at El Alamein.

entries.name: Battle of Fort Sumter
entries.desc: Confederate forces bombarded the Union-held Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor on 12–13 April 1861, forcing its surrender without loss of life on either side, in the opening engagement of the American Civil War.
entries.tldr: On 12–13 April 1861, Confederate batteries under General P. G. T. Beauregard opened fire on the small Union garrison holding Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, commanded by Major Robert Anderson, after the fort refused to surrender. After roughly 34 hours of bombardment, with the fort's walls battered and provisions nearly exhausted, Anderson surrendered; remarkably, no one was killed in the exchange itself. The attack rallied Northern opinion behind Lincoln, who called for 75,000 volunteers, and marked the opening of the Civil War.

entries.name: Battle of Taranto
entries.desc: On the night of 11–12 November 1940, British carrier aircraft crippled the Italian fleet at anchor at Taranto in the first all-aircraft ship-to-ship attack in naval history, later studied by planners of Pearl Harbor.
entries.tldr: On the night of 11–12 November 1940, twenty-one obsolete Fairey Swordfish biplanes launched from the British carrier HMS Illustrious attacked the Italian fleet at anchor in its harbor at Taranto. The raid sank or crippled three battleships for the loss of just two aircraft, in the first all-aircraft ship-to-ship attack in naval history. Japanese naval officers studied the operation closely, and it is widely credited as an influence on the planning of the attack on Pearl Harbor a year later.

entries.name: War of Jenkins' Ear
entries.desc: The War of Jenkins' Ear was fought between Great Britain and Spain from 1739 to 1748. Most of the fighting took place in New Granada and the Caribbean Sea, with major operations over by 1742.

entries.name: Treaty of Versailles (1871)
entries.desc: The Treaty of Versailles of 1871 ended the Franco-Prussian War, with France ceding Alsace-Lorraine and paying a large indemnity to the newly proclaimed German Empire. The harsh terms fueled lasting French resentment.

entries.name: Battle of Maiwand
entries.desc: On 27 July 1880, Afghan forces under Ayub Khan defeated a British-Indian brigade near Kandahar, one of Britain's costliest defeats of the Second Anglo-Afghan War, though British troops recaptured Kandahar weeks later.
entries.tldr: During the Second Anglo-Afghan War, a British-Indian brigade under General Burrows marched to intercept a much larger Afghan force led by Ayub Khan near Maiwand. Afghan artillery, manned partly by trained deserters, outmatched the British guns, and repeated cavalry charges broke the British line, turning the retreat into a rout. The brigade suffered devastating losses, among Britain's worst single-day defeats of the colonial era. Kandahar was recaptured weeks later, but Maiwand endured in memory partly via a mention in Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories.

entries.name: War of the Breton Succession
entries.desc: The War of the Breton Succession (1341–1364) was a civil war between the Houses of Blois and Montfort for the Duchy of Brittany, entangled with the wider Hundred Years' War. The Montfort line prevailed.

entries.name: Battle of Azaz
entries.desc: In 1125, a Crusader army under Baldwin II of Jerusalem defeated a Seljuk and Artuqid coalition near Azaz, relieving pressure on Antioch and Aleppo and checking Muslim efforts to reunite northern Syria.
entries.tldr: In June 1125, a Crusader coalition led by Baldwin II, King of Jerusalem, marched to relieve the besieged fortress of Azaz in northern Syria, a buffer protecting the Crusader states of Antioch and Edessa. Baldwin's force decisively defeated a Seljuk and Artuqid army under Aq Sunqur al-Bursuqi, using a feigned retreat to draw the Turkish cavalry out of position before counterattacking. The victory relieved pressure on Antioch and temporarily halted Muslim efforts to unite northern Syria against the Franks, one of the last major Crusader field wins before the tide turned.

entries.name: Battle of Berezina
entries.desc: Between 26 and 29 November 1812, Napoleon's retreating army forced a crossing of the Berezina River under Russian attack. It survived encirclement but suffered catastrophic losses in the disaster of the Russian campaign.
entries.tldr: Fought between 26 and 29 November 1812 along the Berezina River in present-day Belarus, the battle came as Napoleon's shattered Grande Armée, already devastated by cold and hunger during its retreat from Moscow, tried to cross the icy river while pursued by three converging Russian armies. French engineers built makeshift bridges under fire, and though most surviving French troops escaped encirclement, the crossing descended into chaos as stragglers were crushed or drowned. Losses were so catastrophic that the word bérézina still means a total disaster in French.

entries.name: First Silesian War
entries.desc: The First Silesian War (1740–1742) saw Prussia seize most of Silesia from Austria under Frederick the Great. Austria's defeat, confirmed by the Treaty of Berlin, marked Prussia's rise as a major European power.
entries.tldr: Frederick the Great invaded the Habsburg province of Silesia within weeks of inheriting the Prussian throne, exploiting Maria Theresa's disputed succession to the Austrian crown. Prussian victories at Mollwitz and Chotusitz secured the province, and the 1742 Treaty of Berlin confirmed Prussian control over most of it. The seizure roughly doubled Prussia's population and revenue overnight, launching the Austro-Prussian rivalry that would define German politics for the next century.

entries.name: Defense of the Polish Post Office in Danzig
entries.desc: On 1 September 1939, Polish postal workers defended their post office in Danzig against German attack on the invasion's first day; most surviving defenders were later executed by German forces.
entries.tldr: On 1 September 1939, the opening day of the German invasion of Poland, a small garrison of Polish postal workers barricaded themselves inside their post office in the Free City of Danzig and held off attacking SS and police units for nearly fifteen hours. German forces eventually broke through using flamethrowers and artillery, forcing a surrender. Most of the surviving defenders were court-martialed and executed by the Germans, a war crime not formally addressed by German courts until decades later. The defense became a symbol of Polish resistance on the very first day of the war.

entries.name: Battle of Khaybar
entries.desc: In 628 CE, Muhammad's forces besieged the Jewish community at the Khaybar oasis, who surrendered and were allowed to keep farming the land in exchange for tribute, until their later expulsion under Caliph Umar.
entries.tldr: Muhammad led roughly 1,600 followers against the fortified oasis of Khaybar, home to Jewish tribes who had opposed him after his earlier expulsion of other Jewish communities from Medina. The Muslims besieged and captured the oasis's fortresses one by one over several weeks, including one reportedly stormed by Ali ibn Abi Talib. The defeated inhabitants surrendered and were permitted to remain and farm the land in return for handing over half their produce as tribute. That arrangement lasted until Caliph Umar expelled the Jewish community from Khaybar roughly a decade later.

entries.name: League of the Three Emperors
entries.desc: The League of the Three Emperors (1873–1887) allied Germany, Russia, and Austria-Hungary under Bismarck's diplomacy to isolate France. Balkan rivalry between Austria-Hungary and Russia eventually broke it apart.
entries.tldr: Otto von Bismarck engineered this alliance among the conservative monarchies of Germany, Russia, and Austria-Hungary primarily to keep republican France diplomatically isolated after the Franco-Prussian War. It rested on the three emperors' shared interest in suppressing nationalist and socialist movements at home. The pact collapsed over Balkan rivalry between Austria-Hungary and Russia, especially the 1875-78 crisis over Bulgaria. Its failure showed how Balkan nationalism could fracture even careful great-power diplomacy.

entries.name: Battle of Fontenoy
entries.desc: On 11 May 1745, a French army under Marshal Saxe defeated an allied British, Dutch, and Hanoverian force near Fontenoy during the War of the Austrian Succession, opening France's conquest of the Austrian Netherlands.
entries.tldr: On 11 May 1745, Marshal Maurice de Saxe, commanding French forces despite being gravely ill and directing the battle from a wicker litter, defeated an allied army of British, Dutch, and Hanoverian troops near Fontenoy during the War of the Austrian Succession. The battle opened with a famous exchange between opposing guards officers inviting each other to fire first, before a grinding contest the French narrowly won thanks to well-placed artillery. The victory let France overrun much of the Austrian Netherlands.

entries.name: Battle of the Kalka River
entries.desc: In 1223, Mongol forces under Jebe and Subutai defeated a coalition of Rus' princes at the Kalka River, a shock defeat that previewed the full Mongol invasion of Rus' lands over a decade later.
entries.tldr: In May 1223, a Mongol reconnaissance force under the generals Jebe and Subutai, returning from a campaign near the Caspian Sea, encountered a large coalition of Rus' princes and their Cuman allies near the Kalka River in modern Ukraine. Using a feigned retreat to draw the pursuing Rus' forces out of formation, the Mongols turned and annihilated the disorganized coalition, killing several princes and much of the army. The defeat previewed the far larger Mongol invasion of the Rus' lands over a decade later, though the Mongols withdrew eastward without pressing their advantage.

entries.name: Battle of Rossbach
entries.desc: On 5 November 1757, Frederick the Great's outnumbered Prussian army routed a combined French and Imperial force during the Seven Years' War, a lopsided defeat that later spurred French military reforms.
entries.tldr: On 5 November 1757, Frederick the Great's outnumbered Prussian army routed a combined French and Holy Roman Imperial force near Rossbach in Saxony, inflicting a humiliating defeat in barely half an hour of fighting. Prussian cavalry under Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz struck the allied column while it was still maneuvering, throwing it into panicked flight for the loss of only a few hundred Prussian casualties. The stinging defeat forced France to reassess its military organization, and the victory boosted Frederick's reputation as one of the era's greatest battlefield commanders.

entries.name: Fourth Anglo-Dutch War
entries.desc: The Fourth Anglo-Dutch War (1780–1784) broke out when Britain accused the Dutch Republic of covertly aiding the American Revolution. The war ruined Dutch trade and left the Republic reliant on France.
entries.tldr: Britain declared war on the Dutch Republic in 1780 after discovering secret Dutch trade and loan negotiations with the rebelling American colonies, seizing on a pretext to crush a commercial rival. Fought almost entirely at sea and in colonial waters, the conflict devastated Dutch shipping and overseas trade, most notably at the Battle of Dogger Bank. The 1784 Treaty of Paris left the Republic economically weakened and diplomatically dependent on France for the rest of the century.

entries.name: Japanese invasions of Korea
entries.desc:
