Japanese occupation of Gyeongbokgung
Korea under Japanese rule
entries.tldr: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, having unified Japan, launched a massive invasion of Korea in 1592 intending to use it as a corridor for conquering Ming China, and Japanese forces initially overran much of the peninsula rapidly. Korean naval commander Yi Sun-sin's innovative 'turtle ships' repeatedly cut Japanese supply lines at sea, while Ming Chinese reinforcements and guerrilla resistance ground the invasion to a stalemate. A second invasion attempt in 1597 fared no better, and the wars ended in 1598 after Hideyoshi's death, leaving Korea devastated but independent.

entries.name: Battle of Cresson
entries.desc: On 1 May 1187, a small force of Templars and Hospitallers was destroyed by an Ayyubid raiding party under Saladin near the Spring of Cresson. It foreshadowed the far larger Crusader disaster at Hattin two months later.
entries.tldr: On 1 May 1187, Grand Master Gerard de Ridefort led a small force of Templars and Hospitallers into an ambush by a larger Ayyubid raiding party sent by Saladin's son near the Spring of Cresson in Galilee. Nearly the entire Christian force was killed, including the Hospitaller Grand Master Roger de Moulins, while Ridefort escaped with a handful of survivors. The defeat did not check Ridefort's recklessness, and he pushed King Guy toward the disastrous confrontation at Hattin two months later.

entries.name: Battle of Forbie
entries.desc: On 17–18 October 1244, an Ayyubid and Khwarazmian army crushed a combined Crusader and Ayyubid force near Forbie, killing or capturing most of the Crusader army, which could no longer mount another major offensive.
entries.tldr: On 17–18 October 1244 near La Forbie in Galilee, an army of Khwarazmian mercenaries allied with the Ayyubid sultan of Egypt crushed a coalition of Crusader knights and the Ayyubid rulers of Damascus and Homs, who had allied against Cairo. Nearly the entire military strength of the Crusader kingdom, including most of the Templars and Hospitallers present, was killed or captured, a defeat some historians rank as more damaging than Hattin. The Crusader states never fully recovered their military capacity afterward.

entries.name: Battle of Blore Heath
entries.desc: Fought on 23 September 1459 in Staffordshire, this early battle of the Wars of the Roses saw a Yorkist force under the Earl of Salisbury defeat a larger Lancastrian army sent to intercept it.
entries.tldr: Fought on 23 September 1459 in Staffordshire, the battle was among the earliest engagements of the Wars of the Roses, as a Yorkist force under Richard Neville, Earl of Salisbury, marching to join Richard, Duke of York, at Ludlow, was intercepted by a larger Lancastrian army under Lord Audley. Outnumbered, Salisbury's troops used a feigned retreat to lure the Lancastrian cavalry into a costly downhill charge across a stream, then routed the survivors and killed Audley. The win let Salisbury reach York's muster, though the Yorkist cause suffered reversal weeks later at Ludford Bridge.

entries.name: First Anglo-Sikh War
entries.desc: The First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–1846) was fought between the Sikh Empire and the British East India Company over control of Punjab. British victory forced the Sikhs to cede territory and accept a reduced, tributary state.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1845 to 1846, the war erupted when the powerful Sikh Empire, weakened by instability after Ranjit Singh's death, clashed with the expanding British East India Company along the Sutlej River. Despite fierce resistance from the disciplined Khalsa army, British forces won a series of costly battles, aided by betrayal within the Sikh command. The Treaty of Lahore forced the Sikhs to cede territory, pay a large indemnity, and accept a British resident. The settlement left the Sikh Empire a diminished, tributary state fully annexed after a second war three years later.

entries.name: Battle of Debrecen
entries.desc: The Battle of Debrecen, called by the Red Army the Debrecen Offensive Operation, was a battle taking place from 6 to 29 October 1944 on the Eastern Front in Hungary during World War II.
entries.tldr: Fought from 6 to 29 October 1944 in eastern Hungary, this was part of the Soviet Red Army's offensive to push German and Hungarian forces toward Budapest. Marshal Rodion Malinovsky's 2nd Ukrainian Front tried to encircle Axis forces around Debrecen using fast cavalry-mechanized groups, triggering one of the largest tank engagements on the Eastern Front's southern flank. German counterattacks partly cut off the advancing Soviet spearheads, turning a clean encirclement into a costly struggle. The Red Army still captured Debrecen, opening the road toward Budapest.

entries.name: Second Geneva Convention
entries.desc: The Second Geneva Convention of 1949 extended humanitarian protections to wounded, sick, and shipwrecked members of armed forces at sea. It updated earlier rules governing naval warfare.
entries.tldr: Adopted alongside three companion conventions after World War II exposed gaps in existing humanitarian law, extending to naval warfare the protections the First Geneva Convention had already established for wounded soldiers on land. It requires belligerents to collect, protect, and care for the wounded, sick, and shipwrecked at sea, and to respect hospital ships and their crews regardless of nationality. It builds on an earlier 1907 Hague Convention that had adapted the original 1864 Geneva principles to naval combat. Nearly every state in the world is now a party to it.

entries.name: Battle of Kleidion
entries.desc: On 29 July 1014, Byzantine emperor Basil II crushed the Bulgarian army and blinded thousands of captives, breaking Bulgarian resistance and paving the way for Byzantium to annex Bulgaria by 1018.
entries.tldr: After decades of war with the First Bulgarian Empire, Byzantine emperor Basil II trapped and destroyed the Bulgarian army at the Kleidion mountain pass. Byzantine sources claim Basil blinded roughly 14,000 captured soldiers, leaving one eye in every hundredth man to guide the rest home, though modern historians question the numbers. Bulgarian tsar Samuel reportedly collapsed and died upon seeing his returning, blinded army. The victory broke organized Bulgarian resistance, and Basil completed the conquest of Bulgaria within four years, earning the later epithet 'Bulgar-Slayer.'

entries.name: Siege of Malta
entries.desc: The Great Siege of Malta in 1565 saw the Knights Hospitaller and Maltese defenders withstand a months-long Ottoman assault. Their survival halted Ottoman expansion in the western Mediterranean.
entries.tldr: In May 1565 an Ottoman armada carrying tens of thousands of troops landed on Malta to seize the island from the Knights Hospitaller, based there since losing Rhodes decades earlier. Grand Master Jean Parisot de Valette led a heavily outnumbered garrison of knights and Maltese defenders through nearly four months of siege and repeated assaults before a relief force arrived from Sicily. The Ottoman withdrawal was seen across Christian Europe as a deliverance and became a celebrated symbol of resistance. Valette later founded the city of Valletta on the site to commemorate the victory.

entries.name: Battle of Falkirk
entries.desc: On 22 July 1298, an English army under Edward I defeated Scottish forces under William Wallace, whose schiltron formations were broken by English archers, ending Wallace's leadership of the Scottish resistance.
entries.tldr: On 22 July 1298, King Edward I of England personally led an army against Scottish forces under William Wallace near Falkirk, a year after Wallace's victory at Stirling Bridge. English longbowmen broke apart Wallace's tightly packed schiltron formations of spearmen before cavalry finished off the disordered Scots. The defeat forced Wallace to resign as Guardian of Scotland, and he spent his remaining years as a fugitive before capture and execution in 1305.

entries.name: Paraguayan War
entries.desc: The Paraguayan War, or War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870), pitted Paraguay against the allied forces of Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay. Paraguay's defeat cost it much of its population and territory.
entries.tldr: Paraguayan dictator Francisco Solano López invaded Brazil and Argentina in a dispute over regional influence in Uruguay, uniting the two larger powers with Uruguay itself into the Triple Alliance against him. Despite early Paraguayan advances, the far larger allied forces eventually overwhelmed Paraguay's army, and López refused to surrender even as his country was devastated. He was killed in 1870 still resisting, and Paraguay lost an estimated 60 to 70 percent of its prewar population, plus large stretches of territory, making it the deadliest interstate war in South American history.

entries.name: Battle of Berestechko
entries.desc: In 1651, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth defeated a Cossack and Crimean Tatar army near Berestechko, the largest battle of the Khmelnytsky Uprising. The Tatars' withdrawal forced harsher peace terms on the Cossacks.
entries.tldr: Fought over late June and early July 1651 in what is now western Ukraine, the battle was the largest engagement of the Khmelnytsky Uprising, pitting the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth against the combined forces of Cossack hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky and his Crimean Tatar allies under Khan Islam III Giray. When the khan abruptly withdrew his cavalry, reportedly after a dispute with Khmelnytsky, the exposed Cossack army suffered a severe defeat, and Khmelnytsky himself was briefly detained by his own retreating allies. The Commonwealth's win forced a harsher peace treaty later that year.

entries.name: Treaty of Alcáçovas
entries.desc: The Treaty of Alcáçovas (1479) ended the War of the Castilian Succession between Castile and Portugal. It also divided their rival claims to Atlantic exploration, foreshadowing the later Treaty of Tordesillas.
entries.tldr: Signed in 1479, the Treaty of Alcáçovas ended the War of the Castilian Succession, fought after Isabella I's contested accession to the Castilian throne, in which Portugal had backed a rival claimant. Beyond settling the succession, it divided the Atlantic's newly explored and yet-to-be-explored territories between the two crowns, granting Portugal exclusive rights south of the Canaries, Guinea, and the Azores, while Castile kept the Canary Islands. This early division of overseas claims set a precedent for the more famous 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas after Columbus's voyages.

entries.name: Battle of Badon
entries.desc: A battle traditionally dated to around 500 CE in which Britons are said to have defeated invading Anglo-Saxons. Its historicity is disputed; it is chiefly known through its later link to the legend of King Arthur.
entries.tldr: Traditionally dated to around 500 CE, the Battle of Badon is described by the 6th-century writer Gildas as a major British victory that halted the advance of Anglo-Saxon settlers for a generation. Neither its location nor its precise historicity is established by modern scholarship, and Gildas himself names no British commander. The battle became attached centuries later to the legend of King Arthur, first credited to him by the 9th-century Historia Brittonum, though most historians treat that link as later literary invention rather than contemporary fact.

entries.name: Battle of the Vorskla River
entries.desc: On 12 August 1399, Golden Horde forces under Edigu crushed a Lithuanian-led coalition at the Vorskla River, halting Grand Duke Vytautas's eastward expansion and securing Tatar dominance over the steppe for years.
entries.tldr: On 12 August 1399, a Golden Horde army led by the khan Timur Qutlugh and his general Edigu crushed a large coalition led by Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania, which included Polish and Teutonic contingents, along the Vorskla River in modern Ukraine. Vytautas had been backing a rival claimant to the Golden Horde's throne and hoped to extend Lithuanian influence over the steppe, but his coalition was routed with heavy losses, including many Lithuanian nobles. The defeat halted Lithuania's eastward expansion for a generation.

entries.name: Battle of Tricamarum
entries.desc: On 15 December 533, Byzantine general Belisarius decisively defeated the Vandal army, effectively ending the Vandal Kingdom and returning North Africa to Roman rule.
entries.tldr: On 15 December 533, the Byzantine general Belisarius decisively defeated the army of the Vandal king Gelimer near Carthage during Emperor Justinian I's campaign to reconquer North Africa. Gelimer fled into the mountains and eventually surrendered the following year, ending nearly a century of independent Vandal rule. The victory restored North Africa to Roman control and stood as one of the signature triumphs of Justinian's ambitious reconquest of the western Mediterranean.

entries.name: Battle of Durbe
entries.desc: On 13 July 1260, Samogitian forces defeated the Livonian Order near Durbe in present-day Latvia. The defeat triggered major uprisings against crusader rule in both Prussia and Livonia.
entries.tldr: On 13 July 1260, an army of pagan Samogitians ambushed and destroyed a large force of the Livonian Order, a Baltic branch of the Teutonic Knights, near Durbe in what is now western Latvia, killing the order's Land Master and many senior knights. News of the crushing defeat spread through the recently conquered Baltic territories and triggered the Great Prussian Uprising as well as revolts in Courland and Livonia. The uprisings dragged on for over a decade before the order regained control.

entries.name: Battle of the Dukla Pass
entries.desc: Fought from September to October 1944, Soviet and Czechoslovak forces attacked German defenses at the Dukla Pass in the Carpathians, a costly offensive meant to support the Slovak National Uprising.
entries.tldr: Fought from September to October 1944, Soviet and Czechoslovak forces launched a costly offensive through the Dukla Pass in the Carpathian Mountains, intended to break through to Slovakia and link up with the Slovak National Uprising then underway against German forces. German defenders, well entrenched in the mountainous terrain, inflicted heavy losses and slowed the advance through autumn rains and difficult ground. The offensive eventually pushed through but arrived too late to save the uprising, which collapsed in late October.

entries.name: Falaise Pocket
entries.desc: In August 1944 Allied forces encircled German troops near Falaise, Normandy, trapping much of Army Group B in the final battle of the Normandy campaign. Its collapse hastened the liberation of France.
entries.tldr: In August 1944, advancing Allied armies encircled much of the German Seventh Army and Fifth Panzer Army near the Norman town of Falaise, trapping tens of thousands of troops attempting to retreat eastward. Canadian, Polish, American, and British forces closed the gap under intense fighting, subjecting the trapped Germans to devastating air and artillery bombardment. Thousands escaped before the pocket fully closed, but the battle destroyed enormous quantities of men and equipment, effectively ending organized German resistance in Normandy and opening the way to Paris.

entries.name: Battle of Anchialus
entries.desc: In 708, Bulgarian Khan Tervel routed a Byzantine army led by Emperor Justinian II near Anchialus, forcing the emperor to retreat. The defeat confirmed Bulgaria's standing as a power on the Byzantine frontier.
entries.tldr: In 708, Bulgarian Khan Tervel led an army against a Byzantine force that Emperor Justinian II had personally brought north, ostensibly to punish Tervel despite the khan having helped restore him to his throne only years before. Tervel's cavalry ambushed and routed the imperial army near Anchialus, forcing Justinian to flee back to Constantinople by sea. The humiliating defeat was one of several failures that soon contributed to the unpopular emperor's overthrow, and it confirmed Bulgaria's standing as a power Byzantium could not simply dictate to.

entries.name: Battle of Nahāvand
entries.desc: In 642, Rashidun Muslim forces under an-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin decisively defeated the Sasanian army; the defeat broke organized Persian resistance and opened the Sasanian Empire to Muslim conquest.
entries.tldr: In 642, Rashidun Arab forces under an-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin decisively defeated a large Sasanian Persian army near Nahavand in western Iran, in a battle Muslim tradition calls the "Victory of Victories." An-Nu'man was killed in the fighting but his forces prevailed, shattering the last major organized Sasanian resistance. The defeat opened the Iranian plateau to Muslim conquest and effectively sealed the fate of the centuries-old Sasanian Empire. Within years the last Sasanian emperor, Yazdegerd III, was killed as a fugitive, and Persia came under Muslim rule.

entries.name: Convention of Peking
entries.desc: Signed in 1860 to end the Second Opium War, this set of treaties between Qing China and Britain, France, and Russia ceded Kowloon to Britain, opened new treaty ports, and legalized the opium trade in China.
entries.tldr: Signed in October 1860, this set of treaties ended the Second Opium War between Qing China and the allied forces of Britain and France, with Russia also securing concessions as a mediator. China ceded the Kowloon Peninsula to Britain, opened Tianjin as a treaty port, permitted Christian missionary activity, and legalized the opium trade it had fought two wars trying to suppress. Russia used the occasion to press separate claims, gaining vast territory in the Amur and Ussuri regions. The convention deepened China's 'century of humiliation' under unequal treaties.

entries.name: Geneva Protocol
entries.desc: The Geneva Protocol of 1925 banned the use of chemical and biological weapons in war, responding to the horrors of gas warfare in the First World War. It did not, however, prohibit their production or stockpiling.
entries.tldr: Negotiated in the aftermath of the First World War's mass gas casualties, the 1925 protocol formally banned the first use of chemical and biological weapons in international conflict. It grew directly out of horror at attacks like the German use of chlorine gas at Ypres in 1915. Crucially, the treaty prohibited only wartime use, not the production, stockpiling, or research of such weapons, a loophole that let major powers continue building chemical arsenals throughout the twentieth century.

entries.name: War of the Fourth Coalition
entries.desc: The War of the Fourth Coalition (1806–1807) saw Napoleon's France defeat a coalition led by Prussia and Russia. Prussia's crushing defeat led to the humiliating Treaties of Tilsit.

entries.name: Siege of Szigetvár
entries.desc: The 1566 Siege of Szigetvár saw Croatian commander Nikola Zrinski's garrison hold the fortress against Suleiman the Magnificent's army before it fell. The delay is credited with slowing the Ottoman advance on Vienna.
entries.tldr: In August 1566 Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent led a massive Ottoman army against the small Hungarian fortress of Szigetvár, defended by Croatian nobleman Nikola Zrinski and a garrison of a few thousand men. The defenders held out for over a month before Zrinski led a final charge into the Ottoman ranks rather than surrender, and the fortress fell only after being reduced to ruins. Suleiman died of illness during the siege, and the delay is credited with slowing that year's Ottoman advance enough to spare Vienna. The siege became a foundational legend of Croatian and Hungarian national memory.

entries.name: Battle of Peleliu
entries.desc: Fought from September to November 1944 for an airfield on the island of Peleliu, this battle produced some of the highest casualty rates of the Pacific War and remains debated for its limited strategic value.
entries.tldr: American Marines and Army troops fought from September to November 1944 to seize a small airfield on the coral island of Peleliu, expecting a quick victory that instead became one of the war's bloodiest campaigns per square mile. Japanese defenders under Colonel Kunio Nakagawa abandoned beach defense for a network of fortified caves and tunnels in the island's ridges, inflicting heavy American casualties over weeks of combat. The operation's strategic value was questioned even before it ended, and it remains a case study in objectives worth less than planners assumed.

entries.name: Battle of Civitate
entries.desc: On 18 June 1053, Norman forces in southern Italy defeated a coalition army assembled by Pope Leo IX and captured the pope. The victory secured Norman rule and led the papacy to instead ally with the Normans.
entries.tldr: Fought on 18 June 1053 near Civitate in southern Italy, the battle saw a coalition army assembled by Pope Leo IX, combining Swabian mercenaries and Italian levies, confront Norman adventurers who had been carving out territory at the expense of Byzantine and Lombard rulers. Despite being outnumbered, the Normans under leaders including Humphrey of Hauteville and Richard of Aversa won decisively, and Leo himself was captured, though treated with deference. The defeat forced the papacy to abandon fighting the Normans and instead pursue an alliance, reshaping medieval southern Italy.

entries.name: Castellammarese War
entries.desc: Fought from 1930 to 1931 between rival Mafia factions led by Joe Masseria and Salvatore Maranzano, this power struggle ended with both men's deaths and reorganization of the American Mafia into the Five Families system.
entries.tldr: From 1930 to 1931, rival Italian-American Mafia factions fought for control of organized crime in New York, pitting old-guard boss Salvatore Maranzano against Joe 'the Boss' Masseria. Masseria was gunned down in a Coney Island restaurant in April 1931 after his own lieutenant, Lucky Luciano, secretly switched sides. Maranzano briefly declared himself 'boss of bosses' before Luciano had him assassinated just months later. Luciano then dismantled the old hierarchy and organized the survivors into the Five Families structure that has governed New York's Mafia ever since.

entries.name: Treaty of Tientsin
entries.desc: The Treaty of Tientsin (1858) was a set of unequal treaties Qing China signed with Britain, France, Russia, and the United States after the Second Opium War. It opened further ports and legalized the opium trade.

entries.name: First Battle of the Isonzo
entries.desc: The First Battle of the Isonzo was fought between the armies of Italy and Austria-Hungary on the northeastern Italian Front in World War I, between 23 June and 7 July 1915.
entries.tldr: Fought between 23 June and 7 July 1915, this was the opening battle in a grueling series of eleven clashes between Italy and Austria-Hungary along the Isonzo River on the mountainous northeastern Italian Front. Italian commander Luigi Cadorna's frontal assaults against fortified Austro-Hungarian positions in difficult alpine terrain achieved little beyond heavy casualties on both sides. The pattern of costly, inconclusive offensives repeated through the following battles of the Isonzo over the next two years. The front became notorious for extreme conditions and attritional fighting.

entries.name: Anglo-Egyptian War
entries.desc: The British conquest of Egypt, also known as the 2nd Anglo-Egyptian War, occurred in 1882 between mostly Egyptian and Sudanese forces under Ahmed 'Urabi and the United Kingdom.
entries.tldr: In 1882, Britain intervened militarily in Egypt after a nationalist uprising led by army officer Ahmed 'Urabi threatened foreign financial control and the Suez Canal. A British fleet bombarded Alexandria, and an expeditionary force under General Garnet Wolseley decisively defeated 'Urabi's army at the Battle of Tel el-Kebir. The victory left Egypt under de facto British military occupation for decades, even though it remained nominally part of the Ottoman Empire. The war marked the start of Britain's long, informal rule over Egypt.

entries.name: First Anglo-Mysore War
entries.desc: The First Anglo-Mysore War (1767–1769) pitted the Sultanate of Mysore under Hyder Ali against the East India Company and its allies in southern India. It ended in a stalemate treaty restoring prewar territory.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1767 to 1769, this conflict pitted the Sultanate of Mysore, under its ambitious ruler Hyder Ali, against the British East India Company and a coalition of regional allies in southern India. Hyder Ali proved a formidable commander, at one point advancing his cavalry to the outskirts of Madras and forcing the Company to negotiate from weakness. The resulting treaty restored each side's prewar territory and included a mutual defense pact the British later broke. The stalemate set up decades of further Anglo-Mysore wars that ended only with Mysore's defeat in 1799.

entries.name: Third Anglo-Maratha War
entries.desc: The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1819) was the final and decisive conflict between Britain and the Maratha Empire. The war left the Company in control of most of India.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1817 to 1819, this was the culminating conflict between the British East India Company and the Maratha Confederacy, the last major independent power resisting British expansion across much of India. Company forces defeated the Maratha peshwa and allied chieftains in a series of campaigns, exploiting divisions among the Maratha states. The war's end dissolved the Maratha Confederacy as a political entity and left the Company the dominant power across most of the subcontinent. It marked a decisive step toward British paramountcy in India that lasted until independence in 1947.

entries.name: Franco-Spanish War
entries.desc: Franco-Spanish War may refer to any war between France and Spain, including:
entries.tldr: The name covers several distinct wars fought between the kingdoms of France and Spain across the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries, most notably the 1635–1659 conflict fought alongside the Thirty Years' War. That war pitted Bourbon France against Habsburg Spain for European dominance and ended with the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees, which ceded Roussillon and parts of the Spanish Netherlands to France and sealed France's rise as the continent's leading power.

entries.name: Third Anglo-Mysore War
entries.desc: The Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790–1792) pitted Tipu Sultan of Mysore against a coalition of the East India Company, the Marathas, and Hyderabad. Defeat forced Tipu to cede half his territory at the Treaty of Seringapatam.
entries.tldr: From 1790 to 1792, Tipu Sultan of Mysore fought a coalition of the British East India Company, the Maratha Empire, and the Nizam of Hyderabad, allied against him after years of prior Anglo-Mysore conflict. British and allied forces besieged Tipu's capital at Seringapatam, forcing his surrender in 1792. Under the Treaty of Seringapatam, Tipu ceded roughly half his territory and paid a large indemnity, handing over two sons as hostages to guarantee the terms. The defeat weakened Mysore ahead of the final Anglo-Mysore war that ended Tipu's rule and life in 1799.

entries.name: Anglo-Egyptian treaty of 1936
entries.desc: This treaty between Britain and Egypt ended Britain's military occupation of most of Egypt but let British troops remain to defend the Suez Canal Zone, and paved the way for Egypt to join the League of Nations.
entries.tldr: Signed in August 1936 amid rising fears of Italian aggression in the region, this treaty formally ended Britain's decades-long military occupation of Egypt while permitting British forces to remain in the Suez Canal Zone to defend the waterway. It granted Egypt greater sovereignty, including the right to build its own army, and cleared the way for Egypt's admission to the League of Nations that year. Nationalist sentiment still viewed the continued British troop presence as an affront to full independence.

entries.name: Anglo-Persian War
entries.desc: Fought in 1856–1857 after Persia besieged Herat in violation of an earlier pledge to Britain, this war ended with the Treaty of Paris, under which Persia withdrew its claim to Herat and Afghanistan.
entries.tldr: War broke out in late 1856 after Qajar Persia besieged and captured the Afghan city of Herat, breaking an earlier pledge to Britain not to interfere there. Concerned about Persian, and by extension Russian, influence encroaching toward British India, Britain declared war and landed a force that captured the port of Bushire and defeated Persian troops near the Tigris. The 1857 Treaty of Paris ended the conflict, with Persia withdrawing from Herat and renouncing any claim to Afghan territory.

entries.name: Fourth Anglo-Mysore War
entries.desc: The Fourth Anglo-Mysore War was a conflict in South India during which the Mysore State fought against the East India Company, Maratha Empire and the Hyderabad State in 1798–99.
entries.tldr: Governor-General Richard Wellesley, alarmed by Tipu Sultan of Mysore's contacts with revolutionary France, launched a coordinated invasion with Maratha and Hyderabad allies in 1799. British and allied forces stormed Tipu's capital at Seringapatam, where Tipu died defending the breach. His death ended Mysore's independent power, and the East India Company partitioned the kingdom, restoring a client Wodeyar dynasty under close British control.

entries.name: Battle of Mortimer's Cross
entries.desc: The Battle of Mortimer's Cross was fought on 2 February, 1461 near Kingsland, Herefordshire, not far from the Welsh border. It was a major battle of the Wars of the Roses.
entries.tldr: Fought on 2 February 1461 near Kingsland in Herefordshire, this Wars of the Roses battle saw the young Yorkist claimant Edward, Earl of March, defeat a Lancastrian force loyal to the Tudor and Wiltshire families. Before the fighting, a rare atmospheric phenomenon showing three suns in the sky was interpreted by Edward as a good omen, and he later adopted the "sun in splendour" as a personal badge. The victory helped clear Edward's path to London, where he was soon proclaimed King Edward IV. Owen Tudor, grandfather of the future Henry VII, was captured and executed afterward.

entries.name: Battle of Ager Sanguinis
entries.desc: On 28 June 1119, an Artuqid army under Ilghazi annihilated the Crusader field army of Antioch near Sarmada, killing its ruler Roger of Salerno. Antioch survived only because the Turks failed to press their advantage.
entries.tldr: On 28 June 1119, the Artuqid ruler Ilghazi led a Muslim army that ambushed and virtually annihilated the field army of the Crusader Principality of Antioch near Sarmada, so severe a disaster the site became known as the Field of Blood. Antioch's regent Roger of Salerno was killed along with most of his knights, leaving the principality almost undefended. Antioch survived only because Ilghazi's coalition, more interested in plunder than conquest, failed to follow up with an assault on the city itself.

entries.name: Aragonese Crusade
entries.desc: A 1284–1285 papal-sanctioned invasion of the Crown of Aragon by France, launched to punish King Peter III for seizing Sicily from the Angevins. The campaign collapsed after disease and defeat forced a French retreat.
entries.tldr: Declared by Pope Martin IV, the Aragonese Crusade of 1284–1285 authorized the French crown to invade Aragon and depose King Peter III as punishment for seizing Sicily from the Angevins during the Sicilian Vespers uprising. A large French army under King Philip III crossed the Pyrenees and besieged the Catalan city of Girona, initially making progress. An outbreak of dysentery, combined with an Aragonese naval victory that cut off supplies, forced a disastrous French retreat in which Philip III died.

entries.name: Battle of Karbala
entries.desc: On 10 October 680, Umayyad forces killed Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, and his companions near the Euphrates, a trauma that deepened the Sunni–Shia split and is commemorated annually as Ashura.
entries.tldr: Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, had refused to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid I and set out for Kufa with a small band of family and supporters. Umayyad forces under Umar ibn Sa'd intercepted them at Karbala, cut them off from the Euphrates, and after days of siege killed Husayn and nearly all the men in his party. The surviving women and children, including Husayn's son Ali Zayn al-Abidin, were taken captive to Damascus. The massacre became the central grief narrative of Shia Islam, mourned each year on Ashura with processions and passion plays.

entries.name: Battle of Taierzhuang
entries.desc: The Battle of Taierzhuang took place during the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1938. It was fought between the armies of the Republic of China and the Empire of Japan at the peak of the Xuzhou Campaign.
entries.tldr: Fought in the spring of 1938 as part of the wider Xuzhou Campaign, this battle saw Chinese forces under General Li Zongren surround and destroy a Japanese division that had advanced too aggressively into the walled town of Taierzhuang. It was the first major Chinese victory of the Second Sino-Japanese War and delivered a significant boost to national morale after a string of defeats. Japan nonetheless went on to capture Xuzhou soon after, limiting the battle's strategic impact.

entries.name: Battle of Lutter
entries.desc: On 27 August 1626, Catholic League forces under Tilly defeated Christian IV of Denmark during the Thirty Years' War, forcing Denmark's withdrawal and exposing northern Germany to imperial control.
entries.tldr: King Christian IV of Denmark had entered the Thirty Years' War to support Protestant forces in Germany, but his army was intercepted near Lutter am Barenberge by Catholic League forces under the veteran commander Johann Tserclaes von Tilly. Tilly's infantry and cavalry outmaneuvered the Danish force, inflicting heavy losses and capturing much of its artillery. The defeat forced Christian to withdraw from Germany within two years, ending Denmark's phase of the war. The victory let Tilly and the rising commander Albrecht von Wallenstein extend Catholic control across northern Germany.

entries.name: Byzantine–Ottoman wars
entries.desc: A prolonged series of conflicts from the late 13th century onward between the shrinking Byzantine Empire and the rising Ottoman Turks, ending with the fall of Constantinople in 1453 and the empire's extinction.
entries.tldr: Beginning in the late thirteenth century as the nascent Ottoman beylik expanded from Anatolia into Byzantine Thrace, this long series of wars steadily stripped the Byzantine Empire of its remaining territory. Byzantium, weakened by civil wars and chronic poverty, could offer only sporadic resistance despite occasional Western crusading aid. The conflict culminated in Mehmed II's capture of Constantinople in 1453, extinguishing the thousand-year-old Roman state. Ottoman forces then absorbed the last Byzantine remnants in the Peloponnese and Trebizond within a decade.

entries.name: Battle of Idistaviso
entries.desc: In 16 CE, Roman legions under Germanicus defeated Germanic tribes led by Arminius near the Weser River. Despite the victory, Rome abandoned further campaigns beyond the Rhine soon after.
entries.tldr: In 16 CE, the Roman general Germanicus led his legions to victory over a Germanic coalition under Arminius, the chieftain who had annihilated three Roman legions at Teutoburg Forest seven years earlier, in a battle near the Weser River recorded by the historian Tacitus. Roman infantry and cavalry inflicted heavy casualties, and the victory was celebrated as partial vengeance. Despite the success, Emperor Tiberius recalled Germanicus and ended further campaigns beyond the Rhine.

entries.name: Deluge
entries.desc: A deluge is a large downpour of rain, often a flood.
entries.tldr: Known in Polish as the Potop, the Deluge was a series of devastating mid-seventeenth-century invasions of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth by Sweden, Russia, Transylvania, and Cossack forces beginning in 1655. Swedish occupation proved especially destructive, sacking cities and looting art and libraries, killing a substantial share of the population. Polish resistance rallied, most famously at the defense of the Jasna Góra monastery, and the invaders were gradually expelled by 1660. The Commonwealth never fully recovered, marking the start of its long decline.

entries.name: Kalmar War
entries.desc: The Kalmar War (1611–1613) was fought between Denmark–Norway and Sweden. Though Denmark–Norway soon gained the upper hand, it was unable to defeat Sweden entirely.
entries.tldr: Christian IV of Denmark-Norway invaded Sweden in 1611 to check Swedish expansion around the Arctic coast and reassert Danish dominance in the Baltic, exploiting the recent accession of the young Gustavus Adolphus to the Swedish throne. Danish forces captured the fortress of Kalmar and the port of Älvsborg, giving the war its name, but proved unable to force a full Swedish surrender. The 1613 Peace of Knäred required Sweden to pay a large ransom to recover Älvsborg but left the underlying Baltic rivalry between the two powers unresolved.

entries.name: First Russo-Turkish War
entries.desc: The Russo-Turkish War of 1568–1570, fought over control of the Astrakhan Khanate, was the first of twelve wars between Russia and the Ottoman Empire. Russia's defense of Astrakhan checked Ottoman expansion northward.
entries.tldr: An Ottoman-Crimean expedition attempted to seize Astrakhan from Muscovy in 1569, aiming to link the Ottoman and Crimean khanates via a canal between the Don and Volga rivers and open a route toward Central Asia. Russian defenders and a harsh winter forced the retreating army to abandon the siege with heavy losses. The failure checked Ottoman ambitions in the region and opened the long, grinding series of Russo-Turkish wars that would recur for the next three centuries.

entries.name: Russo-Polish War
entries.desc: This is a list of armed conflicts between Poland and Russia.
entries.tldr: Also known as the Thirteen Years' War, fought after Ukrainian Cossacks under Bohdan Khmelnytsky placed themselves under Russian protection, drawing Muscovy into war against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth for control of Ukraine. Russian and Cossack forces overran much of Lithuania and Ukraine while Sweden simultaneously invaded Poland from the west during the same crisis. The 1667 Truce of Andrusovo split Ukraine along the Dnieper, giving Russia Smolensk and left-bank Ukraine, including Kyiv. The settlement marked a lasting shift of power from the Commonwealth toward Russia.

entries.name: Battle of Towton
entries.desc: The Battle of Towton took place on 29 March 1461 during the Wars of the Roses, near Towton in North Yorkshire. Yorkist forces decisively defeated Lancastrian supporters of Henry VI, securing the English throne for Edward IV.
entries.tldr: Fought during a blinding snowstorm on Palm Sunday, 29 March 1461, this clash between Yorkist and Lancastrian forces is often considered the largest and bloodiest battle ever fought on English soil, with estimates running well into the tens of thousands of dead. Edward IV's Yorkist army pressed a decisive advantage as the wind-driven snow favored their archers, eventually routing the Lancastrian forces loyal to Henry VI. The overwhelming victory secured Edward's hold on the English throne for the following decade.

entries.name: Battle of Pavia
entries.desc: The Battle of Pavia, fought on the morning of 24 February 1525, was the decisive engagement of the Italian War of 1521–1526 between the Kingdom of France and the Habsburg Empire of Charles V.
entries.tldr: On the morning of 24 February 1525, Habsburg imperial forces under Charles V's commanders trapped and destroyed a French army besieging Pavia, in the decisive engagement of the Italian War of 1521-26. King Francis I fought on personally after his forces collapsed and was captured, reportedly writing to his mother that "all is lost save honour and life." The battle showcased the growing dominance of massed arquebus fire over heavy cavalry charges. Francis's year-long captivity in Madrid forced France into a humiliating treaty, though he repudiated its terms soon after release.

entries.name: War of the League of Cambrai
entries.desc: The War of the League of Cambrai, fought from December 1508 to December 1516, pitted France, the Holy Roman Empire, the Papal States, and Venice against each other as part of the wider Italian Wars.

entries.name: Battle of Marj Ayyun
entries.desc: The Battle of Marj Ayyun was fought near the Litani River in June 1179 between the Kingdom of Jerusalem under Baldwin IV and the Ayyubid armies of Saladin, ending in a decisive Muslim victory.
entries.tldr: Baldwin IV of Jerusalem, the young 'Leper King,' led a raiding force against Saladin's Ayyubid army near the Litani River after a fortress-building dispute reignited fighting between the two states. A premature charge by part of the Crusader force, launched without waiting for the rest of the army, let Saladin's disciplined troops isolate and defeat the Christians in detail. Several prominent nobles were captured, and Baldwin himself narrowly escaped. The defeat weakened Jerusalem's position ahead of further clashes with Saladin leading up to the disaster at Hattin.

entries.name: Fifth Russo-Turkish War
entries.desc: The Russo-Turkish War of 1735–1739 pitted Russia against the Ottoman Empire over the Crimean Tatars and access to the Black Sea, joined in 1737 by the Habsburg monarchy on Russia's side.
entries.tldr: Fought from 1735 to 1739, this war saw Russia, later joined by the Habsburg monarchy, campaign against the Ottoman Empire over control of Crimea and access to the Black Sea. Russian forces under Field Marshal Münnich achieved striking early successes, including the capture of the Crimean capital Bakhchysarai, but disease and logistics forced repeated withdrawals. Austria's poor performance and a separate peace with the Ottomans left Russia to settle on modest terms. The 1739 Treaty of Belgrade returned most conquered territory, though Russia gained rights on the Sea of Azov.

entries.name: Smyrniote crusades
entries.desc: The Smyrniote crusades (1343–1351) were two Crusades sent by Pope Clement VI against the Beylik of Aydin under Umur Bey, targeting the coastal city of Smyrna in Asia Minor.
entries.tldr: Pope Clement VI organized these naval crusades against the Turkish beylik of Aydin, ruled by the emir Umur Bey, whose fleets were raiding Christian shipping and towns in the Aegean. A combined fleet of Venetian, Cypriot, Hospitaller, and papal forces captured the port of Smyrna in 1344, and Umur Bey was killed years later attempting to retake it. The Christian-held enclave around Smyrna's harbor fortress persisted for decades under Hospitaller control. The campaigns were among the last crusading efforts against Anatolian Turkish states before the Ottomans came to dominate the region.

entries.name: Battle of Tolvajärvi
entries.desc: The Battle of Tolvajärvi began on 12 December 1939 and lasted about a week and a half between Finland and the Soviet Union, marking the first large Finnish offensive victory of the Winter War.
entries.tldr: Beginning on 12 December 1939 and lasting about ten days, Finnish forces under Colonel Paavo Talvela encircled and routed the Soviet 139th Division in the freezing forests near Lake Tolvajärvi. It was the first significant Finnish offensive victory of the Winter War, following a series of defensive stands elsewhere on the front. The win gave a considerable boost to Finnish morale and demonstrated the effectiveness of small, mobile units against the Red Army's larger but less adaptable formations.

entries.name: Battle of Kruty
entries.desc: The Battle of Kruty took place on January 29 or 30, 1918, near Kruty railway station northeast of Kyiv, Ukraine, during the Ukrainian War of Independence.
entries.tldr: As Bolshevik forces advanced on Kyiv during the Ukrainian War of Independence, a small, hastily assembled force of cadets and students defended the rail junction at Kruty against a far larger Red Army column. The defenders held for several hours before being overwhelmed and forced to retreat, and captured student volunteers were reportedly executed afterward. The engagement did little to slow the advance on the capital, but the sacrifice of young, poorly trained volunteers made it a lasting symbol of Ukrainian resistance, commemorated annually as a day honoring fallen defenders.

entries.name: Battle of the Boyne
entries.desc: The Battle of the Boyne, fought in 1690 across the River Boyne near Drogheda in Ireland, pitted the deposed King James II against King William III, ending in William's victory.
entries.tldr: Fought on 1 July 1690 (Old Style) across the River Boyne near Drogheda in Ireland, this battle pitted the Catholic King James II, seeking to reclaim the English, Scottish, and Irish thrones, against his son-in-law and rival, the Protestant King William III. William's larger army forced a crossing of the river and outflanked James's positions, driving the Jacobite forces into retreat. James fled to France shortly after, effectively ending his cause in Ireland, and the victory is commemorated by Ulster Protestants in the annual Orange Order marches of 12 July.

entries.name: Battle of Dublin
entries.desc: The Battle of Dublin was a week of street battles in Dublin from 28 June to 5 July 1922, marking the beginning of the Irish Civil War between the Provisional Government and anti-Treaty IRA forces.
entries.tldr: From 28 June to 5 July 1922, Provisional Government forces led by Michael Collins besieged and bombarded the anti-Treaty IRA garrison in Dublin's Four Courts, using artillery borrowed from the British army. A week of street fighting followed, destroying the Public Record Office and killing prominent republican Cathal Brugha in a final defiant charge. The government's victory marked the opening battle of the Irish Civil War, setting the pattern for the guerrilla conflict that followed.

entries.name: Franco-Dutch War
entries.desc: The Franco-Dutch War, 1672 to 1678, was fought primarily between France and the Dutch Republic, with both sides backed at different times by a variety of allies.
entries.tldr: Louis XIV invaded the Dutch Republic in 1672 to punish its opposition to French expansion, triggering a national crisis so severe the Dutch call it the 'Disaster Year.' William of Orange rallied resistance by opening the dikes to flood the countryside and halt the French advance, while Spain, Austria, and Brandenburg joined the Dutch side. The 1678 Peace of Nijmegen gave France territorial gains, including Franche-Comté, but confirmed William's rise as the Republic's leader.

entries.name: Battle of Patay
entries.desc: The Battle of Patay, fought on 18 June 1429 during the Hundred Years' War, was the culmination of the Loire Campaign, where French forces inflicted heavy casualties on the English army.
entries.tldr: On 18 June 1429, French forces guided by Joan of Arc caught a retreating English army by surprise near Patay during the Loire Campaign of the Hundred Years' War. French cavalry under commanders such as La Hire and the Duke of Alençon overran the English longbowmen before they could form their usual defensive stakes, inflicting a rout that killed or captured most of the English force. The victory reversed the momentum built by earlier English successes like Agincourt and cleared the way for Charles VII's coronation at Reims weeks later.

entries.name: Treaty of 1818
entries.desc: The Treaty of 1818, an international treaty signed between the United States and the United Kingdom, resolved standing boundary and fisheries disputes and allowed joint occupation of Oregon Country.
entries.tldr: Signed in 1818 between the United States and the United Kingdom, this treaty resolved several outstanding disputes left from the War of 1812 and earlier agreements. It fixed the border along the 49th parallel from Minnesota to the Rockies, granted American fishermen rights in parts of British North American waters, and set up joint occupation of the disputed Oregon Country. That joint occupation lasted until the two countries divided the territory permanently in 1846. The treaty is remembered as an early example of peaceful boundary settlement between the two nations.

entries.name: Battle of Culloden
entries.desc: The Battle of Culloden took place on 16 April 1746 near Inverness in the Scottish Highlands, where a Jacobite army under Charles Edward Stuart was decisively defeated, ending the 1745 rising.
entries.tldr: On 16 April 1746, government forces under the Duke of Cumberland crushed the Jacobite army of Charles Edward Stuart, 'Bonnie Prince Charlie,' on Drummossie Moor near Inverness in under an hour. Exhausted, outnumbered Highlanders charged into artillery and disciplined musket volleys, and government bayonet drill broke the clan regiments. It was the last pitched battle fought on British soil and ended the Jacobite cause. The brutal aftermath, which earned Cumberland the nickname 'Butcher,' led to laws suppressing Highland dress and clan authority.

entries.name: Indo-Pakistani War of 1947–1948
entries.desc: The India–Pakistan war of 1947–1948 was fought between India and Pakistan over the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, the first of several wars between the two newly independent nations.
entries.tldr: Days after independence in 1947, the Muslim-majority princely state of Jammu and Kashmir was invaded by Pashtun tribal militias backed by Pakistan, prompting its Hindu maharaja to accede to India in exchange for military aid. Indian troops airlifted into Srinagar halted the advance, and fighting continued along a shifting front for over a year. A United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 1949 established the Line of Control dividing Kashmir, a division that remains the source of ongoing India-Pakistan tension.

entries.name: Battle of Toulouse
entries.desc: The Battle of Toulouse (721) was fought between the Duchy of Aquitaine and the Umayyad Caliphate near Toulouse, France, resulting in an Aquitanian victory that halted the Umayyad advance.
entries.tldr: In 721, Duke Odo of Aquitaine surprised and routed the besieging army of the Umayyad governor As-Samh ibn Malik outside the walls of Toulouse, killing As-Samh in the fighting. The Aquitanian victory halted the first major Umayyad thrust into Francia and bought roughly a decade before a later Muslim invasion force would be turned back again at Tours in 732. It remains a lesser-known but strategically important check on early Islamic expansion into western Europe.

entries.name: French Revolution
entries.desc: The French Revolution was a period of political and societal change in France beginning with the Estates General of 1789 and ending with the Coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799, reshaping modern political thought.
entries.tldr: Financial collapse and grievances over aristocratic privilege forced Louis XVI to summon the Estates-General in 1789, which the Third Estate transformed into a National Assembly demanding a constitution. The fall of the Bastille, the abolition of feudal privileges, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man followed within months, but escalating radicalism brought the monarchy's execution, the Terror under Robespierre, and years of war. Napoleon's 1799 coup ended the revolutionary decade while keeping many of its reforms.

entries.name: Battle of the Caucasus
entries.desc: The Battle of the Caucasus was a series of Axis and Soviet operations in the Caucasus during the Eastern Front of World War II, following the German capture of Rostov-on-Don in July 1942.
entries.tldr: Following Germany's summer 1942 drive toward the Caucasus oilfields, this months-long campaign saw German Army Group A push deep into the mountainous region before being halted at Malgobek and the foothills of the main Caucasus range in late 1942. As the German position at Stalingrad collapsed to the north, threatening to cut off the overextended Caucasus force, German forces withdrew in stages during early 1943 under Soviet pressure, giving up most of the territory they had seized. The failed campaign cost Germany enormous resources without securing the oil supplies it desperately needed.

entries.name: Battle of Lugdunum
entries.desc: The Battle of Lugdunum, fought on 19 February 197 at Lugdunum (Lyon), pitted Roman emperor Septimius Severus against usurper Clodius Albinus, establishing Severus as sole emperor.
entries.tldr: Following the assassination of Emperor Commodus and the chaotic Year of the Five Emperors, Septimius Severus and the Britain-based usurper Clodius Albinus, former allies, turned on each other for sole control of Rome. Their armies, among the largest ever fielded in a Roman civil war, met at Lugdunum, modern Lyon, in a battle so close-fought that Severus was nearly killed after being thrown from his horse. His forces eventually broke Albinus's lines, and Albinus took his own life rather than be captured. The victory left Severus unchallenged as emperor and founder of the Severan dynasty.

entries.name: Battle of Trenton
entries.desc: The Battle of Trenton was a pivotal American Revolutionary War battle on 26 December 1776 in Trenton, New Jersey, where Washington's Continental Army defeated Hessian forces after crossing the Delaware.
entries.tldr: In the early hours of 26 December 1776, George Washington's Continental Army, having crossed the ice-choked Delaware River the previous night, launched a surprise attack on the Hessian garrison holding Trenton, New Jersey. Caught off guard after Christmas celebrations, the Hessians were quickly overwhelmed, and nearly 900 were captured for minimal American losses. Coming after a string of demoralizing defeats, the victory revived flagging revolutionary morale and helped Washington reenlist troops whose terms were about to expire.

entries.name: Storming of the Bastille
entries.desc: Parisian revolutionaries stormed the Bastille fortress-prison on 14 July 1789, a flashpoint that ignited the French Revolution.
entries.tldr: On 14 July 1789, a crowd of Parisians seeking arms and gunpowder attacked the Bastille, a royal fortress-prison that had come to symbolize the arbitrary power of the monarchy. After a chaotic battle the garrison surrendered, and its governor was killed by the crowd despite promises of safe conduct. Though the prison held only a handful of inmates at the time, the fall of the Bastille became the defining symbolic moment igniting the French Revolution. The date is still celebrated annually in France as Bastille Day, the national holiday.

entries.name: Second Northern War
entries.desc: Sweden invaded and nearly conquered the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, drawing in Russia, Brandenburg-Prussia, and Denmark–Norway.
entries.tldr: Began when Sweden's King Charles X Gustav invaded the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth during a period Poles call "the Deluge," rapidly overrunning most of the country and forcing the Polish king to flee abroad. Sweden's early success drew in Russia, Brandenburg, Denmark, and the Habsburgs, each pursuing its own rival interests as the war widened. Poland eventually recovered with allied help, and the 1660 Treaty of Oliva confirmed Sweden's other possessions while ending its claim to the Polish throne. The war devastated Poland-Lithuania and marked the peak of Sweden's great-power status.

entries.name: Battle of Cambrai
entries.desc: A British WWI offensive near Cambrai, France, featured the first large-scale, successful use of tanks in combined-arms warfare.
entries.tldr: Launched on 20 November 1917 near Cambrai, France, the British offensive is best remembered for the first large-scale use of tanks in a coordinated combined-arms assault, deployed alongside infantry and artillery without the usual lengthy bombardment that warned defenders. The surprise attack broke deep into German lines on the first day, prompting church bells to ring back in Britain, but mechanical breakdowns and stiffening resistance stalled the advance, and a German counterattack recovered most of the lost ground. Cambrai still proved the tank's potential for decades of warfare to come.

entries.name: Quasi-War
entries.desc: An undeclared naval conflict between the United States and Revolutionary France, fought mainly in Caribbean and Atlantic coastal waters.
entries.tldr: An undeclared naval conflict after Revolutionary France, angered by American neutrality and unpaid debts, began seizing US merchant ships and demanded bribes just to negotiate, the so-called XYZ Affair. Congress authorized reprisals, and the newly created US Navy fought French privateers and warships across the Caribbean and Atlantic without a formal declaration of war. The 1800 Convention of Mortefontaine ended the fighting and voided the old Franco-American alliance from the Revolutionary War era. It was the young republic's first armed conflict as an independent nation.

entries.name: Battle of the Iron Bridge
entries.desc: Rashidun Muslim forces defeated the Byzantine army near a fortified bridge over the Orontes River, securing the conquest of Syria.
entries.tldr: Fought in 637 near Antioch, this battle saw a Rashidun Muslim army defeat a Byzantine force defending a fortified crossing over the Orontes River known for its iron-reinforced gate, hence the name. The Muslim victory removed one of the last major Byzantine field forces standing between the invaders and the great city of Antioch, which surrendered shortly afterward. The battle consolidated the Rashidun conquest of Syria that had begun with the earlier victory at Yarmouk, extending Muslim control over the region's major cities and effectively ending centuries of Byzantine rule in northern Syria.

entries.name: Greco-Turkish War of 1897
entries.desc: Greece and the Ottoman Empire fought over Crete; despite an Ottoman battlefield win, an autonomous Cretan state emerged from the settlement.
entries.tldr: Greek nationalists and Cretan insurgents pushed Athens into war with the Ottoman Empire in 1897 over the future of Crete, where a rebellion against Ottoman rule had been simmering for years. Ottoman forces under German-trained commanders defeated the poorly prepared Greek army in Thessaly within weeks. Despite the battlefield outcome, the Great Powers intervened diplomatically, and the postwar settlement created an autonomous Cretan State under nominal Ottoman sovereignty, a step toward the island's eventual union with Greece.

entries.name: Second Barons' War
entries.desc: English barons led by Simon de Montfort rebelled against King Henry III to force him to rule through a council of nobles.
entries.tldr: Fought when a faction of English barons led by Simon de Montfort, angered by King Henry III's disregard for reforms agreed in the Provisions of Oxford, rose in rebellion. Montfort's forces captured Henry and his son Edward at the Battle of Lewes in 1264, and Montfort then summoned a parliament that for the first time included elected town representatives. Prince Edward escaped captivity and defeated and killed Montfort at the Battle of Evesham in 1265. Though the rebellion ultimately failed, Montfort's parliament is remembered as a step toward representative government.

entries.name: Battle of Achelous
entries.desc: Bulgarian forces under Tsar Simeon I crushed a Byzantine army near the Achelous river, a major Bulgarian victory over Byzantium.
entries.tldr: In 917, Bulgarian forces under Tsar Simeon I ambushed and crushed a Byzantine army near the Achelous river as it marched to confront the Bulgarians in the Balkans. The Byzantine commander Leo Phokas fled the field, and the rout was one of the most devastating Byzantine defeats of the medieval period, with heavy losses among veteran troops. The victory let Simeon press deep into Byzantine territory and strengthened his claim to the title of Emperor of the Bulgarians, marking the peak of Bulgarian power.

entries.name: Battle of Galicia
entries.desc: Russian forces routed the Austro-Hungarian army in Galicia during the opening weeks of World War I, capturing Lemberg.
entries.tldr: Fought across a broad front in Austrian Galicia during August and September 1914, this series of engagements pitted the Russian Imperial Army against Austria-Hungary's forces in one of the largest campaigns of the war's opening months. Poor Austro-Hungarian coordination let Russian armies encircle and rout much of the defending force, capturing the regional capital Lemberg, present-day Lviv, and inflicting huge casualties. The defeat crippled Austria-Hungary's army so severely it never fully recovered its offensive capability.

entries.name: Second Russo-Turkish War
entries.desc: Russia and the Ottoman Empire fought over control of right-bank Ukraine amid Turkish expansion in the late 17th century.
entries.tldr: Fought over control of right-bank, or western, Ukraine, as Russia intervened to support a Cossack hetman against Ottoman and Crimean Tatar forces that had recently gained influence there. Ottoman forces besieged the Cossack fortress of Chyhyryn, eventually capturing it after a long and costly campaign. The 1681 Treaty of Bakhchisarai established a twenty-year truce, with the Dnieper River fixed as a rough boundary between Russian and Ottoman spheres. It was one of several 17th-century wars fought over the contested Ukrainian borderlands.

entries.name: First Battle of the Masurian Lakes
entries.desc: German forces drove Russian troops out of East Prussia days after the German victory at Tannenberg.
entries.tldr: In September 1914, weeks after their crushing victory at Tannenberg, German forces under Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Ludendorff struck the Russian First Army in East Prussia's lake district. Exploiting superior rail mobility and intelligence from intercepted Russian radio signals, the Germans forced a fighting retreat that drove Russian troops entirely out of German territory. Russian casualties were heavy, though the army escaped the encirclement that had doomed the Second Army at Tannenberg. The victory cemented the duo's reputation as Germany's premier commanders in the east.

entries.name: Battle of Mühlberg
entries.desc: Holy Roman Emperor Charles V decisively defeated the Protestant Schmalkaldic League near Mühlberg, Saxony.
entries.tldr: On 24 April 1547, Holy Roman Emperor Charles V's imperial army surprised and crushed the forces of the Protestant Schmalkaldic League near Mühlberg in Saxony, capturing the League's leader, Elector John Frederick I of Saxony. The victory temporarily broke Protestant political power within the empire and let Charles impose the short-lived Augsburg Interim settlement. Titian's equestrian portrait of Charles V, painted soon after, commemorated the triumph. Protestant resistance revived within years, and the conflict was not resolved until the Peace of Augsburg in 1555.

entries.name: Battle of the Piave River
entries.desc: The Italian Army decisively defeated Austria-Hungary along the Piave River, a turning point on the Italian Front in World War I.
entries.tldr: Fought in June 1918, this Austro-Hungarian offensive across the Piave River aimed to knock Italy out of the war before American reinforcements could bolster Allied lines. Italian defenders, reinforced by British and French divisions, held their positions and launched counterattacks, aided by flooding that isolated and trapped many Austro-Hungarian units on the Italian-held bank. The decisive Italian victory, sometimes called the 'Battle of the Solstice,' broke the strained Austro-Hungarian army's offensive capacity and set the stage for its collapse at Vittorio Veneto that year.

entries.name: Battle of Vittorio Veneto
entries.desc: A decisive Italian offensive shattered the Austro-Hungarian army, effectively ending fighting on the Italian Front.
entries.tldr: Fought from late October to early November 1918, this Italian-led offensive shattered the already war-weary Austro-Hungarian army along the Piave and into the Veneto region. Coordinated attacks by Italian, British, French, and American units broke Austro-Hungarian resistance and triggered mass surrenders and desertions as the multiethnic empire began to disintegrate. The collapse forced Austria-Hungary to sign an armistice on 3 November 1918, ending fighting on the Italian Front just days before the wider Armistice on the Western Front.

entries.name: Battle of Zorndorf
entries.desc: Prussian forces under Frederick the Great fought Russian troops to a bloody, inconclusive standstill during the Seven Years' War.
entries.tldr: Fought on 25 August 1758 during the Seven Years' War, Prussian forces under Frederick the Great attacked a Russian army near the village of Zorndorf in a battle notable for its brutality and confusion, with both sides' cavalry and infantry becoming entangled in chaotic close-quarters fighting. Neither side achieved a breakthrough, and both suffered enormous casualties relative to army size, roughly a third of each force killed or wounded. Both commanders claimed victory, but it is generally regarded as a bloody standstill.

entries.name: Battle of Mollwitz
entries.desc: Frederick the Great's Prussian army won its first battle, against Austria, in the opening clash of the First Silesian War.
entries.tldr: Fought on 10 April 1741 near the Silesian village of Mollwitz, this was the first battle of Frederick the Great's reign, opening the First Silesian War against Austria. Prussian infantry discipline held the field even after Frederick himself fled early, fearing the battle lost, when Austrian cavalry routed his cavalry wing. The victory let Prussia seize and hold Silesia, a resource-rich province it kept for two centuries. It also taught Frederick hard lessons about cavalry that reshaped his later campaigns.

entries.name: Mexican-American War
entries.desc: The United States invaded Mexico following the annexation of Texas, resulting in major territorial expansion of the US Southwest.
entries.tldr: After the United States annexed Texas in 1845, a border dispute with Mexico over whether the boundary lay at the Nueces River or the Rio Grande escalated into open war the following year. American forces under Winfield Scott captured Mexico City itself in 1847, forcing Mexico's surrender. The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ceded roughly half of Mexico's territory to the US, including present-day California, Nevada, Utah, and much of Arizona and New Mexico, for $15 million, reopening the fight over slavery in new states.
